tools.name: AdapterRemoval
tools.description: Trims adapter sequences and low-quality bases from reads and merges overlapping read pairs.

output.name: Trimming and collapsing statistics
output.description: Read pairs in, mates merged, reads discarded and sequences retained, from an AdapterRemoval .settings report. The counts balance exactly, which is what lets a read-fate flow be drawn from them without apportioning anything. One row per report, so a pipeline that trims per lane gets one row per lane.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: collapse_vs_length
  title: Collapse rate against retained length
  description: |-
    Each point is one AdapterRemoval report, usually a lane or a library: the mean length of its retained sequences against the share of read pairs merged into a single sequence, sized by the sequences retained. It answers whether the insert sizes of a library are short enough for mates to overlap.
    How to read: short fragments make the mates overlap, so a high collapse rate goes with a short retained length. That is the expected shape of an ancient or degraded DNA library. A low collapse rate with long retained sequences means the inserts are longer than the reads and the mates cannot merge.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median collapse rate of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of AdapterRemoval.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: Average retained length (bp)
    y_title: Share of pairs collapsed
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: average_retained_length
    y: collapse_rate
    label: sample
    color: sample
    size: retained_reads

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Sequences retained per report
  description: |-
    Each bar is one AdapterRemoval report: the number of sequences it wrote out, which is the input of the mapper. It answers how much data each report contributes after trimming and collapsing.
    How to read: reports of one library type should be of similar size. A very short bar is a report that lost most of its reads to discarding, so check its discard rate before pooling it.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median number of sequences retained per report of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of AdapterRemoval.
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: retained_reads
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Report
      retained_reads: Sequences retained
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: retained_reads

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Read pairs processed
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of read pairs given to AdapterRemoval across the reports, and the strip steps down to the pairs whose mates overlapped and the pairs merged into one sequence. It answers how much of the input survives each step.
    How to read: a short step from overlapping to collapsed means most overlapping pairs were merged. A large drop from input to overlapping means long inserts, which is normal for modern DNA and unusual for ancient DNA.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  column: total_read_pairs
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: attrition
  attrition_cols:
  - well_aligned_read_pairs
  - collapsed_pairs
  caption: pairs, from input to overlapping to collapsed

  aggregation: median
  aggregations:

- component: card
  title: Retained length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across reports of the mean length of a retained sequence, in base pairs, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the sequences handed to the mapper are.
    How to read: short sequences map ambiguously and long ones map better. A report well below its peers may have been over-trimmed or be a degraded library.
  column: average_retained_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Discard rate
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across reports of the share of reads dropped on quality or length, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much data trimming throws away.
    How to read: a low share means the library trims cleanly. A report far above its peers has many reads too short or too poor to keep, which points to adapter dimers or degraded input.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  column: discard_rate
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

renders._yaml:
- component: table
  title: Trimming and collapsing statistics
  description: |-
    One row is one AdapterRemoval report, with its read counts at each step, retained length, collapse rate and discard rate. It gives the exact values behind the tiles and answers which reports lose or merge the most reads.
    How to read: sort by discard rate to find the reports that lose the most reads, then by collapse rate to see how many pairs were merged. The counts balance, so pairs in, mates merged and reads discarded add up to the sequences retained. It complements the collapse rate and discard rate tiles.

  id: genes_vs_exons
  title: Genes against exons per transcript
  description: |-
    Each point is an annotation and a transcript type, with the number of genes on the horizontal axis (log scale) and the exons per transcript on the vertical axis, sized by mean gene length and coloured by transcript type. It answers how complete the gene models of each annotation look.
    How to read: a fragmented annotation shows many short, few-exon models, so it sits low on the vertical axis. Points of one transcript type that sit apart from the others are the annotation to inspect first. AGAT publishes no cut-off for these values.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median exons per transcript of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of AGAT.

  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Genes
    y_title: Exons per transcript
    log_x: true
    top_n_labels: 6
    legend_pos: bottom
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
  roles:

    y: exons_per_transcript
    label: genome
    color: feature_type
    size: mean_gene_length

The longest-isoform view keeps one transcript per gene, so it is the one to compare annotations that kept different numbers of isoforms.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  version: 1.1.0
  title: AGAT metrics per annotation
  description: |-
    Each panel is one sp_statistics metric, and each bar in it the value for one annotation in the longest-isoform view, which keeps one transcript per gene. It answers how annotations compare metric by metric.
    How to read: every panel has its own value axis, so compare bars within a panel, not across panels. Without a metric filter the first nine metrics in AGAT's order are shown; pick metrics and a feature type with the filters to see others.
    Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because each panel holds a different quantity and a cohort median of a handful of annotations says little.
    Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  code: |-
    # one isoform view, so a bar is one number: the longest-isoform view when present
    view = "longest" if (df["isoforms"] == "longest").any() else "all"
    d = df.filter(pl.col("isoforms") == view).drop_nulls(["value"])
    # the first metrics in AGAT's order, unless the metric filter picked others
    keep = d.sort("metric_order")["metric"].unique(maintain_order=True).head(9).to_list()
    d = d.filter(pl.col("metric").is_in(keep)).sort(["metric_order", "genome"])
    fig = px.bar(
        d.to_pandas(),
        x="genome",
        y="value",
        color="genome",
        facet_col="metric",
        facet_col_wrap=3,
        facet_row_spacing=0.12,
        category_orders={"metric": keep},
        labels={"genome": "Annotation", "value": "Value", "metric": "Metric"},
    )
    fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=", 1)[-1]))
    fig.update_yaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
    fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, title_text="")
    fig.update_layout(
        legend_title_text=f"Annotation ({view} isoforms)",
        margin={"t": 32, "l": 48, "r": 16, "b": 24},
    )

_render.title: AGAT metrics per annotation
_render.description:
Each panel is one sp_statistics metric, and each bar in it the value for one annotation in the longest-isoform view, which keeps one transcript per gene. It answers how annotations compare metric by metric.
How to read: every panel has its own value axis, so compare bars within a panel, not across panels. Without a metric filter the first nine metrics in AGAT's order are shown; pick metrics and a feature type with the filters to see others.
Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because each panel holds a different quantity and a cohort median of a handful of annotations says little.
Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
_render.code:
# one isoform view, so a bar is one number: the longest-isoform view when present
view = "longest" if (df["isoforms"] == "longest").any() else "all"
d = df.filter(pl.col("isoforms") == view).drop_nulls(["value"])
# the first metrics in AGAT's order, unless the metric filter picked others
keep = d.sort("metric_order")["metric"].unique(maintain_order=True).head(9).to_list()
d = d.filter(pl.col("metric").is_in(keep)).sort(["metric_order", "genome"])
fig = px.bar(
    d.to_pandas(),
    x="genome",
    y="value",
    color="genome",
    facet_col="metric",
    facet_col_wrap=3,
    facet_row_spacing=0.12,
    category_orders={"metric": keep},
    labels={"genome": "Annotation", "value": "Value", "metric": "Metric"},
)
fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=", 1)[-1]))
fig.update_yaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, title_text="")
fig.update_layout(
    legend_title_text=f"Annotation ({view} isoforms)",
    margin={"t": 32, "l": 48, "r": 16, "b": 24},
)

tools.name: anota2seq
tools.description: Generally applicable transcriptome-wide analysis of translational efficiency using anota2seq.

output.name: Translational regulation mode per gene
output.description: One row per contrast and gene with the four anota2seq analyses side by side and one regulatory mode: translation, buffering, mRNA abundance or not regulated, assigned with anota2seq's default selection thresholds.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fold_change_plane
  title: Ribosome-bound against total mRNA change
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene in one contrast: its change in total mRNA on the horizontal axis and in ribosome-bound mRNA on the vertical axis, coloured by regulatory mode. It answers whether a gene changes by transcript level, by translation or is buffered.
    How to read: genes riding the diagonal change with their mRNA level (mRNA abundance). Genes above or below it change translation beyond their mRNA, and buffered genes lie flat along the horizontal axis, where mRNA moves but ribosome-bound mRNA does not. Open the volcano for the statistics of the translation calls.
    Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where ribosome-bound and total mRNA change equally, so translational efficiency is unchanged. It is a geometric reference. The modes follow the anota2seq default selection, an adjusted p-value below 0.15 and, for translation and buffering, a change of at least log2(1.2).
    Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30926999/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Total mRNA log2 fold change
    y_title: Ribosome-bound mRNA log2 fold change
    reference_line: diagonal
    reference_label: no change in translational efficiency

_render.title: Ribosome-bound against total mRNA change
_render.description:
Each point is a gene in one contrast: its change in total mRNA on the horizontal axis and in ribosome-bound mRNA on the vertical axis, coloured by regulatory mode. It answers whether a gene changes by transcript level, by translation or is buffered.
How to read: genes riding the diagonal change with their mRNA level (mRNA abundance). Genes above or below it change translation beyond their mRNA, and buffered genes lie flat along the horizontal axis, where mRNA moves but ribosome-bound mRNA does not. Open the volcano for the statistics of the translation calls.
Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where ribosome-bound and total mRNA change equally, so translational efficiency is unchanged. It is a geometric reference. The modes follow the anota2seq default selection, an adjusted p-value below 0.15 and, for translation and buffering, a change of at least log2(1.2).
Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30926999/

output.name: Arriba breakpoint links
output.description: The same Arriba calls as the fusion table, read as pairs of genomic loci: the two "chr:pos" breakpoints are split into bindable chromosome and position columns, the read evidence is summed into one link weight, and the event class and confidence come through unchanged. This is the row shape a chord diagram binds, so a run's fusions can be read as a partner map across the genome instead of as a list of names.

  roles:
    chrom_a: chrom_a
    pos_a: pos_a

output.name: Arriba fusion calls
output.description: Fusion calls Arriba retained, one row per call. The recipe labels each fusion from its two partner genes, sums the split reads, discordant mates and local coverage into one evidence block, derives a log-scaled support and the fraction of local reads that support the call, and splits the contig out of each breakpoint so the partners can be read as a chromosome flow.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: evidence_dot_plot
  title: Evidence for each fusion
  description: |-
    Each dot is a fusion in one confidence class: its colour is the read support on a log scale and its size is the share of local reads that support it. It answers which calls rest on strong evidence and how confident Arriba is in them.
    How to read: a large, dark dot in the high-confidence column is a well supported call. A call with few supporting reads in the low-confidence column is weak and Arriba's authors advise treating such calls with skepticism unless other evidence corroborates them. Check the table for the breakpoints and domains of the calls you keep.
    Lines and annotations: the colour scale is log10 of supporting reads plus 1, a transform of this catalog's recipe, where supporting reads are the split reads plus the discordant mates Arriba reports. The confidence classes low, medium and high are assigned by Arriba.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: confidence
    gene: fusion
    mean_expression: log_support
    frac_expressing: support_fraction

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: partner_chrom_sankey
  title: Partner chromosomes
  description: |-
    Each flow joins the chromosome of the 5' partner on the left to the chromosome of the 3' partner on the right, with its width the number of fusions. It answers whether the fusions are within one chromosome or between chromosomes.
    How to read: a flow that returns to the same chromosome is a local rearrangement such as a deletion, an inversion or a duplication. A flow to another chromosome is a translocation. Many flows from one chromosome may point to a hot region or to a recurrent artefact worth checking.
  kind: sankey
  config:
    value_label: Fusions
  roles:
    steps:
    - chrom_5p
    - chrom_3p

tools.name: ASCAT
tools.description: Derives allele-specific copy number profiles of tumour cells, accounting for normal cell admixture and tumour aneuploidy.

output.name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
output.description: ASCAT's called segments, turned into the canonical copy-number profile contract. Per the ASCAT documentation the .cnvs.txt file carries sample, chr, startpos, endpos, nMajor and nMinor, one row per segment. The major and minor allele counts become an absolute copy number, a log2 ratio against a diploid baseline and the segment's expected B-allele frequency, so copy-neutral LOH reads as a BAF split even though the total copy number never moves.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ascat_profile
  title: Allele-specific copy-number profile
  description: |-
    Each line is a called copy-number segment: its total copy number as a log2 ratio against two copies on the upper panel, and its expected B-allele frequency on the lower one. It answers where the tumour genome gains, loses or keeps its copy number, and where one allele is lost.
    How to read: segments above the upper dotted line are gains and those below the lower one are losses. A BAF far from 0.5 at an unchanged copy number is copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, which the total copy number alone never shows. Zoom on a chromosome to read the allele-specific counts in the label.
    Lines and annotations: the dotted lines at log2 0.322 and -0.415 are log2(2.5/2) and log2(1.5/2), the total copy numbers of 2.5 and 1.5 where a rounded call leaves two. They are an arithmetic reference defined by this catalog, not an ASCAT cut-off. The dotted line at BAF 0.5 is the balanced state.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20837533/
  kind: cnv_profile
  config:
    gain_threshold: 0.322
    loss_threshold: -0.415
  roles:
    sample: sample
    chrom: chrom
    start: start
    end: end
    log2: log2
    baf: baf
    copy_number: copy_number
    segment: segment
    label: label

How to read: segments above the upper dotted line are gains and those below the lower one are losses. A BAF far from 0.5 at an unchanged copy number is copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, which the total copy number alone never shows. Lines and annotations: the dotted lines at log2 0.322 and -0.415 are log2(2.5/2) and log2(1.5/2), the total copy numbers of 2.5 and 1.5 where a rounded call leaves two. They are an arithmetic reference defined by this catalog, not an ASCAT cut-off. The dotted line at BAF 0.5 is the balanced state.

- component: card

  title: Copy number spread
  description: |-

output.name: Tumour purity and ploidy
output.description: ASCAT's fit for each tumour sample. Per the ASCAT documentation the .purityploidy.txt file carries AberrantCellFraction and Ploidy, one data row per sample. Purity is the share of sequenced cells carrying the tumour genome, ploidy the average copy number of that genome, and every log2 ratio on the copy-number profile is read against them: a low-purity sample flattens the whole track.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: ascat_purity_card
  title: Tumour purity
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median share of sequenced cells that carry the tumour genome (ASCAT's aberrant cell fraction), and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how clean the tumour content is.
    How to read: values near one mean a nearly pure tumour sample. Low purity flattens the copy-number profile and makes calls less certain, so treat the profiles of the lowest samples with care.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20837533/
  column: purity
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: ascat_ploidy_card
  title: Tumour ploidy
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median average copy number of the tumour genome, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers whether the tumours are near diploid or aneuploid.
    How to read: a value near two means a near-diploid genome and values well above it point to whole-genome duplication. A fit that jumps to an odd ploidy with low purity can be wrong, so check the profile of that sample.

tools.name: assembly-scan
tools.description: Assembly summary statistics: contig count and length distribution, N50 and L50, base composition and the contigs past 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb and 1 Mb.

output.name: Assembly statistics
output.description: One row per assembly from assembly-scan's JSON report: contig count, total, median, maximum and N50 contig length, L50, GC and N content, and how many contigs pass 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb and 1 Mb. Contiguity bounds how much of a genome can align in long collinear blocks, so these numbers are read next to the alignment coverage.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: contiguity_scatter
  title: Contiguity of each assembly
  description: |-
    Each point is an assembly: its number of sequences on the horizontal axis and its N50 on the vertical axis, sized by its total length and coloured by the share of N bases. It answers which assemblies are chromosome-level and which are fragmented drafts.
    How to read: the upper left corner holds few, long sequences, the signature of a chromosome-level assembly. Points at the lower right are fragmented, and long alignments between genomes cannot span their breaks. A dark point carries many N bases, which are gaps that cannot align.
    Note: N50 is the sequence length at which half of the assembly is reached, longest first, and the assembly-scan README states no quality cut-off, so none is drawn.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median N50 of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut- off of assembly-scan.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N50,_L50,_and_related_statistics
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    color_col: n_pct
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    x_title: Sequences in the assembly
    y_title: N50 (bp)
    top_n_labels: 8
    reference_line: horizontal

output.name: Fragment length distribution
output.description: The fragment-length histogram of every library in long form. A good ATAC library shows a peak of short fragments followed by a decaying nucleosome ladder; a flat or ladder-free profile has lost that pattern. Each length is classed on the two windows ataqv counts (50 to 100 bp and 150 to 200 bp, ataqv src/cpp/Metrics.cpp), every other length is left outside them.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fragment_ladder
  title: Fragment length ladder
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: the share of reads at each fragment length. It answers whether the library shows the open-chromatin peak and the nucleosome ladder expected of ATAC-seq.
    How to read: a good library has a peak of short fragments followed by a decaying ladder with a bump near one nucleosome. A flat curve with no ladder points to over-tagmentation or damaged chromatin. Compare libraries and open the quality table for the ratio between the two windows.
    Lines and annotations: the shaded bands are the two windows ataqv counts, 50 to 100 bp for short fragments and 150 to 200 bp for mononucleosomal ones, taken from the ataqv source code. The ENCODE ATAC-seq standards also require a nucleosome-free region and a mononucleosome peak.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp and https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Fragment length (bp)
    y_title: Share of all reads
    log_y: true
    shaded_bands:
    - - 50
      - 100
      - Short fragments (50-100 bp)
    - - 150
      - 200
      - Mononucleosomal (150-200 bp)
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: fragment_length
    y: fraction_of_all_reads

_render.title: Fragment length ladder
_render.description:
Each line is a library: the share of reads at each fragment length. It answers whether the library shows the open-chromatin peak and the nucleosome ladder expected of ATAC-seq.
How to read: a good library has a peak of short fragments followed by a decaying ladder with a bump near one nucleosome. A flat curve with no ladder points to over-tagmentation or damaged chromatin. Compare libraries and open the quality table for the ratio between the two windows.
Lines and annotations: the shaded bands are the two windows ataqv counts, 50 to 100 bp for short fragments and 150 to 200 bp for mononucleosomal ones, taken from the ataqv source code. The ENCODE ATAC-seq standards also require a nucleosome-free region and a mononucleosome peak.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp and https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/

output.name: ATAC quality metrics
output.description: One row per ATAC library: TSS enrichment, the share of high-quality autosomal alignments that fall inside peaks, mitochondrial and duplicate fractions, and the peak statistics ataqv computed. These are the numbers an ATAC library is accepted or rejected on, and MultiQC has no module that reports them.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  title: TSS enrichment against reads in peaks
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: its TSS enrichment on the horizontal axis and the percentage of its high-quality autosomal alignments that fall inside peaks on the vertical axis, with the marker sized by the number of peaks. It answers whether a library has both signal and specificity.
    How to read: good libraries sit to the right and above the line. A library high on one axis and low on the other has a good enrichment but poor specificity, or the reverse, and the two cards below give the cut-offs for each.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is 30 percent, the ENCODE ATAC-seq standard of 0.3 for the fraction of reads in peaks (0.2 is acceptable). ataqv computes the percentage on high-quality autosomal alignments, so the two are close but not identical.
    Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: TSS enrichment
    y_title: High-quality alignments in peaks (%)
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 30
    reference_label: ENCODE fraction of reads in peaks, 0.3
  roles:
    x: tss_enrichment
    y: hqaa_overlapping_peaks_percent
    color: sample
    size: total_peaks

renders._yaml:

  title: TSS enrichment
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average TSS enrichment, the signal at transcription start sites over the flanks of the same window. It answers whether the libraries show the open chromatin expected of good ATAC-seq.

  caption: average enrichment, with the lowest and highest library

output.name: TSS coverage profile
output.description: Aggregate read coverage in a window centred on every transcription start site, recentred so 0 is the TSS. The height of the central spike over the flanks is the TSS enrichment score; the shape says whether that enrichment is a sharp signal or a broad shoulder.

    y: coverage

  description: |-

    How to read: boxes of similar height and position mean comparable libraries. A library whose box sits well above or below its replicates has a composition or quality difference to check before comparing conditions.

  dict_kwargs:

    y: log_cpm
    color: condition
    labels:

      condition: Condition
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: log_cpm

renders._yaml:

  id: correlation_heatmap
  title: Sample correlation
  description: |-
    Each cell is the Spearman correlation between two samples over their log2(CPM + 1) gene expression, with the condition as a row annotation and rows and columns clustered. It answers which samples resemble each other.

  kind: complex_heatmap
  roles:
    index: sample_id
    row_annotation_cols:
    - condition

tools.name: BCFtools
tools.description: Utilities for variant calling and for manipulating VCF and BCF files.

output.name: Variant distributions per caller
output.description: The distribution blocks of `bcftools stats`, melted into one long frame so a single `section` filter drives every tile instead of five separate collections. `section` is one of `indel_length` (insertion and deletion length, deletions negative), `substitution` (the A to C, A to G, ... substitution spectrum), `depth` (read depth), `allele_frequency` (non-reference allele frequency) and `singleton_stats` (variants seen in exactly one allele copy). The key column differs per section, which is the price of melting: a numeric distribution puts its x value in `bin` and leaves `label` null, a categorical one puts its x value in `label` and leaves `bin` null, and `depth` fills both because bcftools writes its open-ended top bucket under a non-numeric bin name. `count` is always a count of variant records, but of a different kind per section (sites for indel length and depth, SNPs for allele frequency, substitutions or singletons for the two categorical ones), so summing it within a filtered section is meaningful and summing it across sections is not. Sample and caller are read off the report's own `ID` line, so any layout a pipeline publishes the reports under works. The quality block is left out: it is most of the rows of a real callset, and the VCFtools Ts/Tv-by-quality sweep answers its question.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Variant distributions per caller
  description: |-
    Each panel is one bcftools distribution (indel length, substitution, read depth, allele frequency, singletons), and each bar the number of variant records in one of its bins, grouped by caller. It answers how the call sets of different callers are distributed.
    How to read: every panel has its own axes, because the sections count different kinds of records on different scales; compare callers within a panel. Callers that peak in the same bins agree, and a caller with an extra mode, for instance very low allele frequencies, adds calls the others do not make.
    Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because a median of bin counts says nothing about a distribution.
    Source: https://samtools.github.io/bcftools/bcftools.html
  code: |-
    # the x value of a section: its label when it has one (categorical sections and
    # the open-ended depth bucket), else its numeric bin
    d = df.with_columns(
        pl.coalesce([pl.col("label"), pl.col("bin").map_elements(lambda v: f"{v:g}", return_dtype=pl.Utf8)]).alias("key")
    ).drop_nulls(["key", "count"]).sort(["section", "bin", "label"], nulls_last=True)
    fig = px.bar(
        d.to_pandas(),
        x="key",
        y="count",
        color="caller",
        barmode="group",
        facet_col="section",
        facet_col_wrap=2,
        facet_row_spacing=0.14,
        facet_col_spacing=0.08,
        labels={"key": "Bin", "count": "Variant records", "caller": "Caller", "section": "Section"},
    )
    fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=", 1)[-1].replace("_", " ")))
    fig.update_xaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="", type="category")
    fig.update_yaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
    fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 32, "l": 48, "r": 16, "b": 32})

output.name: Per-caller Ts/Tv ratio
output.description: Per-sample, per-caller transition/transversion ratio from `bcftools stats`. The ratio varies with genome region and gene function, so it is read against the other callers on the same sample; a caller with too few SNPs to score (e.g. a structural-variant caller) reads 0.0 rather than being absent.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Ts/Tv ratio per caller
  description: |-
    Each bar is the ratio of transitions to transversions among the SNPs of one caller on one sample, coloured by sample. It answers whether callers agree on the substitution balance of the SNPs they report.
    How to read: the cited study uses the ratio as a quality indicator for SNP calls, so callers run on the same sample are expected to land close together. A caller far from its peers is adding or losing SNPs of one kind, a sign of noise or bias. A bar of 0 is a caller with too few SNPs to score.
    Note: the ratio varies with genome region, gene function and GC content, so no single cut-off applies and no reference line is drawn.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: caller
    y: ts_tv
    color: sample
    barmode: group
    labels:
      caller: Caller
      ts_tv: Transition/transversion ratio
      sample: Sample

Each bar is the ratio of transitions to transversions among the SNPs of one caller on one sample, coloured by sample. It answers whether callers agree on the substitution balance of the SNPs they report.

Note: the ratio varies with genome region, gene function and GC content, so no single cut-off applies and no reference line is drawn.

renders._yaml:

  id: library_index_purity
  title: Reads against index purity
  description: |-
    Each point is a library in one lane: its number of reads on the horizontal axis and the share of those reads whose index matched exactly on the vertical axis, coloured by lane. It answers whether low-yield libraries are also the ones with poorly read indexes.
    How to read: points should sit near the top of the plot whatever their size. A library low on the axis, or a whole lane shifted down, has many reads that only matched with a mismatch, which can signal index quality problems or index sets that are too close. Compare the lanes of the same library.
    Note: BCL Convert publishes no pass or fail cut-off for index purity, so no line is drawn.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of reads with a perfect index match of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of BCL Convert.
  kind: scatter_xy

    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    log_x: true
    x_title: Reads
    y_title: Reads with a perfect index match (%)
    top_n_labels: 3
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: reads
    y: pct_perfect_index
    label: sample
    color: lane_label

tools.name: bedtools genomecov
tools.description: A set of tools for genomic analysis tasks, specifically enabling genome arithmetic (merge, count, complement) on various file types. Here, genomecov computes the per-base coverage of a set of alignments, one strand at a time.

output.name: Strand coverage in genomic windows
output.description: Read bases of the plus and minus strand coverage bedGraphs in 250 kb windows, one row per library per window, in parts per million of the library's signal, streamed out of files of several million intervals without holding one. Every library gets every window of the chromosomes, a window without reads at 0, so libraries and time points compare on one complete matrix.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: strand_signal_genome_view
  title: Strand signal along the genome
  description: |-
    Each bar is a 250 kb window of the genome, drawn from its start to its end, with the height of the combined plus and minus strand signal of one library and one lane per library. It answers where along the genome a library holds its reads.
    How to read: lanes that follow one another peak at the same windows when libraries capture the same transcription. A window that towers over its neighbours in one lane only is a hotspot of that library, for instance a repeat array, so compare the lanes before reading it as biology.
    Note: the signal is scaled to parts per million of each library, so lanes compare in shape and not in depth. bedtools genomecov defines no cut-off for coverage.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the 95th percentile of the window signal of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of bedtools. Windows above it are the hottest of the rows on show.
    Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    facet_by_sample: true
    score_title: Signal (log2 of parts per million + 1)
    score_threshold_stat: p95
  roles:
    chr: chromosome
    pos: start
    end: end
    score: log2_signal
    sample: sample

tools.name: Bismark

output.name: Alignment summary
output.description: Per-sample Bismark bisulfite alignment: pairs analysed, the unique-best-hit count and mapping efficiency Bismark itself reports, plus how many pairs never aligned or mapped to more than one place. MultiQC draws the bar; the exact counts behind it are only readable here.

renders._yaml:

  title: Mapping efficiency per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the percentage of read pairs Bismark aligned to a unique best position. It answers which libraries mapped poorly.

    Note: Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mapping efficiency of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.

output.name: Binned CpG methylation
output.description: Genome-wide CpG methylation averaged into 10 kb windows, one row per library per window, streamed out of the per-CpG bedGraph without ever holding it in memory. The only coordinate-bound collection a methylseq run can produce, and the matrix every cohort-level panel downstream reads.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: methylation_track
  title: Methylation along the genome
  description: |-
    Each trace is a library: the mean CpG methylation of every 10 kb window along a chromosome. It answers where methylation rises or drops, and whether libraries share the pattern.
    How to read: traces that move together show a shared methylome. A library that departs over a long stretch is a candidate for a copy-number change, a sex or cell-type difference, or a technical problem. Zoom to a chromosome to read the detail.
    Note: windows with too few CpGs in a library are dropped, so gaps are expected in CpG-poor regions.
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: sample
  roles:
    chromosome: chromosome
    position: position
    value: methylation_pct
    end: end
    sample: sample

output.description: % methylation by read position in all three cytosine contexts and both reads, with the context and the read as columns so two small filters replace six tiles. output.name: Window methylation group comparison
output.description: Every eligible 10 kb window (enough CpGs in every library, re-binned from the per-CpG bedGraphs without the drawing stride) tested between the two levels of the first two-level factor of the run's design table, on the arcsine square-root transform of its methylation proportion, corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg over all tested windows. nf-core/methylseq ships no differential-methylation caller at any version, so this is the screen the published files support: a region ranking on library-level replication, not a called DMR set.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: window_volcano
  title: Window methylation volcano
  description: |-
    Each point is a 10 kb window: the methylation difference between the two groups on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which regions differ most, in which direction and how confidently.
    How to read: windows in the upper left and right corners lose or gain methylation with the highest confidence. With only a handful of libraries per group this is a screen, so confirm any region in the genome view before acting.

output.name: Spike-in normalisation factors
output.description: The two Bowtie 2 alignments of a spike-in normalised run, side by side: how much of each library reached the target genome, how much reached the carrier spike-in genome, and the scale factor the pipeline divides the coverage by before two samples are compared.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: spikein_factor_bar
  title: Spike-in scale factor per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the factor its coverage is multiplied by, the normalisation constant divided by the pairs aligned to the spike-in genome. It answers how much each library is scaled before samples are compared.
    How to read: a larger factor means fewer spike-in pairs, so the library is scaled up. Factors that differ widely between replicates of one condition point to uneven spike-in addition, so consider another normalisation.
    Lines and annotations: the constant is 10000, the default normalisation_c of nf-core/cutandrun, and no cut-off is drawn.
     The dashed line is the median scale factor of this table, a reference
    computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bowtie 2.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/nextflow_schema.json
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: scale_factor
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      scale_factor: Scale factor
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: scale_factor

The hero number is the lowest number of pairs aligned to the spike-in genome in any library. It answers whether every library holds enough spike-in to be normalised.
How to read: higher is better. A library under the line has spike-in too low to separate from noise, so another normalisation, such as the read count, is safer.
Lines and annotations: the line is 1000 spike-in reads, the level the nf-core/cutandrun documentation gives for a spike-in signal above noise. The table counts pairs, so it is a close approximation.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
renders.caption: lowest spike-in pair count, with the median and highest

tools.name: BUSCO
tools.description: Gene-content completeness of assemblies against a BUSCO lineage dataset.

output.name: BUSCO completeness per assembly
output.description: One row per assessed assembly from BUSCO's batch summary: the complete, single-copy, duplicated, fragmented and missing percentages against the lineage dataset, plus the contiguity BUSCO measures on the way. Complete single-copy is the headline; a high duplicated share on a haploid target points at retained haplotigs, a high fragmented share at a base-level error rate high enough to break gene models. A pipeline that runs BUSCO on both the assembly and its annotated proteins (nf-core/genomeqc) names the mode in the run, read into busco_mode, so the two scores of one assembly stay two rows.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: completeness_vs_duplication
  title: Completeness against duplication
  description: |-
    Each point is an assessed assembly, with the percent of complete BUSCOs on the horizontal axis and the percent of duplicated BUSCOs on the vertical axis, sized by contig N50 and coloured by lineage dataset. It answers which assemblies are both complete and free of duplication.
    How to read: the best assemblies sit far right and low. Points high on the vertical axis hold the same marker genes twice, which BUSCO explains by a recent genome duplication or by a chimeric assembly of haplotypes. A larger point is a more contiguous assembly.
    Note: BUSCO publishes no pass mark and asks that results be read in the biology of the organism, so no reference line is drawn.
    Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Complete BUSCOs (%)
    y_title: Duplicated BUSCOs (%)
    top_n_labels: 5
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: complete_pct
    y: duplicated_pct
    label: assembly_id
    color: lineage
    size: contig_n50

tools.name: CellBender
tools.description: CellBender is a software package for eliminating technical artifacts from high-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data.

output.name: Ambient-RNA removal metrics
output.description: CellBender's per-sample accounting of ambient-RNA removal: counts removed, cells found against the expected count, and the training convergence parameters.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Share of counts removed as ambient
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median fraction of all counts that CellBender called ambient RNA and removed, over the samples in view. It answers how much of the signal was background.
    How to read: a small fraction means a clean sample and little change to the matrix. A large one means heavy ambient contamination, so compare samples and look at the CellBender report of the outlier before using its matrix.
    Note: CellBender documents no cut-off for this fraction, so no pass mark is drawn. It depends on the target false-positive rate the run used.
    Source: https://cellbender.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage/index.html
  column: fraction_counts_removed
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: median, with the lowest and highest sample

Note: CellBender documents no cut-off for this fraction, so no pass mark is drawn. It depends on the target false-positive rate the run used.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Found against expected cells
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median ratio of cells CellBender found to cells it expected, over the samples in view. It answers whether the called cell count matches the prior the run started from.
    How to read: a ratio near 1 means the call agrees with the expectation, and CellBender asks only for an expected-cells value within a factor of 2. output.name: Cell-cycle phase
output.description: S and G2/M scores per cell from the Tirosh gene sets, and the phase call that follows from them. Tells a cluster that is a distinct cell type apart from one that is the same cell type, cycling.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: phase_scatter
  title: S and G2/M scores per cell
  description: |-
    Each point is a cell: its S-phase score on the horizontal axis and its G2/M score on the vertical axis, coloured by the phase assigned. It answers which cells are cycling and in which phase.
    How to read: a large cloud in the lower left corner is G1 or resting cells, the normal majority of a tissue sample. Arms toward the upper or right regions are cycling cells, so check whether a cluster is mostly cycling before treating it as a distinct cell type.
    Lines and annotations: the two lines sit at a score of 0 on each axis. A cell with both scores negative is called G1, otherwise the higher score gives S or G2M, the rule of scanpy's score_genes_cell_cycle. The gene sets are the S and G2/M sets of Tirosh et al.; the scores here subtract the cell's mean expression instead of expression-matched control genes.

The hero number is the average share of called cells that pass the quality filter, and the gauge shows it out of 100 percent. It answers how clean the called cells are.
How to read: the minimum shows the worst sample. A low value points to many cells with few genes, few UMIs or a high mitochondrial share.
Note: the filter uses median absolute deviation limits computed per sample, see the description of the cell QC tab for the rules.
renders.caption: cells passing QC, of 100%

output.name: Per-cell QC, clusters and embeddings
output.description: One row per called cell: UMI / gene counts, mito / ribo / hemoglobin / top-20 fractions, graph-based and k-means clusters, UMAP / t-SNE / PCA coordinates, CellBender agreement and a MAD-based QC flag. The hub every other cell-level cellranger output joins to.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: umap_qc
  title: UMAP coloured by genes detected
  description: |-
    Each point is a cell on the UMAP, coloured by the log10 of the genes it detects. It answers whether depth or quality follows the cell groups.
    How to read: a smooth colour within each island is expected. A whole island of low values is a cluster of poor cells or a low-RNA cell type, so check the mitochondrial and UMI tiles before trusting it.
  kind: embedding
  config:
    axis_prefix: UMAP
  roles:
    sample_id: barcode
    dim_1: umap_1
    dim_2: umap_2
    color: log10_n_genes
    cluster: graphclust

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: umi_vs_genes
  title: Genes detected against UMI counts
  description: |-
    Each point is a cell: its total UMI count on the horizontal axis and the number of genes it detects on the vertical axis, coloured by its QC status. It answers whether cells follow the expected relation between depth and complexity.
    How to read: genes detected rise with UMIs and flatten at high depth. Cells that sit far below the cloud have many UMIs from few genes, which points to low-complexity cells or doublets, and flagged cells should lie at the edges.
    Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. The QC flags come from limits of 5 median absolute deviations on log counts and genes, set per sample.
    Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    log_x: true
    x_title: UMI counts per cell
    y_title: Genes detected per cell
  roles:
    x: n_umi
    y: n_genes
    color: qc_status

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: cluster_stability
  title: Cluster stability across resolutions
  description: |-
    Each band is a group of cells that moves from a graph-based cluster to a k-means cluster with 6 groups and then one with 10, sized by cell count. It answers how stable the clusters are when the method and the resolution change.
    How to read: a cluster that flows into one group at every step is stable. A cluster that splits evenly across several groups is weakly defined, so treat its identity with care.
  kind: sankey
  config:
    color_mode: source
  roles:
    steps:
    - graphclust
    - kmeans_6
    - kmeans_10

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: umi_histogram
  title: UMI counts per cell
  description: |-
    Each bar counts the cells with a total UMI count in a range, split by QC status. It answers how deep the cells are and where the low-depth tail lies.
    How to read: a single peak with a short left tail is a healthy library. A second peak at low counts is empty droplets or debris that the filter flagged.
    The QC filter flags cells below 5 median absolute deviations under the median of log counts, computed per sample.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median UMI count per cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.
    Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: n_umi
    color: qc_status
    labels:
      n_umi: UMI counts per cell
      qc_status: QC status
  reference_lines:
  - axis: x
    stat: median
    column: n_umi

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: mito_box
  title: Mitochondrial fraction by cluster
  description: |-
    Each box is a cluster and shows the percent of UMIs from mitochondrial genes in its cells. It answers which clusters carry stressed or dying cells.
    How to read: a cluster with a high box is a candidate for broken cells, but some cell types are naturally rich in mitochondria. Check its markers before removing it.
    The QC filter flags a cell when it exceeds 3 median absolute deviations and a fixed 8 percent, a limit the source calls not universal.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mitochondrial fraction of a cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.
    Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: cluster_label
    y: pct_mito
    color: cluster_label
    labels:
      cluster_label: Cluster
      pct_mito: Mitochondrial UMIs (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: pct_mito

Each point is a gene tested in one cluster against all other cells: its log2 fold change on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which genes separate a cluster and how confidently.
How to read: genes in the upper right are strong, confident markers of the cluster, and genes in the upper left are depleted in it. Only the most significant genes per cluster are kept, so the lower part of the plot is truncated.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the cut-off this module's recipe uses to label marker genes, not read from the run. No fold-change line is drawn, because Cell Ranger defines no cut-off for its marker tests.

tools.name: CheckM2
tools.description: Machine-learning prediction of genome completeness and contamination for metagenome-assembled genomes.

output.name: Bin completeness and contamination
output.description: How much of a genome each bin holds and how much of it belongs to something else. Completeness against contamination is the plot metagenome binning is read on: the top-left corner holds the bins worth naming, the right-hand side holds chimeras, and the spread between binners on the same assembly says which binner to trust for this sample.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: completeness_contamination
  title: Completeness against contamination
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin: its predicted completeness on the horizontal axis and its predicted contamination on the vertical axis, coloured by binner and sized by genome size. It answers which bins are worth keeping and which binner delivers them.
    How to read: the bottom right corner holds the bins worth naming, and the top half holds chimeric bins with sequences from more than one organism. Compare the colours to see which binner produces more bins in the good corner for this assembly. A large point is a bin with a genome-sized sequence, so a small complete-looking point deserves a second look.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a completeness of 50% and the horizontal line a contamination of 10%, the limits of a medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard. tools.name: CheckV
tools.description: Assesses the quality of single-contig viral genomes: completeness against complete reference genomes, host contamination at the edges of proviruses, and the MIUViG quality tier.

output.name: Viral genome quality
output.description: CheckV's verdict on every viral sequence: length, provirus call, viral and host genes, estimated completeness and contamination, and the quality tier those give. Completeness against contamination is the plane a viral genome is read on: complete genomes sit top left, proviruses with host flanks to the right.

  id: quality_tiers
  title: Sequences by quality tier
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of viral sequences assessed, and the bar splits them by CheckV quality tier. It answers how much of the viral content is usable.
    How to read: complete and high-quality sequences are ready for analysis. Medium and low-quality ones are partial genomes, and undetermined ones could not be given a tier. Tiers rest on completeness alone.
    Source: https://bitbucket.org/berkeleylab/checkv/raw/master/README.md
  column: contig_length
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - median

  breakdown_col: checkv_quality
  caption: sequences, by CheckV tier

tools.name: CNVkit
tools.description: Infers and visualises copy number from high-throughput DNA sequencing data.

output.name: Copy-number profile
output.description: CNVkit's bin-level copy ratios and its called segments in one long table. Per CNVkit's file-format documentation the .cnr file carries chromosome, start, end, gene, depth, log2 and weight, one row per bin, and the .cns file carries chromosome, start, end, gene, log2, depth, probes and weight, one row per segment, with cn and baf added when cnvkit call has run. The two are folded together and told apart by the segment column, so one component draws the evidence and the call on the same axis.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: cnvkit_profile
  title: Copy-number profile
  description: |-
    Each dot is a genomic bin: its log2 copy ratio against the reference along the chromosomes, with the called segments drawn over the bins and coloured by their integer copy number, and the B-allele frequency of each segment underneath when it is known. It answers which regions of the genome are gained or lost in a sample.
    How to read: a log2 ratio near zero is a neutral, two-copy region. Segments above the gain line are gains and segments below the loss line are losses, and a deep drop is a possible homozygous deletion. Bins scattered widely around a segment mean a noisy sample, so check the bin depth card before trusting small segments.
    Lines and annotations: the gain line at a log2 ratio of 0.2 and the loss line at -0.25 are the inner cut-offs of the default thresholds of cnvkit call, chosen to detect a single-copy change in a diploid tumour at a purity as low as 30%. They assume a diploid genome and are rescaled by purity when it is given.
    Sources: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pipeline.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27100738/
  kind: cnv_profile
  config:
    gain_threshold: 0.2
    loss_threshold: -0.25
    y_range: 3.0
  roles:
    sample: sample
    chrom: chrom
    start: start
    end: end
    log2: log2
    baf: baf
    copy_number: copy_number
    segment: segment
    label: label

tools.name: comBGC
tools.description: Aggregates the biosynthetic gene cluster predictions of antiSMASH, DeepBGC and GECCO into one table per sample plus a run-level summary, with the region coordinates, product class, CDS count and PFAM domains normalised across the three callers.

output.name: BGC region coordinates
output.description: The comBGC regions as coordinates rather than counts: contig, interval, product class and region length in kilobases, one row per predicted cluster. Three tracks read the same rows, so a run whose genome renderer is unavailable still has the lane view and the density profile.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: bgc_genome_track
  title: Cluster regions on the contigs
  description: |-
    Each interval is a predicted biosynthetic gene cluster placed on its contig, with its height giving the region length in kilobases and its colour the product class. It answers where on the assembly the clusters sit and which kinds they are.
    How to read: several clusters on one contig suggest a biosynthetic locus, and a cluster covering a whole short contig is probably truncated by the contig edge. Compare the classes: a contig that carries several different ones is a promising place to look first.
    Note: callers disagree on region boundaries by design, so the same locus can appear as differently sized intervals. No cut-off on region length is published, so no line is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: Region length (kb)
  roles:
    chr: contig
    pos: start
    score: length_kb
    feature: region_id
    end: end
    category: product_class

tools.name: Control-FREEC
tools.description: Copy number and genotype annotation from whole genome and whole exome sequencing data.

output.name: Copy-number ratio windows
output.description: Control-FREEC's per-window copy ratios and the segments they encode. Per the Control-FREEC documentation the _ratio.txt file carries Chromosome, Start, Ratio, MedianRatio and CopyNumber, plus BAF, estimatedBAF, Genotype and UncertaintyOfGT when a SNV file was supplied. MedianRatio is the segment value written on every window the segment covers, so a run of identical values is one segment: the windows and the recovered segments land in the same table, told apart by the segment column.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: controlfreec_profile
  title: Copy number profile
  description: |-
    Each point is a genomic window: its log2 copy ratio along the chromosomes, with the called segments drawn over it and the B-allele frequency underneath. It answers where the genome has gained or lost copies.
    How to read: windows around zero are copy neutral, and a run of windows shifted up or down forms a gain or a loss. Segments are coloured by the predicted copy number. A BAF split away from 0.5 on a shifted segment supports a real alteration and marks loss of heterozygosity.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed lines mark log2 ratios of 0.32 and -0.42, the midpoints between 2 and 3 copies and between 2 and 1 copies. They are an arithmetic reference from Control-FREEC's copy number as ratio times ploidy, taken at ploidy 2, and not thresholds the tool uses to call.
    Note: Control-FREEC calls copy number from the ratio and the ploidy of the run, so for another ploidy or a subclonal sample these lines move.
    Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22155870/
  kind: cnv_profile
  config:
    gain_threshold: 0.32
    loss_threshold: -0.42
  roles:
    sample: sample
    chrom: chrom
    start: start
    end: end
    log2: log2
    baf: baf
    copy_number: copy_number
    segment: segment
    label: label

tools.name: cooler
tools.description: Sparse binary format for genomic interaction matrices.

output.name: Binned contact matrix
output.description: Binned, ICE-balanced intra-chromosomal contact matrix from a cooler dump, joined to its bins. One partition per resolution, keyed by the resolution column, so a tile re-bins itself as the reader zooms; coarser levels are derived by merging bins when the run dumped a single resolution.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: binned_contact_map
  title: Chromosome contact map
  description: |-
    Each cell is a pair of genomic bins on one chromosome, coloured by the balanced contact frequency between them, with position on both axes. It answers how the chromosome folds: which regions touch each other more than their distance predicts.
    How to read: the diagonal is always brightest because neighbouring bins contact most, and contact falls away with distance. Squares along the diagonal are self-interacting domains, and bright spots off the diagonal are loops or long-range contacts. The map re-bins to a finer resolution as you zoom in.
    Lines and annotations: the colour scale is logarithmic, since contact frequency spans several orders of magnitude. The values are balanced with the ICE method, which removes per-bin coverage biases, so a bin is comparable with another.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22941365/
  kind: contact_map
  config:
    log_scale: true
  roles:
    chrom1: chrom1
    start1: start1
    chrom2: chrom2
    start2: start2
    count: count
    resolution: resolution
    sample: sample

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz

  title: Contact probability against distance
  description: |-
    Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the probability that two loci a given distance apart are in contact, on log axes. It answers how fast contacts decay with genomic distance.
    How to read: contacts fall steadily with distance. Chromosomes whose curve departs from the pooled one carry a different folding or a technical bias, and a plateau or bump at long range can point to translocations or poor balancing. Open the slope view for the local decay rate.
    Note: this is the tool's expected contact table re-binned over log-spaced distances, with no cut-off drawn.
  kind: profile
  config:
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
    y_title: Contact probability
  roles:
    series: chrom
    x: distance
    y: contact_probability

  description: |-

output.description: TAD intervals derived from the insulation track's boundary calls, one row per domain per window size, with its span, the bins it covers and the boundary strength at each edge.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_track
  title: TAD domains along the genome
  description: |-
    Each rectangle is a domain, drawn from its start to its end on a chromosome-aware axis, at a height equal to its size in kilobases. It answers how the genome is partitioned into topological domains and how large they are.
    How to read: neighbouring rectangles of similar height are a regular partition. Very large domains often span poorly mappable regions or centromeres, and a run of very small ones suggests noise in the boundary calls.
    Note: domains are derived from the insulation boundary calls, so they change with the window size and the boundary threshold.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    mark: rect
    score_title: Domain size (kb)
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: start
    score: size_kb
    end: end
    sample: sample

output.name: A/B compartment track
output.description: Per-bin first eigenvector (E1) of the intra-chromosomal correlation matrix, the A/B compartment track. Sign marks the compartment, zero-crossings are compartment boundaries. The recipe phases E1 per sample, resolution and chromosome so it correlates positively with bin coverage (1 / balancing weight): the better-covered compartment is A, the same way at every resolution, without a GC or gene track.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: compartment_track
  title: A/B compartment track
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin of a chromosome with its first eigenvector value, coloured by compartment. It answers which parts of the genome are in the active A compartment and which in the inactive B compartment.
    How to read: positive values are A and negative values are B, and the zero-crossings are compartment boundaries. Long alternating stretches that match the expected pattern mean a clean decomposition, and an inverted chromosome arm is worth a check.
    Lines and annotations: the compartment labels are this catalog's convention, A for positive E1 and B for negative. The recipe phases each chromosome so that E1 correlates positively with bin coverage, the better-covered compartment being A, the same way at every resolution. The cooltools documentation instead orients E1 to correlate positively with GC content, the usual convention for Hi-C.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py and https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/compartments_and_saddles.html
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: category
  roles:
    chromosome: chrom
    position: start
    value: E1
    category: compartment

renders._yaml:

  title: Libraries by zygosity class
  description: |-
    Each unit is one library and the ring splits them by the classifier's zygosity class: homozygous wild type, heterozygous, homozygous edited or ambiguous. It answers how many libraries carry the edit on both, one or no allele.
    How to read: a ring dominated by one class is a uniform experiment. A large ambiguous share means the wild type fraction sits between the classifier's bands, so check the outcome composition and the clonality call before trusting the library.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: clonality_mix
  title: Libraries by clonality label
  description: |-
    Each unit is one library and the ring splits them by the clonality label the indel peak structure gives them. It answers whether the edited reads come from one clone or from a mixed population.
    How to read: clonal and likely clonal libraries carry one or two dominant indels, which is what a single edited clone looks like. Polyclonal and ambiguous libraries mix many alleles, and low editing activity means too few edited reads to call a clone.
    Lines and annotations: an indel counts as a peak when it holds more than 5% of the classified reads, and a library is clonal when one peak holds more than 85%. Libraries with too few reads are labelled insufficient data. Both rules are constants of the classifier script.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/templates/clonality_classifier.py
  column: clonality
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:

output.name: Indel position around the cut site
output.description: At every position within the profile window of the cut site, the share of each library's classified reads whose deletion covers it and the share with an insertion starting there. A Cas9 cut shows as a deletion peak straddling offset 0.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: deletion_profile
  title: Deletion coverage around the cut site
  description: |-
    Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of its classified reads whose deletion covers that position. It answers where the deletions fall and how wide the damaged stretch is.
    How to read: an efficient nuclease edit gives a hump centred on the cut site that falls off within a few tens of bases. A hump displaced from the marker points to a misplaced cut site or a second target, and a curve flat near zero means little editing. Compare libraries of one guide, which should overlap.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline reports for the amplicon (the cut site file written by the CIGAR parser). It is a landmark, not a cut-off. This catalog's recipe leaves out positions with no indel and keeps a fixed window of 100 bases either side.

Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of its classified reads whose deletion covers that position. It answers where the deletions fall and how wide the damaged stretch is.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: editing_rate
  title: Editing rate
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of classified reads that carry any edit, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how efficiently the guide edits.
    How to read: a higher rate means more edited reads, and replicates of one guide should agree. A very low rate means the cut did not take or the guide is inactive. Compare with the frameshift share before calling a knockout.
    Note: the rate is the share of classified reads, meaning wild type, template-based and indel reads. The pipeline publishes no cut-off for it.
  column: edited_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

  aggregation: average
  aggregations:

output.name: Indel size distribution
output.description: Share of each library's classified reads at every signed indel size (insertions positive, deletions negative), summed from the indel alleles. The shape is a guide's repair signature.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: size_profile
  title: Indel size distribution
  description: |-
    Each curve is a library: the share of its classified reads carrying an indel of each signed size, with deletions negative and insertions positive. It answers which repair outcomes a guide produces.
    How to read: a few dominant sizes, such as a one base insertion or short deletions, are a reproducible repair signature, and replicates of one guide should overlap. A flat curve spread over many sizes means unspecific damage. Sizes that are multiples of three keep the reading frame, so check the frameshift share before calling a knockout.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at 0 only separates deletions from insertions and is not a cut-off. Sizes beyond 100 bases are not drawn.
  kind: profile
  config:
    reference_x: 0
    reference_label: No length change
    x_title: Indel size (bp, deletions negative)
    y_title: Classified reads (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: size
    y: pct_reads

output.name: Substitution and gap rate per position
output.description: For every amplicon position within the profile window of the cut site, the dominant base and the share of reads carrying another base (substitution) or a gap. Base editors show as a substitution peak upstream of the cut.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: substitution_profile
  title: Substituted bases around the cut site
  description: |-
    Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of aligned reads carrying a base other than the most common one at that position. It answers where bases change around the cut.
    How to read: a flat line near zero is a nuclease run with no substitution signal. A hump near the cut can mean base editing, and isolated spikes are usually single nucleotide variants of the sample or sequencing errors. Compare with the deletion profile to tell editing from noise.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline reports for the amplicon (the cut site file written by the CIGAR parser). This catalog's recipe takes the most common base of the library at each position as the reference, not the genome base, so a homozygous variant shows no substitution.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    reference_x: 0
    reference_label: Cut site
    x_title: Offset from the cut site (bp)
    y_title: Reads with a substituted base (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:

    y: substitution_pct

renders._yaml:

  title: Peak yield and agreement by caller
  description: |-
    Each dot is a sample and peak caller: its colour is the number of peaks the caller made (log10) and its size is the share of those peaks the other caller reproduced. It answers how much each caller called and how much the two agree.
    How to read: large dots mean the other caller confirmed most of the peaks. A small dot with a dark colour is a caller that made many peaks the other did not. Read it with the unique peaks bars before trusting either caller.
    Note: neither caller is a subset of the other, so disagreement is informative and not an error.
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:

    gene: caller
    mean_expression: log10_n_peaks
    frac_expressing: frac_shared

  description: |-
    Each point is a sample and peak caller: the peaks that caller made on the vertical axis against the peaks the other caller made on the horizontal axis, coloured by target. It answers which caller is more productive for each target.
    How to read: a point far from the equal-count diagonal means one caller called many more peaks than the other, so look at its unique peaks and at the target. Each sample appears twice, once per caller, with the axes swapped.

      target: Target

output.name: Fraction of coverage in peaks
output.description: Each sample's fragment coverage split into the part that falls inside its own peaks and the part that does not, in base pairs and as a fraction. SEACR reports no read count, so the numerator is the summed region signal de-scaled by the spike-in factor and the denominator is the fragment-length histogram.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: frip_composition_bar
  title: Fragment coverage inside and outside peaks
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample split into the share of its fragment coverage that falls inside its own called peaks and the share that falls outside them. It answers how much of the signal the peaks capture.
    How to read: a larger in-peaks share means a better signal-to-noise ratio. The nf-core cutandrun documentation reads a FRiP above 0.3 as reasonable and above 0.7 as the highest quality. Low values point to background, few peaks or a peak threshold set very high.
    Note: SEACR reports no read counts, so coverage is the summed region signal scaled by the spike-in factor. The score also depends on the peak caller settings.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: fraction
    color: signal_class
    labels:
      sample: Sample
      fraction: Share of fragment coverage
      signal_class: Signal

tools.name: DamageProfiler
tools.description: Determines DNA damage patterns in ancient DNA reads, a Java replacement for mapDamage.

output.name: Authenticity plane
output.description: One row per library pairing the two ancient-DNA authenticity signals, terminal deamination at the first base of a read and mapped fragment length, so a modern contaminant (long, undamaged), an ancient extract (short, damaged) and over-sheared modern DNA (short, undamaged) separate on one plane. Derived from the two tidied DamageProfiler collections, which a template must declare before this one.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: authenticity_plane
  title: Authenticity plane
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: its mean mapped fragment length on the horizontal axis and the C to T frequency at the first 5' base on the vertical axis, with the marker sized by mapped fragments. It answers whether a library carries the two signals of ancient DNA, short fragments and terminal deamination.
    How to read: a library high on the vertical axis and short on the horizontal one combines damage and fragmentation, as expected for ancient DNA. A long, undamaged library looks modern, which may be a contaminant, and a short but undamaged one may be over-sheared modern DNA. No pass mark is drawn because none is defined by the tool, so judge each library against the others and the extraction history.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median C to T frequency at the first 5' base of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of DamageProfiler.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: Mean fragment length (bp)
    y_title: C to T at the first 5' base
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: mean_length
    y: ct_5p_first
    label: sample
    color: sample
    size: n_reads

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: G to A at the 3' end
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean frequency of G to A substitutions at the first 3' base over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the libraries are at the 3' end.
    How to read: on a double-stranded library the 3' G to A signal reflects deamination at the 5' end of the complementary strand, so it should agree with the 5' C to T signal. A strong 5' signal with no 3' signal is not explained by that pattern, so check how the library was built.
    Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  column: ga_3p_first
  aggregation: average
