output.name: Fragment length distribution
output.description: Mapped fragment length by strand, from DamageProfiler's lgdistribution table. The second authenticity signal after the misincorporation profile: ancient DNA is depurination-fragmented and rarely survives past about 100 bp, so a length distribution that looks like a modern library's is a contamination flag even when the damage curve passes.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fragment_length_profile
  title: Fragment length distribution
  description: |-
    Each line is a library and strand: the fraction of its mapped fragments at each length. It answers how long the surviving DNA fragments are.
    How to read: ancient DNA is fragmented, so a curve piled at short lengths fits it. A curve with a wide tail towards long fragments looks like a modern library, a possible contamination even when the damage curve passes. The two strands of a library should follow each other.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Fragment length (bp)
    y_title: Fraction of mapped fragments
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: length
    y: fraction

_render.title: Fragment length distribution
_render.description:
Each line is a library and strand: the fraction of its mapped fragments at each length. It answers how long the surviving DNA fragments are.

Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/

output.description: Substitution frequency by distance from the read end, 5' and 3', C>T and G>A deamination against every other substitution pooled, the ancient-DNA authentication read.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: eager_damage_profile
  title: Misincorporation profile

  description: |-
    Each cell is the correlation between the genome-wide bin counts of two libraries, with rows and columns clustered. It answers which libraries have the most similar signal.

output.name: Fingerprint metrics
output.description: How concentrated each library's coverage is, as the quality metrics plotFingerprint writes beside its curve: the area under the observed cumulative-coverage curve, the same area for a perfectly uniform library of that depth, and the divergence between the two. Enriched targets sit far from the uniform reference, inputs and failed enrichments sit on top of it.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fingerprint_scatter
  title: Enrichment against divergence from uniform
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: the area under its cumulative-coverage curve on the horizontal axis and its synthetic Jensen-Shannon distance, the distance to a perfect input of the same depth, on the vertical axis, with one colour per library. It answers which libraries are enriched and how strongly.
    How to read: enriched targets sit far left, with a large distance. Inputs and failed enrichments sit near the maximum area with a distance close to zero. A point off the trend is a library whose curve is odd, so open the fingerprint in the MultiQC tab.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line at 0.5 is the maximum value the area can take, as stated by the deepTools documentation. It is the area under the diagonal, which the documentation equates with a perfect input of infinite coverage.
    Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Area under the fingerprint curve
    y_title: Jensen-Shannon distance to a uniform library
    reference_line: vertical
    reference_value: 0.5
    reference_label: Maximum area (uniform library)
  roles:

output.name: Metagene signal profile
output.description: The mean signal of every library across the plotted window, one row per bin. With `computeMatrix scale-regions` the window is the flanking region plus a gene body stretched to a fixed number of bins; with `reference-point` it is a window centred on one anchor. `bin_label` carries deepTools' own anchors, so the marker can be placed without hard-coding the window.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: metagene_profile
  title: Metagene signal profile
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: its mean signal in every bin across the plotted window. It answers where along genes or around an anchor the signal accumulates.
    How to read: an enriched target shows a peak at its expected position, such as the promoter for a promoter mark, and an input stays flat. A library with no peak did not enrich, and a peak in the wrong place points to a mislabelled library.
    The dotted guides are the anchors deepTools names for the run, such as the TSS and TES of a scaled gene body, and the dashed line is the median bin of the table: the background a peak has to rise above.
    Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/plotProfile.html
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_label_col: bin_label
    reference_y_stat: median
    reference_y_label: median bin
    x_title: Position along the plotted window
    y_title: Mean signal
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: bin
    y: signal

output.name: DESeq2 QC PCA
output.description: The principal components nf-core's own deseq2_qc.r computed on the count matrix, read from the file the pipeline publishes rather than recomputed, so the dashboard and the MultiQC report show the same points. A run with several count matrices (one per antibody, merge level or aligner route) gets one PCA per matrix, told apart by the pca_set column.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: volcano
  title: Differential expression volcano
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene in one contrast: its log2 fold change on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which genes change most, in which direction, and how confidently.
    How to read: genes in the upper left and upper right corners are strongly down- and up-regulated with high confidence. A cloud with almost nothing past the lines means little differential signal, so check the QQ view and the sample PCA before trusting the contrast. Open the table tile to inspect the labelled genes.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the adjusted p-value cut-off of 0.05 and the vertical lines mark an absolute log2 fold change of 1 (a fold change of 2). Both are the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults, which also define the up, down and not significant calls on every tile of this tab.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 1.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Log2 fold change
    significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
  roles:
    feature_id: gene_id
    effect_size: log2fc
    significance: padj
    category: contrast

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ma
  title: Fold change against mean expression
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene in one contrast: its mean normalised expression on the horizontal axis (log2 of base mean plus one) and its log2 fold change on the vertical axis. It answers whether the fold changes are real or only come from weakly expressed genes.
    How to read: a healthy MA plot is a flat cloud centred on zero, with the significant genes spread across expression levels. A funnel that widens at low expression is normal noise of low counts. A cloud shifted away from zero points to a normalisation problem, so check the sample distributions.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal lines mark an absolute log2 fold change of 1 (a fold change of 2) and points are highlighted when the adjusted p-value is below 0.05. Both are the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults. DESeq2 itself colours its MA plot at an adjusted p-value of 0.1, its default alpha.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json and https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html
  kind: ma
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    fold_change_threshold: 1.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Log2 fold change
    intensity_label: Mean expression (log2)
  roles:
    feature_id: gene_id
    avg_log_intensity: log2_base_mean
    log2_fold_change: log2fc
    significance: padj

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: qq
  title: P-value QQ plot
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene: its observed raw p-value, as minus log10, against the value expected if no gene differed between the groups. One trace is drawn per contrast. It answers whether the test statistics are well calibrated.
    How to read: points hugging the diagonal for most of the range and lifting off at the far end mean a few real signals over a calibrated null. A curve that leaves the diagonal early, or sits below it, points to inflation or deflation from batch effects, a wrong design or low counts. Compare the contrasts and revisit the PCA when one curve differs.
    Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the expectation when p-values are uniformly distributed under no effect. The shaded band is the 95% confidence interval of that null, so points inside it are consistent with chance.
  kind: qq
  config:
    show_ci: true
    show_identity: true
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    p_value: pvalue
    category: contrast
    feature_id: gene_id

  title: Top changed genes per contrast
  description: |-
    Each bar is a gene: its log2 fold change in a contrast, for the genes with the largest absolute change. It answers which genes drive each contrast and in which direction.
    How to read: long bars to the right are up-regulated and to the left down-regulated; bars are marked when their adjusted p-value passes the cut-off. A strong fold change without significance usually means low or variable counts, so open the MA plot and the table to check it.

  kind: da_barplot
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_label: Log2 fold change
  roles:
    feature_id: gene_id
    contrast: contrast
    lfc: log2fc
    significance: padj

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Significant genes by direction
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct genes called significant, and the bars rank them by direction, up or down. It answers whether the response is mostly induction or repression.

  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: direction
  top_n_count: 3
  filter_expr: col('direction') != 'not significant'
  caption: significant genes, by direction

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: manhattan
  title: Significance along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene placed at its start coordinate, with minus log10 of its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers where on the genome the differentially expressed genes cluster.
    How to read: isolated tall points are single genes, while a tower of points over one region suggests a shared locus effect such as a copy number change or a cluster of related genes. Colour by direction to see whether a region moves one way. Several contrasts overlap here, so filter to one.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, shown as 1.301 on the minus log10 axis. It is the nf-core/differentialabundance default cut-off. The score is capped at 300 where DESeq2 reports an adjusted p-value of 0.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_threshold: 1.301
    score_kind: -log10 adjusted p-value
    color_by_columns:
    - direction
    - gene_biotype
    default_color_by: direction
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    chr: chromosome
    pos: start
    score: neg_log10_padj
    feature: gene_name
    effect: log2fc

output.name: Sample expression distributions
output.description: Per-sample density of the variance-stabilised expression matrix, binned on a grid shared by every sample so the curves are directly comparable, plus each sample's five-number summary. The features sitting at the matrix floor are excluded from the grid, because the spike they form is tall enough to flatten the rest of the curve, and published as a share instead. tools.name: DEXSeq
tools.description: Differential exon / transcript usage testing, finding genes whose exon or isoform usage shifts between conditions. nf-core/nanoseq runs it on Bambu's transcript counts; nf-core/rnasplice runs it on exon bins and on transcript-level salmon counts.

output.name: Differential transcript usage
output.description: DEXSeq differential transcript usage (DTU) as nf-core/rnasplice's dexseq_dtu route writes it: one row per contrast and transcript with its usage log2 fold change (treatment over control), p-value, adjusted p-value and the gene-level q-value.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: dtu_volcano
  title: Transcript usage volcano
  description: |-
    Each point is a transcript in one contrast: the log2 fold change of its usage within its gene on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which isoforms gain or lose share of their gene's expression between conditions, and how confidently.
    How to read: points in the upper right gain usage in the treatment and points in the upper left lose it. Usage is relative to the other isoforms of the gene, so an isoform can change without any change in the gene's total expression. Open the table tile to see the gene behind a labelled transcript.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the cut-off the catalog recipe uses for the significant, up and down calls (its fdr parameter). The DEXSeq vignette illustrates a 10% false discovery rate instead, so 0.05 is the stricter choice. No fold-change line is drawn because the calls use none.
    Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 0.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Usage log2 fold change
    significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
  roles:
    feature_id: transcript_id
    effect_size: log2fc
    significance: padj
    label: gene_id
    category: direction

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: qq
  title: P-value QQ plot
  description: |-
    Each point is a transcript: its observed raw p-value, as minus log10, against the value expected if no isoform changed usage. It answers whether the test statistics are well calibrated.
    How to read: points hugging the diagonal for most of the range and lifting off at the far end mean a few real signals over a calibrated null. A curve that leaves the diagonal early, or sits below it, points to inflation or deflation from a wrong design, batch effects or low counts.
    Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the expectation when p-values are uniformly distributed under no effect. The shaded band is the 95% confidence interval of that null, so points inside it are consistent with chance.
  kind: qq
  config:
    show_ci: true
    show_identity: true
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    p_value: pvalue
    feature_id: feature_id

output.name: Clonal rank abundance

    Source: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Clone rank
    y_title: Relative abundance
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:

    x: rank
    y: p
    lower: lower
    upper: upper

output.name: Clonal diversity profile
output.description: alakazam Hill diversity profile per sample: the bootstrapped diversity d at every order q from richness to inverse Simpson, with its confidence band and the matching evenness.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: diversity_profile
  title: Diversity profile by order
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample: its Hill diversity at every order q, coloured by subject. It answers how diverse each repertoire is and how that changes as common clones weigh more.
    How to read: the horizontal axis is the diversity order q, not a sequencing depth. At q = 0 every clone counts equally (richness), at q = 1 it is the exponential of Shannon entropy and at q = 2 the inverse Simpson index. A curve that falls steeply is dominated by a few clones, a flat one is even, and curves that run apart at high q differ in their dominant clones.
    Sources: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/ and https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/calcDiversity/
  kind: rarefaction
  roles:
    sample_id: sample_id
    depth: q
    metric: d
    group: subject_id

  description: |-

  roles:

    lower: d_lower
    upper: d_upper

  title: Shared clones between samples
  description: |-

  title: Hill diversity per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample: its Hill diversity at the chosen order, with a whisker for the bootstrap confidence interval. It answers which samples differ in diversity beyond the uncertainty of the estimate.
    How to read: pick one order with the filter.     Lines and annotations: the whiskers are the confidence interval alakazam derives by bootstrapping, as shown in its diversity vignette.
    Sources: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/ and https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/calcDiversity/

output.name: Endogenous DNA
output.description: Share of a library's reads that map to the target reference, before and after the quality filter and deduplication, from endorS.py. The headline number of an ancient-DNA screen: it says how much of an extract is the organism rather than the soil, the excavator and the lab.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: endogenous_pre_post
  title: Endogenous DNA before and after filtering
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: the percentage of its reads that map to the target reference on the raw alignment (horizontal) and after the quality filter and deduplication (vertical). It answers how much of the on-target signal survives cleaning.
    How to read: a point near the diagonal loses little to filtering and deduplication. A point far below it is a library whose on-target reads were mostly duplicates or low quality, so its usable depth is smaller than the raw percentage suggests. endorS.py defines no cut-off for a good library.
    Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the points where the percentage is unchanged by filtering. It is a reference defined by the plot itself, not a threshold taken from the tool.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aidaanva/endorS.py/master/README.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Endogenous DNA, raw alignment (%)
    y_title: Endogenous DNA, filtered and deduplicated (%)
    reference_line: diagonal
    reference_label: No loss to filtering
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: endogenous_dna
    y: endogenous_dna_post
    label: sample
    color: sample

tools.name: nf-core/epitopeprediction
tools.description: MHC binding predictions of nf-core/epitopeprediction: every peptide of every sample scored against its alleles by each prediction tool (affinity, IC50, percentile rank and the pipeline's binder call), summarised per peptide, per allele and per tool, the agreement between tools, mutant peptides against their wild type, and the candidate peptides cut from the variants.

output.name: Binding per allele
output.description: One row per sample and allele: distinct peptides scored, peptides at least one tool calls a binder, their share, and the median and best IC50 of the peptides. The allele is normalised to HLA-A*02:01 and carries its locus and MHC class, so it filters and joins like the alleles an HLA typing tool writes.

  description: |-

The affinity score is 1 minus log10 of the IC50 over log10 of 50000.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: sample
    gene: allele
    mean_expression: median_affinity_score
    frac_expressing: binder_rate

output.name: Binding predictions
output.description: One row per sample, peptide, allele and prediction tool that scored it: the 0-1 affinity score, the IC50 in nM behind it, the percentile rank, the pipeline's binder call and an affinity class (strong, binder, weak, non-binding), with the peptide's length and origin (mutant, wild type or input sequence) and, for variant input, its gene and consequence. renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: affinity_rank_scatter
  title: IC50 against percentile rank
  description: |-
    Each point is one prediction of a peptide against an allele: its predicted IC50 on the horizontal axis and its percentile rank on the vertical axis, coloured by the tool. It answers whether a tool's affinity and rank agree and where its binder call falls.
    How to read: a lower IC50 and a lower rank both mean stronger binding, so confident binders sit at the lower left. A tool whose points form a clear edge has a rank cut-off that decides its binder call. A tool with no IC50 does not appear here.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line is 500 nM, an IC50 below which peptides are usually considered binders. The binder call of each tool uses its own rank rule, a rank of 2 or less for MHCflurry, NetMHCpan and MixMHCpred, 5 or less for NetMHCIIpan.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Predicted IC50 (nM)
    y_title: Percentile rank
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    reference_line: vertical
    reference_value: 500
    reference_label: 500 nM, usual binder limit
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    x: ic50_nm
    y: percentile_rank
    label: sequence
    color: predictor

  title: IC50 of one tool against another
  description: |-
    Each point is a peptide scored against an allele by two tools: the IC50 of the first on the horizontal axis and of the second on the vertical axis, coloured by whether both, neither or only one calls a binder. It answers how consistent the tools are.
    How to read: points on the diagonal get the same affinity from both tools. Points far from it, or coloured as one tool only, are peptides whose call depends on the tool and should be confirmed before they are trusted.

  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: IC50 of the first tool (nM)
    y_title: IC50 of the second tool (nM)
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    reference_line: diagonal
    reference_label: Both tools agree
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    x: ic50_a_nm
    y: ic50_b_nm
    label: sequence
    color: agreement

    x_title: Wild-type IC50 (nM)
    y_title: Mutant IC50 (nM)
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    reference_line: diagonal
    reference_label: Mutant equals wild type
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    x: wt_ic50_nm
    y: ic50_nm
    label: sequence
    color: pair_call

tools.name: FAMSA
tools.description: Progressive multiple sequence alignment for large protein families: the aligned rows of every family, and how conserved each residue of the family representative is across its members.

output.name: Family alignment
output.description: The protein module's MSA table: one row per aligned sequence of every family alignment, the family representative first (rank 0), with each row's identity to the representative and the share of the representative it covers. Capped at 500 rows per family in file order.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: family_msa
  title: Family alignment
  description: |-
    Each row is a sequence of a protein family, aligned to the family representative on top, and each column is an alignment position coloured by residue type. It answers how well the members of a family line up and where they differ.
    How to read: columns of one colour are conserved positions, and a block of gaps marks an insertion or a member that does not cover that region. Sequences with a low identity to the representative are the divergent members, which may be fragments or distant relatives. Brush columns to follow the residues on the structure and the sequence track.
    Lines and annotations: this module takes the first row of each alignment file as the family representative and measures each row's identity against it. The consensus row and the conservation bars are computed from the displayed rows, which this module caps at 500 per family in file order, not a FAMSA setting.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27670777/
  kind: msa
  roles:
    msa_id: msa_id
    seq_id: seq_id
    sequence: aligned_sequence
    rank: rank
    identity: identity

output.name: Residue conservation
output.description: The protein module's residue table for every family: one row per residue of the family representative, numbered along its ungapped sequence, with a 0-1 conservation score (entropy of the alignment column over the 20 amino acids, discounted by gaps), its class (conserved, intermediate, variable), the column consensus and its occupancy. The representative sequence rides on every row, which is what a 3D tile folds in resolve mode.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: conservation_track
  title: Conservation along the sequence
  description: |-
    Each position is a residue of the family representative, with a lane for its conservation score and a lane for its conservation class. It answers which stretches of the protein are conserved across the family and which vary.
    How to read: runs of high scores mark constrained regions, often a fold core or an active site, and low runs mark loops or variable linkers. Brush a stretch to light up the same residues on the structure and the alignment.
    Lines and annotations: the score is one minus the normalised Shannon entropy of the alignment column, discounted by the share of gaps, so 1 is an invariant gap-free column. The classes are cut at 0.7 and 0.4 by this catalog's recipe; they are not published cut-offs.
  kind: sequence_track
  config:
    value_label: Conservation score
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    residue: residue
    value: value
    category: category

- component: advanced_viz
  id: conservation_structure
  title: Conservation on the structure
  description: |-
    The 3D structure of the family representative, folded on demand from its sequence and coloured by the residue conservation score. It answers where the conserved residues sit in space.
    How to read: a conserved patch on the surface suggests a binding or catalytic site, while conserved residues buried in the core usually hold the fold. Variable residues on the surface are typical of regions free to change.
    Lines and annotations: the colour is the conservation score, the same one drawn along the sequence, from 0 for a diverse column to 1 for an invariant one.
    Note: the structure is a prediction made from the sequence, not an experimental one.
  kind: molecule_3d
  config:
    color_mode: value
  roles:
    position: position
    entity: entity
    value: value
    category: category
    sequence: sequence

tools.name: FCS-adaptor

tools.name: nf-core/funcscan
tools.description: Run-level joins across the four nf-core/funcscan screens: a per-sample screening hub (ARG, AMP, BGC and CAZyme headline counts), a per-contig annotation summary that puts the four screens on the same locus, and the software versions the run recorded.

output.name: Contig annotation
output.description: One row per annotated contig with how many features each nf-core/funcscan screen put on it, the contig length and coverage when the contig name carries them (SPAdes or MEGAHIT headers, null otherwise), and the feature density that follows. This is the annotation layer the four screens share: they all report the contig a feature sits on, even though the annotation step itself publishes no table.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: contig_feature_scatter
  title: Features against contig length
  description: |-
    Each point is a contig: its length on the horizontal axis and the number of features the four screens put on it on the vertical axis, sized by feature density and coloured by the screen with the most features there. It answers which contigs carry an unusual load of resistance genes, peptides, clusters or CAZymes.
    How to read: long contigs carry more of everything, so the interesting points are the short contigs high on the plot, which are dense loci. A contig with features from several screens is a candidate for a mobile or multi-function element, so open the screening tabs for it.
    Note: length is read from the contig name when the assembler wrote it there, so contigs without it are not drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Contig length (bp)
    y_title: Features on the contig
    log_x: true
  roles:
    x: contig_length
    y: features
    label: contig
    color: top_screen
    size: features_per_kb

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: screen_composition
  title: Findings per screen and sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is the number of findings one screen (resistance genes, peptide candidates, cluster regions or CAZymes) made in a sample, on a log axis, grouped by screen. It answers how the four screens compare within and between samples.
    How to read: the screens differ by orders of magnitude, so read the log axis rather than the bar heights. A screen missing from a sample returned nothing there, which can mean it was not enabled.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  code: |-
    # The colour channel belongs to the screen here, so the dashboard's
    # analysis groups take the facet axis instead: one band of samples per
    # group. Spread into the reshape below too, or the unpivot would drop the
    # annotation column before the facet could read it.
    index_cols = ["sample"] + [c for c in depictio_group_by if c != "sample"]
    grp_col = depictio_group_by[0] if depictio_group_by else None
  
    # wide -> long so each screen becomes its own bar colour
    df_modified = df.unpivot(
        index=index_cols,
        on=["arg_hits", "amp_candidates", "bgc_regions", "cazymes"],
        variable_name="screen",
        value_name="findings",
    ).filter(pl.col("findings") > 0)
  
    labels = {
        "arg_hits": "ARG hits",
        "amp_candidates": "AMP candidates",
        "bgc_regions": "BGC regions",
        "cazymes": "CAZymes",
    }
    df_modified = df_modified.with_columns(
        pl.col("screen").replace_strict(labels, default=pl.col("screen")).alias("screen")
    )
  
    fig = px.bar(
        df_modified.to_pandas(),
        x="sample",
        y="findings",
        color="screen",
        barmode="group",
        log_y=True,
        facet_col=grp_col,
        category_orders={"screen": list(labels.values())},
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        yaxis_title="Findings (log scale)",
        legend_title_text="Screen",
        margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 80},
    )
    if grp_col:
        # Each panel keeps only its own samples, and its title is the group
        # name rather than the annotation column's name and an equals sign.
        fig.update_xaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
        fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1]))
    else:
        fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Sample")

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Fusion allele ratio of each partner
  description: |-
    Each point is a fusion call: the fusion allele ratio against its 5' partner on the horizontal axis and against its 3' partner on the vertical axis. The colour is the protein consequence and the size the number of supporting reads. It answers how much each partner's own expression is taken up by the fusion.
    How to read: a point in the top right is a fusion that is large compared with both wild-type partners, which is the pattern of a driver. A point near an axis means one partner is still expressed mostly in its normal form. Compare with the read counts in the table before trusting a low-support point.
    Lines and annotations: both axes are logarithmic, and a small constant of 0.01 is added to each ratio so that a ratio of zero can be placed. No cut-off is drawn because FusionInspector publishes none for these ratios.
  code: |-
    # FAR can be reported as 0, which a log axis cannot place, so shift both.
    eps = 0.01
    df_modified = df.with_columns(
        (pl.col("far_left") + eps).alias("far_left_shift"),
        (pl.col("far_right") + eps).alias("far_right_shift"),
    )
  
    fig = px.scatter(
        df_modified.to_pandas(),
        x="far_left_shift", y="far_right_shift",
        color="prot_fusion_type", size="supporting_reads",
        size_max=24, opacity=0.8, log_x=True, log_y=True,
        hover_name="fusion",
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="FAR 5' partner (log)",
        yaxis_title="FAR 3' partner (log)",
        legend_title_text="Protein fusion type",
        margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 48},
    )

Each row is a fusion transcript pair with its read support, expression, allele ratios and protein consequence. It answers which calls to follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.
How to read: sort by supporting reads or by expression, and filter by protein consequence to keep the in-frame calls.

output.name: Fusion protein domains
output.description: The Pfam domains FusionInspector annotates on the 5' and 3' partner of each fusion protein, unpivoted from the packed PFAM_LEFT / PFAM_RIGHT fields into one row per domain with its amino-acid span and e-value.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fusion_domains
  title: Domains along the fusion protein
  description: |-
    Each block is a Pfam domain placed along the fusion protein, one lane per partner, and the colour tells which partner contributes it. It answers which protein domains a fusion keeps from each side.
    How to read: look for a kinase or DNA-binding domain kept intact on the 3' side next to a dimerisation domain from the 5' side, which is the classic activating pattern. A domain that is cut short is probably not functional in the fusion.
    Note: FusionInspector reports Pfam domains with their e-values and applies no cut-off of its own to them, so weak hits can appear.
    Source: https://github.com/FusionInspector/FusionInspector
  kind: fusion_structure
  roles:
    fusion_id: fusion
    partner: partner
    feature: domain
    start: domain_start
    end: domain_end
    colour_by: partner

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_lollipop
  title: Domain positions per fusion
  description: |-
    Each stem is a Pfam domain at the amino-acid position where it starts, drawn on one lane per fusion and coloured by the partner that contributes it. It answers how domains are distributed across fusions.
    How to read: domains from the 5' partner cluster at the start of the protein and those of the 3' partner come after the breakpoint. A lane with stems from only one partner is a fusion whose other side adds no annotated domain.
  kind: lollipop
  config:
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    feature_id: fusion
    position: domain_start
    category: partner
    label: domain

tools.name: fusion-report
tools.description: Collects and compares the calls of several fusion detection tools in one report.

output.name: Caller evidence
output.description: Long form of the per-caller evidence strings fusion-report writes next to each fusion: one row per fusion and caller, with the read support that caller reported normalised to a single comparable count.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: evidence_dot_plot
  title: Evidence per caller and fusion
  description: |-
    Each dot is a fusion reported by one caller: its colour is the read support on a log scale and its size is the share of the fusion's total support that this caller holds. It answers which callers back each fusion and how strongly.
    How to read: a fusion with dots in several columns is found by several callers, which is the main reason to trust it. A fusion with a single dot rests on one caller. Compare colours within a caller, since callers count evidence differently.
    Lines and annotations: the colour scale is log10 of supporting reads plus 1, where the read count is normalised from each caller's own evidence fields by the recipe.
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: caller
    gene: fusion
    mean_expression: log_support
    frac_expressing: evidence_fraction

_render.title: Evidence per caller and fusion
_render.description:
Each dot is a fusion reported by one caller: its colour is the read support on a log scale and its size is the share of the fusion's total support that this caller holds. It answers which callers back each fusion and how strongly.
How to read: a fusion with dots in several columns is found by several callers, which is the main reason to trust it. A fusion with a single dot rests on one caller. Compare colours within a caller, since callers count evidence differently.
Lines and annotations: the colour scale is log10 of supporting reads plus 1, where the read count is normalised from each caller's own evidence fields by the recipe.

output.name: Fusion consensus
output.description: One row per fusion and sample, with the knowledge bases that already know it, the Fusion Indication Index fusion-report ranks by and a 0/1 flag per caller the run executed, named after the tool. The sample is read off the file name. The caller flags are the set columns a caller-concordance UpSet reads.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: caller_upset
  title: Caller agreement
  description: |-
    Each bar is a combination of callers and its height the number of fusions that exactly those callers reported, with the bars on the left giving each caller's total. It answers which callers agree on a fusion and which find calls alone.
    How to read: tall bars at high degree, where most callers agree, are the safest fusions to follow up. Fusions seen by one caller only are the most likely false positives, because the callers use different approaches. A caller with a large private bar adds sensitivity and noise in the same measure.
    Lines and annotations: bars are coloured by the number of callers in the combination, the degree of the intersection.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  kind: upset_plot
  config:
    color_intersections_by: degree

_render.title: Caller agreement
_render.description:
Each bar is a combination of callers and its height the number of fusions that exactly those callers reported, with the bars on the left giving each caller's total. It answers which callers agree on a fusion and which find calls alone.
How to read: tall bars at high degree, where most callers agree, are the safest fusions to follow up. Fusions seen by one caller only are the most likely false positives, because the callers use different approaches. A caller with a large private bar adds sensitivity and noise in the same measure.
Lines and annotations: bars are coloured by the number of callers in the combination, the degree of the intersection.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fii_lollipop
  title: Fusions ranked by indication index
  description: |-
    Each lollipop is a fusion placed at its rank in fusion-report's ordering, coloured by how many callers found it and sized by its Fusion Indication Index. It answers which fusions fusion-report puts first and how many callers back them.
    How to read: the leftmost, large lollipops are the best candidates. A top-ranked fusion found by one caller only ranks high on database evidence alone, so look at the caller evidence tab before trusting it.
    Lines and annotations: the index is computed by fusion-report as 0.5 times the share of callers that found the fusion plus 0.5 times a weighted database score, with COSMIC and Mitelman weighted 50 each and FusionGDB2 0. It is a ranking score and not a probability.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  kind: lollipop
  config:
    top_n_labels: 10
  roles:
    feature_id: fusion
    position: rank
    category: tool_support
    effect: fii
    label: fusion

_render.title: Fusions ranked by indication index
_render.description:

Lines and annotations: the index is computed by fusion-report as 0.5 times the share of callers that found the fusion plus 0.5 times a weighted database score, with COSMIC and Mitelman weighted 50 each and FusionGDB2 0. It is a ranking score and not a probability.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Fusion Indication Index per fusion
  description: |-
    Each bar is a fusion with its Fusion Indication Index, coloured by how many callers found it. It answers how strong the combined caller and database evidence is for each fusion.
    How to read: a high bar in the colour of several callers is a fusion both found by the tools and known to the databases. A short bar means few callers or no known database record.
    Lines and annotations: the index mixes caller agreement and database knowledge with equal weight, and database weights of COSMIC 50, Mitelman 50 and FusionGDB2 0.
     The dashed line is the median Fusion Indication Index of this table, a
    reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut- off of fusion-report.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: fusion
    y: fii
    color: tool_support
    labels:
      fusion: Fusion
      fii: Fusion Indication Index
      tool_support: Callers
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: fii

Lines and annotations: the index mixes caller agreement and database knowledge with equal weight, and database weights of COSMIC 50, Mitelman 50 and FusionGDB2 0.
 The dashed line is the median Fusion Indication Index of this table, a
reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut- off of fusion-report.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md

tools.name: GenomeScope
tools.description: Genome size, heterozygosity and repeat content from a read k-mer spectrum.

output.name: Genome profile from reads
output.description: GenomeScope's fit to the read k-mer spectrum: the haploid genome length, the share of it in repeats, the heterozygosity and the read error rate, each as a min to max range. The haploid length is the size an assembly should approach; a high heterozygosity warns that a collapsed assembly will carry duplicated haplotigs, and a poor model fit that the other numbers are not to be trusted.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Haploid genome length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median over read sets of GenomeScope's upper estimate of the haploid genome length, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how large the genome is expected to be before any assembly.
    How to read: an assembly total close to this length is complete in size. A total well above it suggests duplicated haplotypes, and one well below suggests missing sequence. Read sets that disagree point to different genomes or to poor fits.
  column: haploid_length_max
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: upper estimate per read set, with its spread
  headline: true

tools.name: GSEA
tools.description: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA).

output.name: GSEA enrichment report
output.description: Gene sets enriched at one pole of a contrast, from the report tables a pre-ranked GSEA run publishes. Neither the contrast nor the pole is a column of those files, so the recipe recovers both from the file name and stacks every report into one frame. The leading-edge percentage is parsed out of the string GSEA writes for a human reader, and an FDR q-value of zero, which is what GSEA writes below its resolution, is clipped at the run's own floor rather than sent to infinity.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: gsea_dotplot
  title: Enriched gene sets
  description: |-
    Each dot is a gene set: its normalised enrichment score (NES) on the horizontal axis, its size by the number of genes in the set and its colour by the FDR q-value. It answers which pathways move together at one end of the ranked gene list, and in which direction.
    How to read: a set far from zero with a dark colour is strongly and confidently enriched. A positive NES means enrichment at the top of the ranked list and a negative one at the bottom, so compare both poles before concluding. Sets with few genes can reach a high score by chance, so look at the size too.
    Lines and annotations: this plot keeps only sets with an FDR q-value up to 0.25, the cut-off at which the GSEA report highlights sets as most likely to give interesting hypotheses. The report itself still gives results for every set, and the table below lists them all. The user guide advises a stricter 5% when the run has few samples and permutes gene sets rather than phenotypes.
    Source: https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/#GSEA/GSEA_User_Guide/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16199517/
  kind: enrichment
  config:
    padj_threshold: 0.25
    top_n: 20
    default_colour_by: neg_log10_padj
  roles:
    term: term
    nes: nes
    padj: fdr_qvalue
    gene_count: size
    source: phenotype

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ani_vs_alignment
  title: Closest reference identity against alignment fraction
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin: its average nucleotide identity (ANI) to the closest GTDB species representative on the horizontal axis and the fraction of the genome aligned to it on the vertical axis, coloured by phylum. It answers how confidently a bin matches a known species.
    How to read: points to the upper right, with high identity and alignment, are assigned to a species. A point with a low alignment fraction or low identity is a novel lineage or a poor bin, and may stop at a higher rank. The ANI needed is specific to each species, typically 95 percent, so no vertical line is drawn.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the minimum alignment fraction of 0.5, the GTDB-Tk default (--min_af) for assigning a genome to a species during the ANI screen. The species-specific ANI radius is typically 95 percent.
    Source: https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/faq.html and https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/commands/classify.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Average nucleotide identity to the closest reference (%)
    y_title: Alignment fraction to the closest reference
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 0.5
    reference_label: Minimum alignment fraction (0.5)
    top_n_labels: 5
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: closest_ani
    y: closest_af
    label: bin_id
    color: phylum

renders._yaml:

  id: arg_island_track
  title: Resistance genes along contigs
  description: |-
    Each arrow is one resistance gene hit placed on its contig, pointing in the direction of the gene and coloured by the screening tool that reported it. It answers whether resistance genes sit together on the same contig.
    How to read: several arrows head to tail on one contig suggest a resistance island or a mobile cassette, which an aggregate over drug classes cannot show. Arrows of different colours on the same locus are the same gene found by several tools, so agreement between tools raises confidence in the call.
    Note: hAMRonization does not harmonise gene names or drug classes across tools, so one gene can appear under different symbols.
    Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  kind: gene_arrow_track
  roles:
    contig: contig
    feature_id: gene_symbol
    start: start
    end: stop
    strand: strand
    class: tool
    label: gene_symbol

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: pr_curve
  title: Precision and recall across thresholds
  description: |-
    Each point is the precision and recall of the SNP calls that pass one variant quality threshold, joined into a curve. It answers how much recall is given up to buy precision when the callset is filtered harder.
    How to read: a curve that stays near the top right across thresholds means the quality score separates true from false calls well. A curve that drops fast as recall falls means filtering removes true calls as readily as false ones. Pick the threshold where precision stops improving.
    Lines and annotations: the area under the curve is computed from the swept points of this table, so it is a data-defined summary and not a published cut-off. Recall is TP over TP plus FN and precision is TP over TP plus FP, as hap.py defines them.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  kind: roc_pr_curve
  roles:
    recall: recall
    precision: precision
    threshold: quality

tools.name: HiC-Pro
tools.description: Maps, pairs and filters Hi-C reads down to valid 3C products, then splits the survivors into cis and trans contacts. Its `stats/` directory is the run's valid-pair funnel, one small key/value file per processing stage.

output.name: Read-pair fates
output.description: The same HiC-Pro statistics as one weighted row per read-pair fate, mapping to restriction-fragment filter to contact class, so the funnel can be drawn as a flow and the cis/trans split as a composition.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: pair_flow_sankey
  title: Fate of the read pairs
  description: |-
    Each band is a group of read pairs flowing from how they mapped, through the restriction-fragment filter, to the contact class they end in. It answers where the sequenced pairs are lost on the way to valid contacts.
    How to read: a thick band into Lost at an early step is the main source of loss. A large dangling end or religation band points to a problem in the digestion or ligation, and a thin valid pairs band means most of the sequencing did not yield contacts. Compare samples through the table tile.
    Lines and annotations: dangling ends are unligated fragments with both reads on the same restriction fragment, religation is the ligation of juxtaposed fragments, and only valid pairs between two different fragments become contacts. No cut-off is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  kind: sankey
  config:
    value_label: Read pairs
  roles:
    steps:
    - mapping
    - filtering
    - contacts

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  title: Valid-pair funnel
  description: |-
    The hero number is the read pairs sequenced, and the stages below it show how many remain after pairing, the restriction-fragment filter, de-duplication, the cis split and the long-range cut. The strip gives the median and the largest sample. It answers how much of the sequencing ends as useful long-range contacts.
    How to read: each stage should keep a sizeable share of the one before. A sharp drop at the restriction-fragment filter points to the digestion or ligation, and one at de-duplication to a low-complexity library.
    Lines and annotations: long-range contacts are cis pairs more than 20 kb apart and short-range ones are 20 kb apart or less, as HiC-Pro counts them.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/scripts/merge_valid_interactions.sh
  column: total_pairs
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: attrition
  attrition_cols:
  - reported_pairs
  - valid_pairs
  - valid_pairs_rmdup
  - cis_pairs
  - cis_long_range
  caption: pairs left at each stage

output.name: Cumulative coverage
output.description: BamTools' per-depth base counts turned into the fraction of bases covered at least each depth, one curve per DNA sample. A tumor sequenced deeper than its normal sits to the right; a curve that drops early marks a sample below the depth the somatic callers need.

  description: |-
    Each curve is a DNA sample: the fraction of bases covered at least to each depth. It answers how much of the target is sequenced deeply enough to call variants.
    How to read: a curve that stays high and drops late means deep, even coverage. A tumour sequenced deeper than its normal sits to the right. A curve that drops early marks a sample too shallow for the somatic callers you plan to use.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. BamTools documents no coverage floor, so judge the depth against the requirements of your callers.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/bam-tools/README.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Coverage depth (x)
    y_title: Fraction of bases at or above depth
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: coverage
    y: fraction_at_least

tools.name: HMMER
tools.description: Profile hidden Markov model searches: which protein families each sequence carries, where on the sequence each domain sits, and how confident the hit is.

output.name: Family profile HMM
output.description: The profile HMM of every protein family as a long table, one row per match state and letter: the emission probability, the letter height in bits, the state's information content, insert and delete behaviour, occupancy and the consensus, RF and CS annotation. Where the family's hmmalign alignment and representative are known, each state also says which residue of the representative it sits on, so a state selected in the logo selects that residue in the family's residue table and structure.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: family_logo
  title: Family profile logo
  description: |-
    Each column is a match state of the family's profile HMM, drawn as a stack of amino acids whose height is the state's information content in bits. It answers which positions of the family are conserved and which residues are allowed there.
    How to read: tall stacks are conserved positions, often the functional or structural core of the family, and low flat stacks tolerate substitutions. The lanes under the logo show how often a state is occupied and how likely and how long insertions are, so a gappy region is a poor place to trust the alignment. Select a state to see the residue it matches in the representative structure.
    Lines and annotations: the total height of a stack is the state's relative entropy in bits, as in hmmlogo. The tile draws only residues more frequent than background, hmmlogo's above-background option. The consensus, RF and CS rows come from the profile file annotation.
    Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  kind: hmm_logo
  config:
    height_mode: relent_abovebg
    show_consensus: true
  roles:
    entity: entity
    position: position
    model: hmm_name
    state: hmm_position
    letter: hmm_letter
    emission: emission
    insert_prob: insert_prob
    insert_length: insert_length
    occupancy: occupancy
    consensus: consensus
    rf: rf
    cs: cs

output.name: Family member coverage of the HMM
output.description: One row per member of every family alignment (hmmalign against the family HMM): the stretch of the model it covers (first and last match state, and the share of the model between them), the member's residues at those two states and its length. The columns of a domain hit table without the search statistics (E-value and score are null), so the lane under an HMM logo draws the members' coverage and a domain architecture shows which members are fragments.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: member_architecture
  title: Family member coverage of the model
  description: |-
    Each row is a member of a family alignment: a backbone for its sequence with a bar for the stretch that aligns to the family HMM, coloured by family. It answers whether the members cover the whole model or only part of it.
    How to read: members whose bar spans the whole backbone are full-length. A zigzag edge marks a member that starts after the first or ends before the last match state of the HMM, so it is a fragment or a truncated sequence. Many fragments suggest the family needs a closer look before building a structure or a logo from it.
    Lines and annotations: the zigzag edge is drawn from the first and last HMM state each member covers against the length of the model, with no score cut-off, since an hmmalign alignment carries no E-value.
    Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  kind: domain_architecture
  config:
    color_by: label
  roles:
    entity: entity
    start: ali_from
    end: ali_to
    label: label
    protein_length: protein_length
    hmm_from: hmm_from
    hmm_to: hmm_to
    hmm_length: hmm_length
    hmm_coverage: hmm_coverage

output.name: Domain hits (hmmsearch)
output.description: One row per domain hit of an hmmsearch run: the sequence, the family HMM and the database it came from, the envelope span on the sequence, the independent E-value and bit score of the domain, and how much of the HMM the alignment covers. renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_score_scatter
  title: Domain score against model coverage
  description: |-
    Each point is a domain hit: the share of the family HMM its alignment covers on the horizontal axis and its bit score on the vertical axis, coloured by the database the family comes from. It answers which hits are both complete and confident.
    How to read: hits in the upper right cover the whole model with a high score, the reliable family assignments. Hits to the left only touch part of the model and are fragments or partial domains. A high score with low coverage can still be a true short match, so check the architecture tile.
    Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. A score threshold is specific to each family, and Pfam stores gathering bit score thresholds inside each model, which hmmsearch applies only on request with its cut_ga option.
    Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Share of the HMM covered
    y_title: Domain bit score
    top_n_labels: 10
  roles:
    x: hmm_coverage
    y: dom_score
    label: label
    color: source

renders._yaml:

  id: tss_distance

  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample: the fraction of its peaks that fall in each bin of distance to the nearest transcription start site, 250 bp wide as set by this catalog's recipe. It answers whether the peaks concentrate at promoters.

    reference_x: 0
    reference_label: TSS
    shaded_bands:

      - 100
      - Promoter-TSS window
    x_title: Distance to nearest TSS (bp)
    y_title: Fraction of peaks
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: distance_to_tss
    y: fraction

output.name: SAV run summary per lane and read
output.description: Cluster density, clusters passing filter, phasing and prephasing, Q30 share, yield and PhiX error rate for every lane and read, from the InterOp summary table (interop_summary --csv=1), the numbers Sequencing Analysis Viewer shows.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: lane_read_error
  title: Error rate and Q30 per lane and read
  description: |-
    Each dot is a read of a lane: its colour is the PhiX error rate and its size the share of bases at Q30 or above. It answers which lane and read combinations sequenced well.
    How to read: a large, pale dot is a read with high quality and a low error rate. A small, dark dot is a weak read to compare with the other lanes. Index reads have no PhiX error rate, so their colour is empty.
    Source: https://support-docs.illumina.com/SW/SAV/Content/SW/SAV/Metrics.htm
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: lane_label
    gene: read_label

    frac_expressing: frac_q30

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: phasing_scatter
  title: Phasing against prephasing
  description: |-
    Each point is a lane of one read: the phasing rate (horizontal) against the prephasing rate (vertical), coloured by the read. It answers whether the chemistry keeps molecules in step along the read.
    How to read: points near the origin are reads where clusters stay in step. A point that sits far from the others is a lane whose chemistry or flow cell deviates, and it is the one to compare with its Q30 and error rate. Index reads report a phasing and prephasing of 0 in the InterOp summary, so read them as not measured rather than perfect.
    Note: the rates are the values Real-Time Analysis uses, estimated from the first 25 cycles of each read.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median prephasing of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Illumina Interop.
    Source: https://support-docs.illumina.com/SW/SAV/Content/SW/SAV/Metrics.htm
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Phasing (% per cycle)
    y_title: Prephasing (% per cycle)
    legend_pos: bottom
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
  roles:
    x: phasing
    y: prephasing
    label: lane_label
    color: read_label

tools.name: InterProScan
tools.description: Protein signature matches from the InterPro member databases, with the integrated InterPro entry, GO terms and pathways of every match.

output.name: InterPro signature matches
output.description: One row per signature match: the protein, the member database (analysis), the signature and its description, the matched span, the match E-value or score, and the InterPro entry, GO terms and pathways it is integrated into. Spans follow the domain table convention (start, end, label, source), so a sequence track can draw them.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: signature_matches
  title: Signature matches
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of signature matches, with the number of distinct proteins that have one beside it, and the bars rank the member databases that report them. It answers how much of the protein set is annotated and by which database.
    How to read: proteins without a match write no row, so compare the protein count with the input size to see the unannotated share. A database that dominates may simply be the one with the broadest signatures.
    Source: https://interproscan-docs.readthedocs.io/en/v5/OutputFormats.html
  column: entity
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - nunique
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: source
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: matches, by member database
  headline: true

  id: insert_length_profile
  title: Insert length distribution
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample: the share of its full-length non-chimeric reads in each 100 bp bin of insert length. It answers what transcript sizes the library captured.

A curve piled at short lengths points to degraded RNA or fragmentation, and a hard cut on the right to a size selection.   kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Insert length (bp)
    y_title: Share of FLNC reads per 100 bp (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:

    x: length_bp
    y: pct

  title: Allele frequency along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a variant at its genome position, with its allele frequency on the vertical axis, coloured by its predicted effect. It answers where along the genome variants sit and how many are fixed rather than minor.

  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_threshold: 0.75
    score_kind: Allele frequency
    color_by_columns:
    - EFFECT
    - sample
    default_color_by: EFFECT
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    chr: CHROM
    pos: POS
    score: AF
    feature: GENE

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: variant_genome_view
  title: Variants along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a variant call at its genome position, with its allele frequency on the vertical axis, coloured by variant type (SNV, insertion or deletion). It answers where in the genome calls cluster and how many are near-fixed.
    How to read: points above the line are the high-frequency calls that would be integrated into a consensus, and points below it are minor variants. A stretch with many low-frequency calls can mean a mixed sample or a poorly covered region, so check the depth track.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an allele frequency of 0.75, the cut-off nf-core/viralrecon documents for variants integrated into the consensus genome. iVar's own default minimum frequency to report a variant is 0.03, and viralrecon runs it at 0.25.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: Allele frequency
    score_threshold: 0.75
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: pos
    score: af
    feature: variant_key
    sample: genome_id
    category: variant_type

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: af_vs_depth
  title: Allele frequency against depth
  description: |-
    Each point is a variant call: the read depth at its position on the horizontal axis and its allele frequency on the vertical axis, coloured by frequency class. It answers which calls rest on enough reads to be trusted.
    How to read: fixed calls sit at the top at any depth. Calls at low frequency and low depth, in the bottom left, are the least reliable because a handful of reads decides the frequency. Minor calls at high depth are credible intra-host variants.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an allele frequency of 0.75, the cut-off nf-core/viralrecon documents for variants integrated into the consensus genome. The Fixed, Major and Minor classes (at least 0.9, 0.5 to 0.9 and under 0.5) are this table's own grouping, not published cut-offs. viralrecon calls variants from a depth of 10 reads by default, while iVar's own default minimum depth is 0.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    log_x: true
    x_title: Total read depth at the position
    y_title: Allele frequency
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 0.75
    reference_label: Consensus cut-off (0.75)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: total_dp
    y: af
    label: variant_key
    color: frequency_class

tools.name: Jellyfish
tools.description: K-mer counting and the read k-mer spectrum.

output.name: Read k-mer spectrum
output.description: The k-mer multiplicity histogram of each read set, cut past the main peak. The main peak sits at the k-mer depth of the sequencing; a second peak at half that depth is the heterozygous share of the genome, and a long right tail the repeats. It is the curve GenomeScope fits, so a genome size estimate can be checked against it by eye.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: kmer_spectrum
  title: Read k-mer spectrum
  description: |-
    Each point is a multiplicity: how many distinct k-mers occur that many times in the reads, with one curve per read set on a log vertical axis. It answers what sequencing depth the reads reach and whether the genome is heterozygous or repetitive.
    How to read: the k-mers piled up near a multiplicity of 1 are mostly sequencing errors. The main peak is the depth of the genome, a smaller peak at half of it is the heterozygous share, and peaks at three and four times that half are repeats.
    Note: GenomeScope needs at least 15x coverage of the haploid genome to fit well.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tbenavi1/genomescope2.0/master/README.md and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32188846/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: K-mer multiplicity (times seen in the reads)
    y_title: Distinct k-mers
    log_y: true
  roles:
    series: read_set
    x: multiplicity
    y: kmers

tools.name: LAST
tools.description: Pairwise genome alignment: how much of a target genome each query aligns to one-to-one, at what identity and divergence, with which substitution spectrum and fitted scoring parameters, and where on the target the long alignments land.

output.name: One-to-one alignment identity
output.description: One row per pairwise genome alignment from the one-line summary last-split writes for MultiQC: aligned length, percent identity with and without gap columns, and the sequence count and length of both genomes. The share of each genome the one-to-one alignment covers is derived alongside, so a distant genome (lower identity) can be told apart from a fragmented one (lower coverage at the same identity).

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: identity_vs_coverage
  title: Identity against coverage of the target
  description: |-
    Each point is a query genome aligned to the target: the share of the target its one-to-one alignment covers on the horizontal axis and the percent identity on the vertical axis. Size is the aligned length and colour the number of sequences in the query. It answers whether a genome is distant or only fragmented.
    How to read: identity falls with divergence, so a distant genome sits low. Coverage also falls with divergence and with assembly gaps, so a point to the left of genomes of similar identity lost coverage to a fragmented assembly, which the colour confirms. Open the distance and parameter tiles for the same pairs.
    Note: there is no standard way to compute nucleotide identity, so the value here is the one nf-core/pairgenomealign reports (gaps counted as mismatches).
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median alignment identity of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of LAST.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    color_col: query_sequences
    x_title: Target covered by the one-to-one alignment (%)
    y_title: Alignment identity (%)
  roles:

    y: percent_identity
    label: query
    size: aligned_bp

The hero number is the median share of the target genome covered by the one-to-one alignment, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how much of the target the queries reach.
How to read: coverage below 100 percent is expected, since a one-to-one alignment leaves out duplicated and unalignable regions. A low tail marks genomes that are divergent or fragmented.
renders.caption: coverage across genomes

  caption: genome length, with its spread

output.name: Substitution matrix and distances
output.description: The substitution table last-split counts over the one-to-one alignment, summarised per genome pair: alignment blocks, identical and substituted columns, transitions against transversions, gap columns on either side, the p-distance with its JC69, F81, K80 and T92 corrections, and the substitution spectrum (the share of each of the 12 directed substitutions). Distances rank the queries by divergence from the target; the spectrum shows whether the substitution process looks alike across them.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: substitution_spectrum
  title: Substitution spectrum by query
  description: |-
    Each cell is the share of one directed substitution (a target base aligned to a different query base) among all substitutions in the one-to-one alignment of a query genome. It answers whether the substitution process looks alike across the queries.
    How to read: transitions (A to G, G to A, C to T, T to C) usually hold the largest shares, and genomes of similar divergence cluster together. A query whose row differs from the rest points to a different mutation process or a lower quality assembly.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  kind: complex_heatmap
  roles:
    index: query
    value_columns:
    - A_to_C_pct
    - A_to_G_pct
    - A_to_T_pct
    - C_to_A_pct
    - C_to_G_pct
    - C_to_T_pct
    - G_to_A_pct
    - G_to_C_pct
    - G_to_T_pct
    - T_to_A_pct
    - T_to_C_pct
    - T_to_G_pct

_render.title: Substitution spectrum by query
_render.description:

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: saturation_scatter
  title: Transition to transversion ratio against distance
  description: |-
    Each point is a query genome: its p-distance to the target on the horizontal axis and its ratio of transitions to transversions on the vertical axis. Size is the number of alignment blocks and colour the number of gap columns on the query side. It answers whether the distant genomes are saturated.
    How to read: the ratio falls as multiple substitutions at one site hide the transitions, so distant genomes sit low and to the right. A point off that trend is a pair whose alignment or assembly deserves a look.
    Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because the expected ratio depends on the species pair and the tool publishes no cut-off.
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    color_col: query_gap_columns
    x_title: Substitutions per aligned column (p-distance)
    y_title: Transitions to transversions ratio
  roles:
    x: p_distance
    y: ts_tv_ratio
    label: query
    size: blocks

output.name: Synteny links
output.description: The one-to-one alignment read as links between a target locus and a query locus, from the PSL export (--export_aln_to psl), which carries coordinates but no sequence. Each alignment is placed at its midpoint on both genomes, weighted by its matching bases and classed by orientation; query sequence names are prefixed so shared names such as chr1 stay two arcs. The longest alignments of each pair are kept, the collinear blocks a synteny ring shows.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: synteny_ring
  title: Synteny between target and query
  description: |-
    Each chord is one of the longest one-to-one alignments, linking its locus on a target chromosome to its locus on a query chromosome, coloured by orientation and weighted by its matching bases. It answers which chromosomes of the two genomes share long collinear blocks.
    How to read: bundles of chords between the same two chromosomes are conserved synteny. Chords that fan out from one chromosome point to rearrangements, and inverted chords mark blocks that are reversed in the query.
    Note: only the longest alignments of each pair are kept, so short blocks do not appear.
  kind: genome_chord
  config:
    colour_by: category
  roles:
    chrom_a: chrom_a
    pos_a: pos_a
    chrom_b: chrom_b
    pos_b: pos_b
    label: label
    weight: weight
    category: category
    sample: query

_render.title: Synteny between target and query
_render.description:
Each chord is one of the longest one-to-one alignments, linking its locus on a target chromosome to its locus on a query chromosome, coloured by orientation and weighted by its matching bases. It answers which chromosomes of the two genomes share long collinear blocks.
How to read: bundles of chords between the same two chromosomes are conserved synteny. Chords that fan out from one chromosome point to rearrangements, and inverted chords mark blocks that are reversed in the query.
Note: only the longest alignments of each pair are kept, so short blocks do not appear.

tools.name: LINX
tools.description: Clusters structural variants into events, chains them, and annotates the genes they disrupt and the fusions they create.

output.name: Fusion partners along the fused transcript
output.description: Each LINX fusion laid out as two partner lanes along the fused transcript in exon units: the 5' partner's exons up to the fused exon and the 3' partner's exons from its fused exon are kept, the rest are drawn as lost, and the breakpoint sits between them. LINX publishes no residue coordinates per fusion, which is why the axis is the exon rank.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fusion_exon_layout
  title: Exons kept in each fusion
  description: |-
    Each fusion is drawn as two partner lanes in exon units: the exons the fused transcript keeps and the exons it loses are drawn as separate blocks, and the breakpoint sits between the two partners. The colour is the phasing of the fusion. It answers which exons each partner contributes to a fusion.
    How to read: a fusion keeps the 5' partner's exons up to its last fused exon and the 3' partner's exons from its first fused exon on, the FusedExonUp and FusedExonDown LINX reports. Many lost exons on the 3' partner mean a large part of its protein is missing.
    Note: LINX publishes no residue coordinates per fusion, so the axis is the exon rank and not the amino-acid position.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/linx/README.md
  kind: fusion_structure
  roles:
    fusion_id: fusion
    partner: partner
    feature: feature
    start: start
    end: end
    breakpoint: breakpoint
    retained: retained
    colour_by: phased

tools.name: MACS2
tools.description: Model-based analysis of ChIP-seq data, for peak calling.

output.name: Broad peak calls
output.description: Every MACS2 broad peak of every sample in one table, with the region width, its centre and the fold enrichment, p-value and q-value MACS2 reported for it. A broad call has no summit, so the region centre stands in for it.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: broad_peak_significance
  title: Broad region significance along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a broad region at its centre: the chromosome and position on the horizontal axis and its mean significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers where the broad domains lie and how confident each call is.
    How to read: tall points are the most confident regions, and a column of points across samples is a domain called in several libraries. For a broad call the q-value is the mean over the whole region and not a value at a summit. Open the table to inspect a labelled region.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a q-value of 0.05, the default q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak, shown as 1.301 on this axis. MACS2 also links nearby regions with a separate broad cut-off, and its documentation suggests 0.01 as the q-value for broad marks, so a run may use a stricter line.
    Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_kind: -log10 q-value
    score_threshold: 1.30103
    color_by_columns:
    - sample
    default_color_by: sample
    hover_cols:
    - fold_enrichment
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    chr: chr
    pos: midpoint
    score: neg_log10_qvalue
    feature: peak_id
