renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: peak_significance
  title: Peak significance along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a peak at its summit position: the chromosome and position on the horizontal axis and its significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers where the strongest calls lie and whether samples call the same regions.
    How to read: tall points are the most confident peaks, and a column of points across samples is a region called in several libraries. Peak calls from one sample sit in a dense band just above the cut-off, so read this tile for positions and not for the density of calls. Open the table to inspect a labelled peak.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a q-value of 0.05, the default q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak, shown as 1.301 on this axis. A run can set its own cut-off, and the line then no longer matches what the caller used.
    Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_kind: -log10 q-value
    score_threshold: 1.30103
    color_by_columns:
    - sample
    default_color_by: sample
    hover_cols:
    - fold_enrichment
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    chr: chr
    pos: summit
    score: neg_log10_qvalue
    feature: peak_id

  title: Peak enrichment along the genome
  description: |-
    Each mark is a peak placed on its chromosome, with its fold enrichment at the summit over the local background on the vertical axis, one colour per sample. It answers how strong the enrichment is along the genome and where libraries agree.
    How to read: higher marks are peaks with more signal over the control, and overlapping marks of different colours are peaks found in several samples. Pick a chromosome to read it in detail.

  config:
    color_by: sample
    smoothing_window: 0

  description: |-
    Each point is a peak: its fold enrichment at the summit on the horizontal axis and its significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers which peaks are both strongly enriched and confidently called.
    How to read: peaks in the upper right are strong and confident, and are the ones to follow up. A peak with high enrichment but low significance sits in a region with few reads, and the reverse is a broad, modest enrichment. Open the table for the labelled peaks.

    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Fold enrichment
    significance_label: -log10 q-value

tools.name: nf-core/mag
tools.description: Aggregate per-bin and per-contig tables of the nf-core/mag metagenome assembly and binning pipeline.

output.name: Bin summary
output.description: Everything four tools know about each recovered bin in one row: how complete and how clean CheckM2 thinks it is, how it is assembled, what Prokka found in it and what GTDB-Tk calls it. It is the table the whole binning question is settled on, and the only place the MIMAG tier is computed with its RNA criteria included rather than from completeness alone.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: mimag_scatter
  title: Bin completeness against contamination
  description: |-
    Each point is a recovered bin: its completeness on the horizontal axis and its contamination on the vertical axis, both estimated by CheckM2, sized by assembly length and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers which bins are good enough to report as genomes.
    How to read: the best bins sit at the bottom right, complete and clean. Bins above the horizontal line are too contaminated for any tier, and bins left of the vertical line are fragmentary. Open the bin table for the lineage and assembly of a bin before trusting it.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line is 50 percent completeness and the horizontal line 10 percent contamination, the limits of the medium-quality MIMAG tier. The high-quality tier needs more than 90 percent completeness and under 5 percent contamination, together with the 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA genes and at least 18 tRNAs, so a bin can look high quality here and still be medium.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Completeness (%)
    y_title: Contamination (%)
    top_n_labels: 0
    legend_pos: bottom
    quadrants:
      x: 50
      y: 10
      labels:
      - Contaminated
      - Contaminated
      - Low quality
      - Medium quality or better
  roles:
    x: completeness
    y: contamination
    label: bin_id
    color: mimag_tier
    size: total_length

The hero number is the median completeness of the bins, as estimated by CheckM2, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much of a genome a typical bin holds.
How to read: a median above 50 percent means most bins are at least medium quality on this criterion. A long lower tail marks fragmentary bins.
Lines and annotations: the MIMAG standard asks for at least 50 percent completeness for a medium-quality bin and more than 90 percent for a high-quality one.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
_render.caption: median, with its spread

output.name: Contig coverage
output.description: How deeply each contig is covered, once per sample whose reads were mapped back onto the assembly. Length against depth is the plot a binner sees before it decides anything: contigs of one organism sit in a band, and a contig deep in one sample and flat in another belongs to something only one of them carries. Contigs under 1 kbp are left out by the recipe, below the 1500 bp nf-core/mag bins from by default.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_vs_depth
  title: Contig length against depth
  description: |-
    Each point is a contig: its length on the horizontal axis and its read depth in one sample on the vertical axis, sized by its mean depth over all samples and coloured by the sample whose reads were mapped. It answers how coverage varies between contigs and between samples.
    How to read: contigs of one organism sit in a band of similar depth, which is the signal a binner uses. A contig deep in one sample and flat in another belongs to an organism only the first carries. Long contigs with very low depth may be poorly supported.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/mag. This catalog's recipe leaves contigs under 1 kbp out of the table, below the 1500 bp nf-core/mag uses by default as its minimum contig size for binning.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mag/master/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    log_x: true
    x_title: Contig length (bp)
    y_title: Depth in this sample (X)
    top_n_labels: 0
    density_threshold: 5000
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: contig_length
    y: depth
    label: contig_id
    color: read_sample
    size: mean_depth

tools.name: MCQUANT
tools.description: Single-cell quantification of multiplexed tissue images: one row per segmented cell with its mean intensity in every channel of the panel, its centroid in the image and its morphology (area, axes, eccentricity, solidity), per image and per segmentation method, with per-image summaries of cell counts, sizes and marker intensities, the correlation between markers and how far two segmenters agree on the same image.

output.name: Marker intensity per cell
output.description: The MCQUANT cell table melted on its marker columns: one row per cell and marker with the cell's mean intensity in the channel and the same through asinh(x / 150), which puts markers of very different brightness on one axis, the marker's position in the panel and whether it is a nuclear stain or a marker. The cell key matches the cell table, so a selection of cells reaches their intensities.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: marker_box
  title: Marker intensity per cell
  description: |-
    Each box is the spread of the cells' mean intensity in one marker channel, one box per marker and segmentation method. It answers which markers carry signal and how bright they are against the rest of the panel.
    How to read: a marker whose box sits near zero has little signal or a failed stain, and a very wide box points to a marker expressed in only a subset of cells. Compare the segmentation methods within a marker: a shift between them means the masks capture different amounts of cytoplasm or neighbours. Open the table tile to inspect single cells.
    Note: intensities are shown on the asinh(x / 150) scale, a fixed cofactor of this catalog module and not read from the run. It keeps markers of very different brightness on one axis.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/labsyspharm/quantification/master/README.md
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: marker
    y: asinh_intensity
    color: segmenter
    labels:
      marker: Marker
      asinh_intensity: Intensity, asinh(x / 150)
      segmenter: Segmentation method

  id: spatial_cells
  title: Cells in the image
  description: |-
    Each point is a segmented cell placed at its centroid in the registered image, coloured by segmentation method or by the intensity of a marker chosen in the controls. It answers where cells and marker signal sit in the tissue.
    How to read: marker positive cells should form the structures the marker is known for, and a patchy or empty region may be a stitching gap or an out-of-focus tile. Compare two segmentation methods on the same image to see where one finds cells the other misses.

  kind: spatial_cells
  roles:

    x: X_centroid
    y: Y_centroid

    sample: sample
    area: Area

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: shape_scatter
  title: Cell size against shape
  description: |-
    Each point is a segmented cell: its area in pixels on the horizontal axis and its eccentricity on the vertical axis, coloured by segmentation method. It answers whether the masks hold cells of plausible size and shape.
    How to read: most cells form a compact cloud. Points far to the right are large objects, often merged cells, and points at the top of the axis are elongated slivers, often fragments or debris. Compare the methods: one cloud shifted from the other means different masking rules.
    Note: eccentricity is that of the ellipse with the same second moments as the mask, from 0 for a circle towards 1 for a line. Neither quantity has a published cut-off, so no reference line is drawn.
    Source: https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/api/skimage.measure.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Cell area (pixels)
    y_title: Eccentricity
    top_n_labels: 5
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: Area
    y: Eccentricity
    label: cell_key
    color: segmenter

output.name: Marker correlation
output.description: Marker by marker Pearson correlation of the cells' asinh intensities, over every cell a segmentation method found in the run: one row per segmenter and marker, one column per marker of the panel. Markers expressed by the same cells correlate; a marker without signal has no correlation. The marker columns are only known at ingest, so a heatmap draws every numeric column.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: correlation_heatmap
  title: Marker correlation
  description: |-
    Each cell of the heatmap is the Pearson correlation between two markers across all segmented cells, with the rows annotated by segmentation method and marker role. It answers which markers are expressed by the same cells.
    How to read: strong positive blocks group markers of one cell lineage or compartment, and negative values separate exclusive populations. A marker with no correlation to anything either has no signal or marks a rare population. A nuclear stain should correlate with the other nuclear signals, not with membrane markers.
    Note: correlations are computed on asinh intensities, so a few very bright cells do not dominate them. No cut-off separates strong from weak correlation, so none is drawn.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  roles:
    index: marker_row
    row_annotation_cols:
    - segmenter
    - marker_role

_render.title: Marker correlation
_render.description:

Note: correlations are computed on asinh intensities, so a few very bright cells do not dominate them. No cut-off separates strong from weak correlation, so none is drawn.

tools.name: Melon
tools.description: Taxonomic identification and quantification of long-read metagenomes using marker genes.

output.name: Genome-copy composition
output.description: Melon's marker-gene estimate of the community, as genome copies rather than read counts, with the seven NCBI ranks already split into their own columns. The rows are pooled across the long-read samples the tool ran on: the sample id lives only in melon's output path.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: sunburst
  title: Community composition by lineage
  description: |-
    Each arc is a taxon: the rings run from superkingdom at the centre out to species, sized by its share of the estimated genome copies and coloured by phylum. It answers which lineages make up the community.
    How to read: wide arcs are the dominant lineages, and an arc that fans out into many species is a diverse group. Taxa Melon could not name at a rank are labelled unclassified. Click an arc to zoom in on it.
    Note: abundance is a share of estimated genome copies from marker genes, not of reads, and the rows are pooled across samples.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xinehc/melon/master/README.md
  kind: sunburst
  config:
    colour_by_rank: phylum
  roles:
    ranks:
    - superkingdom
    - phylum
    - class
    - order
    - family
    - genus
    - species
    abundance: abundance

tools.name: Merqury
tools.description: K-mer based assembly consensus quality (QV), k-mer completeness and copy-number spectra.

output.name: Assembly QV and k-mer completeness
output.description: One row per assembly: the consensus quality value Merqury derives from k-mers found in the assembly but not in the reads, and the share of solid read k-mers the assembly recovers. QV is logarithmic (QV 40 is one error per 10 kbp, QV 50 one per 100 kbp); completeness below the expected level points at sequence the assembly lost, completeness near 100 with a low QV at an assembly that kept everything but did not polish it.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: qv_vs_completeness
  title: Consensus QV against k-mer completeness
  description: |-
    Each point is an assembly: the share of solid read k-mers it recovers on the horizontal axis and its consensus quality value (QV) on the vertical axis, sized by its number of k-mers. It answers which assemblies are both complete and accurate.
    How to read: the best assemblies sit top right. High completeness with a low QV is an assembly that kept everything but was not polished; high QV with low completeness is an accurate assembly that lost sequence. Open the copy-number tile to see whether the lost k-mers are absent or only duplicated.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median consensus QV of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Merqury. QV is the Phred-scaled error rate (QV 40 is one error per 10 kb), so compare assemblies of the same project with each other.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/marbl/merqury/2.-Overall-k-mer-evaluation.md and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32928274/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: K-mer completeness (%)
    y_title: Consensus QV
    legend_pos: bottom
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    x: kmer_completeness
    y: qv
    label: assembly_id
    color: assembly_id
    size: total_kmers

output.name: Per-sequence QV
output.description: Merqury's QV for every contig or scaffold of every assembly. Errors are rarely spread evenly: a handful of short, low-QV sequences often carry most of an assembly's error k-mers, and they are the ones to inspect, polish or drop. Sequences with no error k-mer have no finite QV and are flagged error-free.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: sequence_qv_scatter
  title: Sequence QV against size
  description: |-
    Each point is a contig or scaffold: its number of k-mers, a proxy for its length, against its consensus QV. It answers which sequences carry the lowest accuracy and whether they are small or large.
    How to read: errors are rarely even, so a few short low-QV sequences often hold most error k-mers. The lowest points are labelled; inspect, polish or drop them. A low QV on a large sequence matters more than on a short one.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median consensus QV of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Merqury. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/marbl/merqury/2.-Overall-k-mer-evaluation.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: K-mers in the sequence (size)
    y_title: Consensus QV
    log_x: true
    legend_pos: bottom
    top_n_labels: 8
    label_order_col: qv
  roles:
    x: total_kmers
    y: qv
    label: sequence
    color: assembly_id

tools.name: MetaPhlAn
tools.description: Identify clades (phyla to species) present in the metagenome obtained from a microbiome sample and their relative abundance.

output.name: Taxonomic profile

  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample, split into the relative abundance of its most abundant clades at the chosen taxonomic rank, with the rest lumped as Other. It answers which organisms make up each metagenome and how the samples compare.
    How to read: samples with similar bars share a community, and a sample dominated by one taxon is a low-diversity or perturbed community. Switch the rank from kingdom to species to move between the overview and the detail.
    Note: MetaPhlAn reports relative abundance among the clades it detects, so the bars show composition and not absolute counts.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/biobakery/MetaPhlAn/master/README.md and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823356/

  config:
    top_n: 10

    color: sample

Each bar counts the peptidoforms seen in one exact combination of replicates of a sample, and the dots below show which replicates are in it. It answers how much of a sample is seen in every injection.
How to read: a tall bar for all replicates together means a reproducible sample. Tall bars for single replicates mean peptides seen only once, which are the least certain.

    How to read: a histogram piled at the highest count means most peptides are found in every replicate. A pile at 1 means many are seen once.

  aggregation: average
  aggregations:

  caption: peptides, by replicates seen

output.name: Peptide intensity per replicate
output.description: Log10 intensity of every peptidoform in every raw replicate of its sample, long format, from the per-replicate intensity columns of a quantified run. Replicates are numbered in samplesheet ID order within the sample.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Peptide intensity per replicate
  description: |-
    Each box is the distribution of peptide intensities in one replicate of a sample, on a log10 scale, coloured by sample. It answers whether the replicates of a sample were measured at comparable intensity.
    How to read: boxes at similar heights mean a consistent injection amount and sensitivity. A replicate shifted down or up has a loading or sensitivity difference, so treat its intensities with care.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median log10 peptide intensity of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of mhcquant.
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: replicate_label
    y: log10_intensity
    color: sample
    labels:
      replicate_label: Replicate
      log10_intensity: Log10 intensity
      sample: Sample
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: log10_intensity

output.description: Log10 intensity of each peptide in two replicates of the same sample, for every replicate pair, restricted to the peptides quantified in both. A good pair hugs the diagonal.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: replicate_scatter
  title: Intensity agreement between replicates
  description: |-
    Each point is a peptide quantified in two replicates of a sample: its log10 intensity in the first on the horizontal axis and in the second on the vertical axis, coloured by replicate pair. It answers how reproducible the quantification is.
    How to read: a pair that hugs the diagonal is reproducible. A wide cloud or a cloud shifted off the diagonal has noisy or biased intensities, so check the replicate correlation card before comparing samples.
    Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where the two replicates have equal intensity. It is an identity line, not a cut-off.
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Log10 intensity, first replicate
    y_title: Log10 intensity, second replicate
    reference_line: diagonal
    reference_label: Equal intensity
    top_n_labels: 0
  roles:
    x: intensity_a
    y: intensity_b
    label: peptide
    color: pair

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: class_i_share
  title: Peptides in the class I window
  description: |-
    The hero number is the lowest share of a sample's peptides that fall in the class I length window, 8 to 12 residues, and the median sits beside it. It answers whether any sample leaves the window.
    How to read: mhcquant keeps peptides of 8 to 12 residues by default, so the share is 1 unless the run widened the range. A lower share means the run kept longer peptides.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  column: class_i_fraction
  aggregation: min
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: lowest sample, with the median

tools.name: miRDeep2
tools.description: Discovers known and novel microRNA genes from small RNA sequencing reads.

output.name: Novel miRNA precursors
output.description: miRDeep2's novel precursor calls merged across samples by overlapping locus, one row per hairpin: how many samples report it, its best score and true-positive estimate, the reads on each arm summed over samples, the share of calls with a significant randfold test, any Rfam hit, and the sequences of its strongest call.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: novel_support
  title: Novel precursors by support
  description: |-
    Each point is a novel miRNA precursor merged across samples: the number of samples that report it and its best miRDeep2 score, sized by its total reads and coloured by whether star-arm reads were seen. It answers which candidates are best supported.
    How to read: candidates in the upper right are detected in many samples with a high score. A star-arm read pair is the signature of Dicer processing, so a candidate with star support is stronger than one without. Open the table to read the sequences of the labelled candidates.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median best miRDeep2 score of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of miRDeep2. The README sets a score cut-off of 0 only for which novel candidates its overview table lists.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21911355/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: Samples reporting the precursor
    y_title: Best miRDeep2 score
    legend_pos: bottom
    top_n_labels: 6
  roles:
    x: samples_detected
    y: max_score
    label: precursor_id
    color: star_support
    size: total_reads

output.name: miRDeep2 score-cutoff summary
output.description: miRDeep2's own calibration table, one row per sample and integer score cutoff: novel candidates reported, their estimated false and true positives, known miRBase precursors recovered and the signal-to-noise ratio against permuted structures. The curve miRDeep2's authors read to pick a cutoff.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: signal_to_noise_curve
  title: Signal-to-noise by score cut-off
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample: the signal-to-noise ratio of novel predictions, against permuted structures, at each integer score cut-off. It answers how stringent the score cut-off must be before predictions rise above the noise.
    How to read: pick a cut-off where the curve has risen and flattened, and read the recovery curve beside it to see what that costs in known miRNAs. A flat curve near 1 means the data hold little signal over noise.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The survey covers cut-offs from -10 to 10, and miRDeep2's README sets a default of 0 only for which novel candidates its overview table lists.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: miRDeep2 score cut-off
    y_title: Signal-to-noise ratio
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: score_cutoff
    y: signal_to_noise

    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md

  config:
    x_title: miRDeep2 score cut-off
    y_title: Known miRNAs detected (%)

- component: advanced_viz
  id: isomir_dot_plot
  title: isomiR classes of the top miRNAs
  description: |-
    Each dot is a miRNA in one isomiR class: its colour is the mean share of the miRNA's reads in that class and its size is the fraction of samples where the class is a real part of the reads. It answers which isomiR forms each abundant miRNA carries and whether they are the same across samples.
    How to read: a large dark dot is a class that holds many reads in most samples, such as a miRNA that is mostly 3' trimmed everywhere. A small dot with a dark colour is a class that is common in only part of the cohort, so look at the samples behind it. The classes are not exclusive, since one read can be 3' trimmed and carry an addition.
    Lines and annotations: a class counts as present in a sample when it holds at least 5 percent of that miRNA's reads there, and only samples with at least 10 reads of the miRNA are counted. Both are settings of the recipe, not published cut-offs.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31504201/
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: variant_class
    gene: mirna
    mean_expression: mean_share_pct
    frac_expressing: samples_fraction

How to read: miRNAs in the upper left and upper right corners differ most between the groups, higher in one or the other. Choose groups with several samples each, since a single sample gives no estimate of variation, and treat a result from few samples as exploratory.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a false discovery rate of 0.05 and the vertical lines mark an absolute log2 fold change of 1. These are the tile's own defaults, and no source defines them for miRNA data.

output.name: Cumulative coverage curve
output.description: Share of the reference covered at least at each depth, per mapping, from mosdepth's global distribution: every depth to 100X, then a log-spaced grid. The depth at which a curve falls off is the depth a consensus caller can rely on.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: cumulative_curve
  title: Cumulative coverage curve
  description: |-
    Each line is a mapping: the share of the reference covered at least at each depth, from mosdepth's global distribution. It answers how much of the genome is deep enough to call variants and a consensus.
    How to read: a curve that stays near 100 percent and falls late means even deep coverage. A curve that drops early, or a lower plateau, means part of the genome is thinly covered or not covered at all. Read the value where a curve crosses the marked line to see the breadth at that depth.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is 10X, the default minimum depth at which nf-core/viralrecon calls variants and consensus bases. iVar's own default is 10 reads for a consensus base but 0 for a variant call. mosdepth itself sets no cut-off.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brentp/mosdepth/master/README.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    reference_x: 10
    reference_label: 10X, minimum depth for variant and consensus calls
    x_title: Depth (X)
    y_title: Bases covered at least this deep (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: genome_id
    x: depth
    y: bases_pct

output.description: mosdepth's own headline table, one row per contig with its length, the bases of sequence that landed on it and the mean, minimum and maximum depth. When mosdepth runs against a target file it reports every contig twice, once genome-wide and once over the targets only; the recipe splits that into a `scope` column (genome or region) instead of mixing two very different depths on one axis. output.name: X and Y coverage sex check
output.description: Mean depth on chromosome X and on chromosome Y for every library, from the small per-run table MultiQC's mosdepth module writes, split per sample and alignment stage. The X/Y depth ratio separates the two common karyotypes cleanly: two X and no Y leaves almost no Y signal and a large ratio, one X and one Y sits near 1. `inferred_sex` applies a 10x cut-off in the empty band between them. It is a heuristic on two summary numbers, not a genotype call, and a sex chromosome aneuploidy, a mixed or contaminated library or a very low-depth run can all land on the wrong side of it. Read it as a check against the sex recorded in the sample sheet, and read the raw X and Y depths beside it to see how far from the cut-off a library actually sits.

AdapterRemoval's own MultiQC plot: for each sample, how many reads were kept, discarded or collapsed into a single merged read. It answers how much of the library was lost to trimming and how much of it merged.
How to read: A high retained share means clean libraries. A large discarded share points to adapter dimers or very short inserts, so check the library preparation. A high collapsed share is expected for short inserts and is not a defect.
Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/adapterremoval

output.name: miRNA complexity curve
output.description: Distinct miRNAs detected against reads sampled, per library. A flattened curve says deeper sequencing would find few new miRNAs; a climbing one says the library was sequenced short of its complexity.

  description: |-
    Each line is one library: the number of distinct miRNAs miRTrace detects in a subsample of the given size. It answers whether the library was sequenced deep enough to see its miRNAs.
    How to read: a curve that has flattened means deeper sequencing would add few new miRNAs. A curve still climbing at the library's full depth means the library is under-sequenced. Compare libraries of the same type: a curve that stays far below its peers points to a low-complexity library.

  kind: profile
  config:

    y_title: Distinct miRNAs detected

output.name: Yield above quality cutoffs
output.description: How much of each library survives a quality floor: reads, percentage and megabases above each NanoStat quality cutoff, one row per sample and cutoff. A mean quality hides whether a library is tight around it or bimodal; this ladder does not.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: quality_ladder
  title: Reads kept at each quality cutoff
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: the percentage of its reads whose mean quality is above each cutoff of the NanoStat ladder. It answers how fast a library loses reads as the quality floor rises.
    How to read: a line that stays high and drops late is a library tight around a good quality. A line that falls early is poor, and a steep drop between two rungs means a bimodal library that a single mean quality hides. Pick the cutoff for filtering from the rung where the curve starts to fall.
    Lines and annotations: no pass mark is drawn, because NanoStat defines none. The rungs are the fixed cutoffs of the NanoStat report.
    Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Quality cutoff (Phred Q)
    y_title: Reads above the cutoff (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:

    x: q_cutoff
    y: pct_reads

tools.name: Nextclade

renders._yaml:

  description: |-

tools.name: Nonpareil
tools.description: Estimate average coverage and create curves for metagenomic datasets.

output.name: Coverage curve
output.description: The coverage each library would reach at a given sequencing effort, rebuilt from the gamma model Nonpareil publishes in its merged summary. One curve per sequencing library, decimated to 200 points, with the effort actually sequenced and the effort projected for 95 percent coverage carried on every row.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: coverage_curve
  title: Coverage against sequencing effort
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sequencing library: the average coverage of its metagenome that the reads reach (vertical axis) as the sequencing effort grows (horizontal axis, log scale). It answers how much more sequencing a library needs before it describes its community.
    How to read: a curve that flattens near the top has captured most of the community, and extra sequencing adds little. A curve that still climbs steeply is far from covered, and the projected effort in the summary tiles says how much deeper to go. Compare curves of the same habitat only, since diversity sets the slope.
    Lines and annotations: the curves are redrawn from Nonpareil's fitted model (a gamma distribution on the log of the effort) and not from the measured redundancy points, which nf-core does not publish. Nonpareil projects effort for 95 percent coverage by default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24123672/
  kind: profile
  config:
    log_x: true
    x_title: Sequencing effort (bp)
    y_title: Estimated average coverage
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: library
    x: sequencing_effort
    y: coverage

output.name: Identifications against FDR

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: fdr_profile
  title: Accepted PSMs against FDR
  description: |-
    Each curve is a raw file: the number of target peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) accepted as the target-decoy q-value threshold on the raw Comet score is relaxed. It answers how many identifications each file yields at a given error rate.
    How to read: a curve that rises steeply and early belongs to a file with good spectra, while a flat curve has few confident matches and points to an acquisition or search-space problem. Compare files: one far below its peers is the one to investigate.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is the 1% false discovery rate, the nf-core/mhcquant default fdr_threshold at which peptide hits are selected. This curve applies it to target-decoy competition on the raw Comet score, from the table the pipeline hands to its rescoring engine (Percolator by default). Its counts therefore differ from the final peptide table, which is rescored and filtered at peptide level by default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mhcquant/master/nextflow_schema.json and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17327847/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Target-decoy q-value
    y_title: Accepted target PSMs
    reference_x: 0.01
    reference_label: 1% FDR
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: run_id
    x: q_value
    y: accepted_psms

tools.name: OrthoFinder
tools.description: Phylogenetic orthology inference for comparative genomics: groups the genes of several species into orthogroups, infers orthologues and the rooted species tree.

output.name: Orthogroups shared between species
output.description: One row per orthogroup with a 0/1 column per species, the species it reaches, its genes and whether it is single-copy. Read as an UpSet, it splits the orthogroups into the core every species shares, the ones a clade shares, and the ones a single genome holds alone.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: orthogroup_upset
  title: Orthogroups shared between species
  description: |-
    Each bar is a set of species and counts the orthogroups that contain genes from exactly those species, with the dots below naming the set. It answers which orthogroups every species shares, which a clade shares and which belong to a single species.
    How to read: the bar with every species joined is the core set that all genomes carry. Tall bars for a subset of species point to a clade-specific gene family, and a species with a large single bar holds many genes found nowhere else, which is also what a fragmented or contaminated proteome looks like.
    Lines and annotations: bars are coloured by the number of species in the set, the degree of the intersection.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidemms/OrthoFinder/master/README.md
  kind: upset_plot
  config:
    color_intersections_by: degree
    show_values: true

tools.name: Pangolin
tools.description: Assigns SARS-CoV-2 genomes to global outbreak lineages.

output.name: Lineage report
output.description: Per-sample PANGO lineage report.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Lineage calls by QC status
  description: |-
    Each bar counts the sequences assigned to a Pango lineage, split by whether they passed Pangolin's sequence quality check. It answers which lineages the run found and how many calls rest on usable sequences.
    How to read: a lineage made of passing sequences is a call to trust. Failed sequences get an unassigned lineage, so a large unassigned bar is a data quality problem and not a new variant.
    Lines and annotations: the colour is the QC status, which fails a sequence with more than 30 percent N or shorter than 25000 bases, the defaults of Pangolin's max-ambig and min-length options.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cov-lineages/pangolin/master/pangolin/command.py
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: lineage
    color: qc_status
    labels:
      lineage: Pango lineage
      qc_status: QC status

tools.name: Preseq
tools.description: Software for predicting library complexity and genome coverage in high- throughput sequencing.

output.name: Library complexity curve
output.description: How many distinct molecules each library would yield at a given sequencing depth, with the confidence interval preseq puts around that extrapolation. A curve still climbing at the depth already sequenced means resequencing buys new material; one that has flattened means the library is exhausted.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: complexity_ribbon
  title: Expected distinct molecules by depth
  description: |-
    Each curve is a library: the number of distinct molecules preseq expects to see at a given sequencing depth, with the confidence interval as a band. It answers whether sequencing deeper would still add new molecules.
    How to read: a curve still rising steeply means the library is far from exhausted and resequencing pays off. A curve that has flattened is exhausted, so more reads return duplicates. A wide band means the extrapolation is uncertain, so be careful recommending deeper sequencing from it.
    Note: preseq extrapolates from the reads already sequenced, and the further it goes past that depth the less reliable it is. It publishes no cut-off for a sufficient library.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23435259/ and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/smithlabcode/preseq/master/README.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Total reads sequenced
    y_title: Expected distinct molecules
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: total_reads
    y: expected_distinct
    lower: lower_ci
    upper: upper_ci

tools.name: Prokka
tools.description: Structural and functional annotation of prokaryotic genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes.

output.name: Bin locus map
output.description: Where the genes sit along a bin's contigs, as an arrow per coding sequence, transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA. Pick one bin and one contig and the tile becomes a locus map: operon structure, strand switches, and the ribosomal RNA operon whose presence decides the bin's MIMAG tier.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: locus_map
  title: Gene arrows along a contig
  description: |-
    Each arrow is a coding sequence, transfer RNA or ribosomal RNA placed on a contig of one bin, pointing in the direction of the gene and coloured by feature class. It answers how the genes of a bin are organised.
    How to read: pick one bin and one contig. Runs of arrows on one strand are operons, a switch of direction marks a strand change, and a cluster of ribosomal RNA arrows is the rRNA operon that decides the MIMAG tier of the bin.
    Note: Prokka renames contigs to internal identifiers, so the coordinates are valid within a bin only.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tseemann/prokka/master/README.md and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  kind: gene_arrow_track
  roles:
    contig: contig
    feature_id: feature_id
    start: start
    end: end
    strand: strand
    class: ftype
    label: gene

output.name: Protein x database coverage
output.description: Protein by database matrix: the fraction of each protein's residues covered by the domains of each database the pipeline searched (Pfam, FunFam, NMPFamsDB, MetagRoot, InterProScan). Clustered, proteins group by which databases describe them and how completely; a skipped database is a column of zeros.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: coverage_heatmap
  title: Domain coverage per protein and database
  description: |-
    Each cell is the fraction of a protein's residues covered by the domains of one database, from 0 (no hit) to 1 (every residue covered), with the sample as a row strip. It answers which databases describe each protein and how completely.
    How to read: clustered, proteins that group together are described by the same databases. A protein bright in one column and blank in the others rests on a single source, and a blank row has no annotation at all, so open the domain architecture for it. A skipped database is a column of zeros.
    Lines and annotations: the dendrograms come from hierarchical clustering of the rows and columns. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient coverage.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  config:
    value_columns:
    - pfam
    - funfam
    - nmpfams
    - metagroot
    - interproscan
    row_annotation_cols:
    - sample
  roles:
    index: entity

  id: domain_significance
  title: Domain significance against length
  description: |-
    Each point is a domain span: its length in residues on the horizontal axis and the minus log10 of its independent E-value on the vertical axis, coloured by the database that reports it. It answers which domains are long and confident and which are weak.
    How to read: points high on the plot are strong matches. Long, high spans are whole-protein families and short, high ones are motifs. Weak points of any length are borderline, so check them in a second database.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an E-value of 0.01, the default inclusion threshold of HMMER (per-target and per-domain). HMMER applies it to the full-sequence and conditional E-values, so a few points can sit just below the line. InterProScan matches pass the filters of their own member database, not one shared E-value.
    Sources: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf and https://github.com/ebi-pf-team/interproscan-docs/blob/master/docs/FAQ.rst
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Domain span (residues)
    y_title: -log10 E-value
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 2
    reference_label: E-value 0.01
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    x: span

  description: |-

output.name: Initial cluster sizes
output.description: How the input sequences of each sample fell into MMseqs2 clusters before families are built: the number of clusters of every size, the sequences they hold and those sequences' share of the sample. Families are seeded from the clusters above the pipeline's size threshold, so the tail of this distribution is what the run can turn into families.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: cluster_size_profile
  title: Initial cluster sizes
  description: |-
    Each line is a sample: the number of MMseqs2 clusters of every size before families are built. It answers how the input sequences group and how many clusters are large enough to seed a family.
    How to read: most clusters are tiny, so the curve falls steeply and the count axis is logarithmic. Only the tail to the right of the line can become families, so a sample with almost nothing there will yield few families. Lower the threshold to get more families.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line at 25 is the default minimum cluster size of nf-core/proteinfamilies for seeding a family. The run may have set another value, which this tile does not read.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: profile
  config:
    log_y: true
    reference_x: 25
    reference_label: Default minimum cluster size (25)
    x_title: Sequences in the cluster
    y_title: Clusters
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: cluster_size
    y: n_clusters

tools.name: nf-core/proteinfold
tools.description: Protein structure prediction summaries of nf-core/proteinfold: per-residue confidence of every top-ranked structure, per-model confidence scores (pLDDT, pTM, ipTM, ipSAE) across engines, predicted aligned error matrices and the multiple sequence alignments the MSA-based engines folded from.

output.name: Residue confidence per engine
output.description: The per-residue pLDDT of each engine's top-ranked structure, one curve per engine (and per chain on a complex), averaged over windows past 200 residues. Kept apart from the residue table, with the engine only in the curve label, so that an engine picked on the residue table leaves every engine's curve for the same target on screen.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: plddt_by_engine
  title: Residue confidence along the sequence
  description: |-
    Each curve is the per-residue pLDDT of the top-ranked structure of one engine for one target, with chains of a complex drawn separately. It answers which regions of the sequence an engine places confidently.
    How to read: stretches above 90 are very high confidence, 70 to 90 confident, 50 to 70 low and below 50 very low, which often marks intrinsically disordered regions. Dips between confident stretches usually separate domains or flexible linkers. When engines disagree on a region, treat its placement as unreliable.
    Note: the bands are AlphaFold DB's reading guide and are not drawn on the plot. Curves longer than 200 residues are averaged over windows by this catalog's recipe, a display limit and not an engine setting.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/plddt-understanding-local-confidence/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Residue position
    y_title: pLDDT
    legend_pos: bottom
    residue_axis: true
  roles:
    series: series
    x: position
    y: plddt

output.name: Model confidence scores
output.description: One row per predicted model of every target and engine: its rank (1 is the top-ranked model), mean pLDDT, the share of residues placed confidently (pLDDT 70 or more) and likely disordered (under 50), and, when the engine writes them, the predicted TM score (pTM) and for a complex the interface TM score (ipTM) and ipSAE.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: plddt_vs_ptm
  title: Local against global confidence
  description: |-
    Each point is a predicted model: its mean pLDDT on the horizontal axis and its predicted TM score on the vertical axis, coloured by engine and sized by the number of residues. It answers whether a model is trustworthy locally and as a whole.
    How to read: models in the upper right are confident on both counts. A high pLDDT with a low pTM means well folded pieces that are badly arranged, and the lower left holds models that are probably wrong. Engines that write no pTM are not drawn.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a mean pLDDT of 70, the AlphaFold DB threshold for a confident residue. The horizontal line is a pTM of 0.5, above which the overall fold of the model might be similar to the true structure.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Mean pLDDT
    y_title: pTM
    top_n_labels: 5
    legend_pos: bottom
    quadrants:
      x: 70
      y: 0.5
      labels:
      - Weak locally, fold likely

Each point is a predicted model: its mean pLDDT on the horizontal axis and its predicted TM score on the vertical axis, coloured by engine and sized by the number of residues. It answers whether a model is trustworthy locally and as a whole.
How to read: models in the upper right are confident on both counts. A high pLDDT with a low pTM means well folded pieces that are badly arranged, and the lower left holds models that are probably wrong. Engines that write no pTM are not drawn.
Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a mean pLDDT of 70, the AlphaFold DB threshold for a confident residue. The horizontal line is a pTM of 0.5, above which the overall fold of the model might be similar to the true structure.

tools.name: PURPLE
tools.description: Purity, ploidy and absolute copy-number fitting for tumor/normal or tumor-only whole-genome and panel data, with the somatic and germline driver catalog and the purity-adjusted somatic variants.

output.name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
output.description: PURPLE's fitted copy-number segments turned into the canonical copy-number profile contract. The absolute, purity-adjusted copy number becomes a log2 ratio against a diploid baseline, the fitted BAF comes through, and the major and minor allele copy numbers are kept for the allele-specific locus view, so loss of heterozygosity reads as a BAF split at unchanged total copy number.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: purple_cn_profile
  title: Copy-number profile
  description: |-
    Each line is a fitted copy-number segment: its purity-adjusted copy number as a log2 ratio against two copies on the upper panel, and its fitted B-allele frequency on the lower one. It answers where the tumor genome gains, loses or keeps its copy number, and where one allele is lost.
    How to read: segments above the upper dotted line are gains and those below the lower one are losses. A BAF that rises towards 1 at an unchanged copy number is loss of heterozygosity, where one allele is gone and the other duplicated. Zoom on a chromosome to see the allele-specific copy numbers.
    Lines and annotations: the dotted lines at log2 0.322 and -0.415 are the copy numbers of 2.5 and 1.5, where the rounded copy number leaves two. They are a reference defined by the recipe, not a PURPLE cut-off. The dotted line at BAF 0.5 is the balanced state, since the BAF of a segment varies between 0.5 and 1.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  kind: cnv_profile
  config:
    gain_threshold: 0.322
    loss_threshold: -0.415
  roles:
    sample: sample
    chrom: chrom
    start: start
    end: end
    log2: log2
    baf: baf
    copy_number: copy_number
    segment: segment
    label: label

renders._yaml:

  title: Minimum against maximum copy number
  description: |-
    Each point is a gene: the lowest and the highest copy number found over its exons, coloured by the call derived from them. It answers which genes are altered and whether the change covers the whole gene or only a part.

    reference_label: Minimum equals maximum
    x_title: Minimum copy number over the gene
    y_title: Maximum copy number over the gene
    top_n_labels: 10
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:

  kind: lollipop
  config:
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:

    label: label
    effect: value

output.name: Tumor purity, ploidy and QC
output.description: PURPLE's fit for each tumor, one row per tumor: purity, ploidy, fit status and sex, the genome-wide mutational load (microsatellite indels per Mb and MSI status, tumor mutational burden and load, structural-variant burden, whole-genome duplication), joined with the checks of the .purple.qc file (QC status, copy-number segments, deleted genes, contamination, LOH fraction, TINC level). Every copy number and allele frequency downstream is read against this fit.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: purity_gauge
  title: Tumor purity
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median tumor purity, the share of tumor cells in the sample, over the tumors in view. It answers whether the sample holds enough tumor for a reliable fit.
    How to read: a high purity gives clean copy-number and allele-frequency signals, and a low one blurs them. The lowest and highest values are listed beside it.
    Lines and annotations: the marker is a purity of 0.2, below which PURPLE raises its low-purity warning.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  column: purity
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: threshold
  threshold_value: 0.2
  threshold_direction: min
  caption: median, against the 0.2 warning level
  headline: true

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Alpha diversity by habitat
  description: |-
    Each box summarises the samples of one habitat for one alpha-diversity metric, and each dot is a sample. It answers whether within-sample diversity differs between habitats.
    How to read: boxes that do not overlap point to habitats with different diversity, and a wide box means the samples of that habitat are heterogeneous. Shannon and Faith's PD grow with richness, and evenness says how equally the features share the reads. Compare with the beta-diversity ordination to see whether the same habitats also differ in composition.
    Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  code: |-
    # reshape wide -> long so each metric becomes a facet panel (stays polars)
    df_modified = df.unpivot(
        index=["sample_id", "habitat"],
        on=["shannon", "observed_features", "faith_pd", "evenness"],
        variable_name="metric",
        value_name="value",
    )
  
    fig = px.box(
        df_modified,
        x="habitat", y="value", color="habitat",
        facet_col="metric", facet_col_wrap=2, points="all",
        category_orders={"metric": ["shannon", "observed_features", "faith_pd", "evenness"]},
        labels={"habitat": "Habitat", "value": "Value"},
    )
  
    fig.update_yaxes(matches=None)  # each panel keeps its own scale
    fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1]))
    fig.update_layout(showlegend=True, legend_title_text="Habitat", boxmode="group", margin=dict(t=10))

output.name: Alpha rarefaction
output.description: Alpha-rarefaction curve (sample × depth × iteration × metric).

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: rarefaction_alpha
  title: Rarefaction curves
  description: |-
    Each line is a sample: its Faith's phylogenetic diversity as the reads are subsampled to a growing depth, averaged over the iterations, with the spread of the iterations as a band. It answers whether the sequencing depth was enough to capture the diversity.
    How to read: a curve that levels out (approaches a slope of zero) means more reads would not reveal new diversity. A curve still climbing at the deepest depth means the diversity was not fully observed, or that sequencing error remains in the data. Choose the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most curves have levelled out, without dropping too many samples.
    Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  kind: rarefaction
  config:
    show_ci: true
  roles:
    sample_id: sample
    depth: depth
    metric: faith_pd
    iter: iter

output.name: Differential abundance
output.description: ANCOM-BC differential-abundance results. The tool writes one CSV per statistic per contrast; the recipe joins + melts them into a long table.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: volcano
  title: Differential abundance volcano
  description: |-
    Each point is a taxon in one contrast: its ANCOM-BC log fold change on the horizontal axis and its q-value (adjusted p-value) on the vertical axis, coloured by contrast. It answers which taxa differ most between the groups, in which direction, and how confidently.
    How to read: taxa in the upper left and upper right corners are less and more abundant than in the reference group, with high confidence. A cloud with almost nothing past the lines means little differential signal. Open the table tile to inspect the labelled taxa.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the q-value cut-off of 0.05 and the vertical lines mark an absolute effect size of 1. Both are the nf-core/ampliseq defaults for its differential-abundance barplot.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 1.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Log fold change
    significance_label: -log10 q-value
  roles:
    feature_id: id
    effect_size: lfc
    significance: q_val
    label: Phylum
    category: contrast

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: distance_heatmap
  title: Sample distances
  description: |-
    Each cell is the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between two samples, computed from their relative abundances. It answers which samples have similar communities and which groups they form.
    How to read: dark blocks along the diagonal are groups of similar samples and the dendrograms show how they cluster. Samples that sit far from every other sample have an unusual community, so check them against the ordination and the habitat metadata.
    Note: Bray-Curtis runs from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities that share nothing.
    Sources: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/ and https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.distance.braycurtis.html
  kind: complex_heatmap
  config:
    cluster_rows: true
    cluster_cols: true
    normalize: none
  roles:
    index: sample

renders._yaml:

  title: Classifier confidence
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median classifier confidence over the ASVs in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how certain the taxonomic assignments are.
    How to read: values close to 1 are firm assignments, and a long lower whisker is a set of ASVs assigned with little support. The classifier only keeps an assignment at a rank when its confidence reaches the minimum set for the run, 0.7 by default, so the lowest values sit near that floor.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qiime2/q2-feature-classifier/master/q2_feature_classifier/classifier.py
  column: confidence
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats

tools.name: QSEE
tools.description: Collects the QC metrics of a WiGiTS run and checks each against its threshold.

output.name: QC verdicts per feature
output.description: One row per sample and checked QC feature (coverage, mapping and base quality, duplicates, purity, deleted genes, contamination, TINC): the source tool, the value, the PASS, WARN or FAIL verdict and the condition that fails it.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: qc_check_count
  title: QC checks run
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of QC checks QSEE ran, with the number of samples beside it, and the bars rank the verdicts PASS, WARN and FAIL. It answers whether the run clears its quality thresholds.
    How to read: a bar of FAIL or WARN checks is the list to open in the table. An overall sample status is FAIL if any check fails, WARN if any warns and PASS otherwise.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/qsee/README.md
  column: sample
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - nunique
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: qc_status
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: checks, by verdict
  headline: true

_render.title: QC checks run
_render.description:
The hero number is the count of QC checks QSEE ran, with the number of samples beside it, and the bars rank the verdicts PASS, WARN and FAIL. It answers whether the run clears its quality thresholds.
How to read: a bar of FAIL or WARN checks is the list to open in the table. An overall sample status is FAIL if any check fails, WARN if any warns and PASS otherwise.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/qsee/README.md
_render.caption: checks, by verdict

renders.title: QC checks run

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/qsee/README.md
renders.caption: checks, by verdict

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: qc_status_bar
  title: Verdicts by source tool
  description: |-
    Each bar counts the QC checks of one source tool (BAM metrics, purity, deleted genes, contamination, TINC and so on), split by verdict. It answers which part of the pipeline raises the QC problems.
    How to read: a tool whose bar is all PASS needs no action. A tool with WARN or FAIL checks points to the stage to investigate, then the table names the feature.
    Lines and annotations: the colours are QSEE's PASS, WARN and FAIL verdicts, each set by comparing the value with the feature's default threshold, which a threshold overrides file can change.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/qsee/README.md

output.name: Coverage across the reference
output.description: Windowed read depth along the whole reference, from Qualimap BamQC's own coverage_across_reference table. Qualimap reports the window centre on the concatenated reference, so the recipe maps each window back onto its contig using the per-contig lengths in the same run's genome_results.txt; without that file the track falls back to a single pseudo-contig.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: reference_coverage_track
  title: Read depth along the reference
  description: |-
    Each point is a window of the reference, drawn at its position on its contig with the read depth Qualimap measured there, one line per library. It answers where along the genome the reads pile up or thin out.
    How to read: a flat line means an even library. Spikes point to repeats, amplified regions or organelle contigs, and long gaps point to regions the reads do not reach. Compare libraries to separate a sample effect from a reference effect.
    Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: sample
  roles:
    chromosome: chromosome
    position: position
    value: coverage
    sample: sample

tools.name: QUAST
tools.description: Reference-free assembly quality statistics for whole assemblies and for individual bins.

output.name: Assembly statistics
output.description: Contig counts, N50 and assembled length for each assembly, one row per assembler and sample. Total length says how much of the community was assembled at all; N50 says whether that length sits in a few long contigs a binner can work with, or in a drift of short ones it cannot.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: n50_vs_length
  title: Contiguity against assembled length
  description: |-
    Each point is one assembly: its total assembled length on the horizontal axis and its contig N50 on the vertical axis, coloured by assembler and sized by the number of contigs. It answers which assembler gives the most contiguous assembly for the length it recovers.
    How to read: points toward the upper right assemble more of the community in longer contigs. A large point low on the axis is a fragmented assembly, many small contigs, which a binner will struggle with. Compare assemblers on the same sample before choosing one.
    Note: QUAST defines no pass mark for N50 or assembled length. The vertical axis is logarithmic.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median contig N50 of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of QUAST.
    Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Assembled length (bp)
    y_title: Contig N50 (bp)
    log_y: true
    top_n_labels: 5
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
  roles:

    color: assembler

tools.name: RepeatMasker
tools.description: Screens DNA sequences for interspersed repeats and low-complexity regions against a repeat library, and masks them.

output.name: Masking summary per assembly
output.description: One row per assembly from the header of RepeatMasker's summary table: sequences, length with and without runs of N, GC and the bases masked, with the interspersed, retroelement, DNA transposon, unclassified and simple repeat shares. A large unclassified share is a library that could not name the repeats; a masked share far from the genome's relatives is a library that missed them or a de novo one that over-called.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: masked_share
  title: Masked share
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median percentage of the assembly masked as repeat, with the lowest and the highest assembly next to it. It answers how repeat-rich the assemblies are.
    How to read: compare an assembly with its close relatives. A share far below them suggests a library that missed repeats, and a share far above a de novo library that over-called. RepeatMasker publishes no expected share.
    Source: https://www.repeatmasker.org/
  column: masked_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: gauge
  coverage_max: 100.0
  caption: median share of the assembly, with the range

Source: https://www.repeatmasker.org/

tools.name: riboWaltz
tools.description: Calculation of optimal P-site offsets, diagnostic analysis and visual inspection of ribosome profiling data.

output.name: P-site frame distribution
output.description: Share of each library's P-sites in the three reading frames, per transcript region. Footprints of translating ribosomes pile into frame 0 of the CDS; the UTRs, which ribosomes do not translate, stay close to a third per frame.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: frame_composition
  title: P-site reading frame per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the share of its P-sites that fall in each of the three reading frames, for one transcript region. It answers whether the footprints show the three-nucleotide periodicity of translating ribosomes.
    How to read: on the CDS, one frame should dominate, usually frame 0. The UTRs are not translated, so they stay close to a third per frame. A CDS that looks like the UTRs means the P-site offsets are wrong or the library lacks periodicity.
    Lines and annotations: a third per frame is the split of reads with no frame preference, a plain expectation of three frames and not a riboWaltz cut-off.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  kind: stacked_bar
  config:
    rank_label: Region
    value_title: P-sites in the frame (%)
  roles:
    sample_id: sample
    taxon: frame
    rank: region
    abundance: pct

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: phasing_plane
  title: CDS share against frame 0 share
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: the share of its P-sites that fall in the CDS against the share of CDS P-sites in frame 0, sized by the number of P-sites, with one colour per library. It answers which libraries are both enriched on coding sequence and phased.
    How to read: good libraries sit top right. A point near the line, or with a negative margin, has no clear periodicity, which usually means the P-site offsets are wrong for that library. A point far left of its peers is dominated by UTR signal, as fragmented RNA would be.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line at a third marks the frame 0 share of a library with no frame preference. It is an arithmetic reference, an even split over three frames, and not a riboWaltz cut-off.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: P-sites in the CDS (%)
    y_title: CDS P-sites in frame 0 (%)
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_value: 33.3
    reference_label: No frame preference (one third)
  roles:
    x: cds_pct
    y: frame0_cds_pct
    label: sample
    size: psites
    color: sample

tools.name: rMATS
tools.description: Differential alternative splicing of annotated and novel events (skipped exons, retained introns, mutually exclusive exons, alternative 3' and 5' splice sites) between two groups of replicated RNA-seq samples.

output.name: Differential splicing events (rMATS)
output.description: rMATS junction-and-exon-count (JCEC) results for the five event types, stacked: one row per contrast and covered event with its gene, alternative region, mean inclusion (PSI) per condition, the treatment-minus-control difference, FDR and the significance call.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: event_volcano
  title: Splicing change against significance
  description: |-
    Each point is a splicing event in one contrast: its change in exon inclusion (delta PSI) on the horizontal axis and its FDR on the vertical axis, coloured by event type. It answers which events change most, in which direction, and how confidently.
    How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment with strong support. A cloud with nothing above the line means little differential splicing, so check the replicate coverage before trusting the contrast. Open the table tile for the labelled genes.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an FDR of 0.05, the level at which rMATS counts an event as significant in its summary. No delta PSI line is drawn: the rnasplice template passes its MIN_DPSI variable to this recipe's min_dpsi parameter with a default of 0, so the call adds no floor on the change. A value above 0 is the user's own working value, not an rMATS default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Xinglab/rmats-turbo/master/README.md
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 0.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Change in inclusion (delta PSI)
    significance_label: -log10 FDR
  roles:
    feature_id: event_id
    effect_size: dpsi
    significance: fdr
    label: gene_name
    category: event_type

tools.name: RSeQC
tools.description: Modules that evaluate high-throughput sequencing data, especially RNA-seq.

output.name: Read distribution over the annotation
output.description: Where each library's reads land on the annotation: coding exons, the two UTRs, introns, the promoter and downstream rings, and everything intergenic. RSeQC publishes the upstream and downstream bands nested inside each other, so the recipe differences them into disjoint rings and adds the unassigned tags explicitly, which makes the composition sum to one.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: distribution_composition
  title: Read distribution over the annotation
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library, split into the share of its mapped tags that fall on each part of the annotation: exons, introns, promoter and downstream bands and intergenic sequence. It answers where the reads of each library land.
    How to read: an RNA-seq library of mature RNA is dominated by exonic reads. A high intronic share points to pre-mRNA or genomic DNA contamination, and a high intergenic share to DNA contamination or an incomplete annotation. Switch the level to read the individual features.
    Note: where features overlap, RSeQC assigns a read to CDS exons first, then UTR exons, then introns, then intergenic regions.
    Source: https://rseqc.sourceforge.net/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22743226/
  kind: stacked_bar
  config:
    default_rank: Region class
    rank_label: Level
    x_title: Library
    value_title: Share of mapped tags
  roles:
    sample_id: sample_id
    taxon: taxon
    rank: rank
    abundance: abundance

tools.name: RTG Tools
tools.description: Real Time Genomics utilities for accurate VCF comparison and manipulation.

output.name: vcfeval benchmark summary
output.description: Per-callset variant-calling accuracy (TP/FP/FN, precision, recall, F1) from rtg-tools vcfeval's aggregated summary. `label` is the callset's samplesheet id, `caller` the tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was compared against. Serves the germline (small/) and somatic (snv/, indel/) routes with the same vocabulary.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: pr_scatter
  title: Precision against recall per callset
  description: |-
    Each point is a callset compared with its truth set: its recall on the horizontal axis and its precision on the vertical axis, coloured by F1 and sized by the true positives it recovers. It answers which callset finds the most true variants without adding false ones.
    How to read: the top right corner is best, with every true variant found and no false call. A point far to the left misses true variants, a point low down adds false calls, so look at the false negative and false positive cards to see which one dominates.
    Lines and annotations: the curved contours are lines of equal F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and the diagonal marks precision equal to recall. They are drawn from the definitions of the metrics, not from a cut-off.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/ and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  kind: pr_benchmark
  roles:
    label: label
    recall: recall
    precision: precision
    f1: f1
    support: tp_comp

_render.title: Precision against recall per callset

  title: True and false calls per callset
  description: |-
    Each cell is a count of variants for one callset: the true positives, the false positives or the false negatives of its comparison with the truth set. It answers how many variants stand behind each precision and recall value.
    How to read: a callset with many more false negatives than false positives loses recall, and the reverse loses precision. Compare cells within a callset first, because callsets of different size are not comparable by raw count.

tools.name: Salmon
tools.description: Salmon is a tool for wicked-fast transcript quantification from RNA-seq data.

output.name: Top variable genes
output.description: The 500 most variable genes of the merged Salmon TPM matrix on the log2(TPM + 1) scale, wide (genes x samples), with the experimental factors as column annotations.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: top_variable_heatmap
  title: Most variable genes across samples
  description: |-
    Each cell is a gene in one sample: its expression as log2(TPM + 1), with genes as rows and samples as columns. It answers which genes separate the samples and whether replicates group together.
    How to read: columns of one condition that cluster together and share a pattern mean the experiment is reproducible. A replicate that clusters away from its group is a candidate outlier, so check the sample overview. Rows with the same pattern across samples are co-regulated genes, the first candidates for a signature.
    Lines and annotations: the coloured bar above the columns is the experimental factor read from the sample sheet or the sample names, and rows and columns are clustered with the tile's default Ward linkage. The matrix holds the 500 genes with the highest variance, a fixed selection of this view.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  roles:
    index: gene_name

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: mapped_reads_bar
  title: Mapped reads before and after the mapping-quality filter
  description: |-
    Each bar is the number of mapped reads of a sample at one stage, before or after the mapping-quality filter. It answers how many reads survive the filter and whether samples differ in depth.
    How to read: a post-filter bar close to the pre-filter one means the filter removed little. A large drop points to many low-quality or multi-mapping reads, so check the reference, the trimming and the library. Very uneven bars across samples call for normalisation downstream.

  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:

    y: mapped_reads
    color: stage

output.name: Alignment distributions
output.description: The distribution blocks of a samtools stats report, which MultiQC never surfaces: the read-length histogram (RL), the coverage-depth histogram (COV), the indel-length spectrum (ID) and, for paired data, the insert-size distribution (IS), with the SN summary block on one row per sample beside them. Each section has its own value column, so three profile tiles read the same collection without a filter between them.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: read_length_profile
  title: Read length distribution
  description: |-
    Each line is a sample: the number of reads at every read length in the alignment. It answers how long the aligned reads are and whether the length is uniform.
    How to read: short-read data draws one sharp peak at the sequenced length, and trimmed reads draw a spread below it. A long flat tail is expected for long-read data. Samples with a different shape were trimmed or sequenced differently.
    Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Read length (bp)
    y_title: Reads
  roles:
    series: series
    x: bin
    y: n_reads
