tools.name: SEACR
tools.description: Calls peaks and enriched regions from sparse CUT&RUN and chromatin profiling data.

output.name: Consensus peak overlap
output.description: Merged consensus intervals per target against the replicates that called a peak on them, as one 0/1 column per replicate. The intersections say how reproducible the peak set is between replicates.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: seacr_consensus_upset
  title: Replicate overlap of consensus peaks
  description: |-
    Each bar is a combination of replicates and counts the merged consensus intervals that every replicate of the combination called a peak on. It answers how reproducible the peak set is between replicates.
    How to read: a tall bar for all replicates together means the peaks are reproducible. Tall bars for single replicates mean that replicate calls peaks the others miss, which is typical of a noisy or over-sensitive library. Compare the set sizes on the left with the intersections.
    Note: SEACR publishes no minimum number of replicates, and the pipeline decides which consensus peaks to keep with its own replicate threshold.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  kind: upset_plot
  config:
    color_intersections_by: degree

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: seacr_consensus_track
  title: Consensus intervals along the genome
  description: |-
    Each mark is a merged consensus interval on its chromosome, coloured by target and high according to the strongest maximum signal among the peaks merged into it. It answers where the replicates agree and how strong the signal is there.
    How to read: clusters of tall intervals are enriched domains, and an isolated tall interval is a candidate site. Compare targets to see which regions they share. Brush a region to filter the tiles of the tab.
    Lines and annotations: the line is the 95th percentile of the maximum signal in the table, a data-defined reference computed from the rows on show and not a SEACR cut-off.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: Maximum signal
    score_threshold_stat: p95
  roles:
    chr: chr
    pos: start
    score: max_signal
    feature: peak_id
    end: end
    category: target

  title: Consensus interval width by replicate support
  description: |-
    Each box is a replicate support level: the spread of the widths of the consensus intervals that this many replicates called. It answers whether intervals confirmed by more replicates are wider or narrower.
    How to read: a box that moves up with support means reproducible calls are broader domains, as expected for a broad mark. Similar boxes mean width does not depend on support. Very wide outliers are merged neighbouring peaks.
    Note: no width cut-off is drawn, because SEACR defines none.

    y: width
    color: support

output.name: Nucleosome fragment classes
output.description: The fragment-length histogram binned into the four nucleosome classes: sub-nucleosomal below 120 bp, mononucleosomal to 250 bp, dinucleosomal to 450 bp and multi-nucleosomal above it, with the share of each per sample and the mononucleosome to sub-nucleosome ratio behind it.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: seacr_fragment_class_stack
  title: Nucleosome classes per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample, split into the share of its fragments in each length class: sub-nucleosomal, mono-, di- and multi-nucleosomal. It answers how much of the library is nucleosome-free against nucleosome-bound.
    How to read: a sharp mark gives a sub-nucleosomal heavy library, and a broad mark a mononucleosomal heavy one, so replicates of one target should look alike. A library dominated by multi-nucleosomal fragments was digested too little.
    Lines and annotations: the classes are cut at 120, 250 and 450 bp. The 120 bp boundary follows the transcription factor sized fragments of the CUT&RUN paper, while 250 and 450 bp are this table's own bins and not a published cut-off.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: fraction
    color: fragment_class
    barmode: stack
    labels:
      sample: Sample
      fraction: Share of fragments
      fragment_class: Fragment class

output.description: The sequenced fragments piled up in 100 bp bins on a 6 kb window centred on the summit of each sample's 500 strongest non-overlapping SEACR regions, per million fragments of the sample: a metagene matrix around the calls and a fragment coverage track under a locus navigator, from the same rows.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: frags_pileup_matrix
  title: Fragment pile-up around peak summits
  description: |-
    Each row is one of the strongest SEACR regions of a sample, each column a 100 bp bin around its summit, and the colour is the fragment coverage per million fragments of the sample. It answers whether the calls stand on a clean, centred pile-up.
    How to read: a bright vertical band at the centre means the signal is centred on the summit. A target with sharp peaks, such as a promoter mark, gives a narrow band, and a broad mark a wide one. Rows that are bright everywhere are broad domains.
    Lines and annotations: the marker at offset 0 is the summit of the region, the midpoint of its maximum signal interval as reported by SEACR. The window, 3 kb each side of it, is a fixed choice of this catalog's recipe, and rows are ordered by total signal.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  kind: signal_matrix
  config:
    reference_label: Peak summit
  roles:
    region_id: peak_id
    position: offset_bp
    value: cpm
    group: sample

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: seacr_peak_signal
  title: Peak signal along the genome
  description: |-
    Each point is a SEACR region at the position of its summit, with the base 10 logarithm of its total fragment coverage on the vertical axis. It answers where in the genome the strongest signal sits.

    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the 95th percentile of the scores in the table, a data-defined reference and not a SEACR cut-off. SEACR gives no significance for a region, since it reports coverage and not a p-value.

    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_kind: log10 total signal
    score_threshold_stat: p95
  roles:
    chr: chr
    pos: summit
    score: log10_total_signal
    feature: peak_id

- component: figure
  id: seacr_signal_scatter
  title: Total against maximum signal
  description: |-
    Each point is a region: its total fragment coverage against the highest coverage inside it, on logarithmic axes and coloured by sample. It answers whether strong regions are strong because they are tall or because they are wide.
    How to read: the points rise together, and a region far below the trend is wide and flat, such as a broad domain. A region far above it is a narrow spike. Compare samples to see which has the taller peaks.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  visu_type: scatter
  dict_kwargs:
    x: total_signal
    y: max_signal
    color: sample
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    labels:
      total_signal: Total signal
      max_signal: Maximum signal
      sample: Sample

tools.name: seqtk
tools.description: Fast processing of FASTA and FASTQ files. Here, the runs of N of an assembly (its scaffolding gaps), counted per genome and binned by length.

output.name: Assembly gap lengths
output.description: The length distribution of the N runs of each assembly, binned on a log10 scale (four bins per decade). Scaffolding methods leave characteristic gap sizes (a fixed filler length, estimated sizes, large reference placeholders), so the curve tells how an assembly was scaffolded, which the gap count does not. The share of each assembly's runs of N per bin is given alongside the count, which puts every assembly on one scale.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: gap_length_matrix
  title: Gap length distribution per assembly
  description: |-
    Each row is an assembly and each column a bin of gap length on a log10 scale, coloured by the share of that assembly's runs of N that fall in the bin. It answers how an assembly was scaffolded and whether two assemblies used the same gap sizes.
    How to read: a single dark cell means one fixed gap length, typical of a filler inserted by a scaffolder. A spread across many bins means estimated gap sizes. The curve on top is the mean over the assemblies shown.
    Note: seqtk cutN reports runs of N, which stand for assembly gaps. Rows are compared as shares, so assemblies with few and with many gaps share one scale.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  kind: signal_matrix
  config:
    reference_position: -1
  roles:
    region_id: genome
    position: log10_gap_length
    value: gaps_pct

tools.name: q2-sidle
tools.description: QIIME 2 plugin that reconstructs one feature table from several amplified 16S regions, so a multi-region run is read as a single community rather than as one community per primer pair.

output.name: Reconstructed features
output.description: The cross-region reconstructed feature table melted to one row per feature and sample, with the Greengenes lineage split into rank columns. This is the community a multi-region run actually resolves, as opposed to the per-primer tables it starts from.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: reconstructed_sunburst
  title: Reconstructed community by rank
  description: |-
    Each arc is a taxon of the reconstructed community, with kingdom in the centre and genus on the outside, sized by its read count and coloured by phylum. It answers which groups make up the community resolved across all amplified regions.
    How to read: wide arcs are the dominant taxa. A large share of arcs labelled Unclassified means the reference database could not name those sequences at that rank, so read the deeper ranks with care.
  kind: sunburst
  config:
    colour_by_rank: Phylum
  roles:
    ranks:
    - Kingdom
    - Phylum
    - Class
    - Genus
    abundance: count

output.description: How many amplified regions mapped to each reconstructed feature and how much kmer support stood behind them. A feature carried by one region is a different claim from one carried by all of them, and this is the table that separates the two.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: reconstruction_support
  title: Region coverage against kmer support
  description: |-
    Each point is a reconstructed feature: the number of amplified regions that mapped to it on the horizontal axis and the kmer support summed over them on the vertical axis. The size is the mean support per region and the colour its spread across regions. It answers how well each feature is backed by the sequenced regions.
    How to read: a point to the right is carried by several regions and is a stronger claim than one carried by a single region. A high point with an uneven colour has most of its support in one region. Follow up the labelled points in the table.
    Note: q2-sidle publishes no minimum number of regions or kmers, so no cut-off is drawn.
    Source: https://q2-sidle.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reconstruction.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    color_col: stdv_kmer_per_region
    x_title: Regions mapped
    y_title: Kmers mapped
    top_n_labels: 5
  roles:
    x: num_regions
    y: total_kmers_mapped
    size: mean_kmer_per_region
    label: feature_id

renders.title: Region coverage against kmer support
renders.description:
Each point is a reconstructed feature: the number of amplified regions that mapped to it on the horizontal axis and the kmer support summed over them on the vertical axis. The size is the mean support per region and the colour its spread across regions. It answers how well each feature is backed by the sequenced regions.
How to read: a point to the right is carried by several regions and is a stronger claim than one carried by a single region. A high point with an uneven colour has most of its support in one region. Follow up the labelled points in the table.
Note: q2-sidle publishes no minimum number of regions or kmers, so no cut-off is drawn.
Source: https://q2-sidle.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reconstruction.html

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Features by regions mapped
  description: |-
    Each bar counts the reconstructed features that were mapped by a given number of amplified regions. It answers how many features rest on one region and how many on all of them.
    How to read: a distribution piled on the highest value means the regions agree and the reconstruction is well supported. A tall bar at one region means many features are single-region claims.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: num_regions
    labels:
      num_regions: Regions mapped
      count: Features

tools.name: SIGS
tools.description: Fits a tumor's 96-context SNV counts to COSMIC mutational signatures.

output.name: Mutational signature allocation
output.description: The number and share of the tumor's SNVs SIGS allocates to each COSMIC signature, one row per tumor and signature. Clock-like, APOBEC, homologous-recombination and mismatch-repair signatures each point at a different mutational process.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: signature_share_bar
  title: Share of SNVs per signature
  description: |-
    Each bar is the percent of a tumor's SNVs that SIGS allocates to one COSMIC mutational signature. It answers which mutational processes shaped the tumor.
    How to read: tall bars are the dominant processes, for instance clock-like, APOBEC, homologous recombination deficiency or mismatch repair signatures, so read each signature's aetiology in COSMIC. The MISALLOC bar is the share the fitted signatures do not explain.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/sigs/README.md
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: signature
    y: percent
    color: sample
    labels:
      signature: COSMIC signature
      percent: Share of SNVs (%)
      sample: Tumor

Each bar is the percent of a tumor's SNVs that SIGS allocates to one COSMIC mutational signature. It answers which mutational processes shaped the tumor.
How to read: tall bars are the dominant processes, for instance clock-like, APOBEC, homologous recombination deficiency or mismatch repair signatures, so read each signature's aetiology in COSMIC. The MISALLOC bar is the share the fitted signatures do not explain.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/sigs/README.md

tools.name: simpleaf (alevin-fry)
tools.description: SimpleAF is a program to simplify and customize the running and configuration of single-cell processing with alevin-fry.

output.name: Barcode-rank curve (simpleaf/alevin-fry)
output.description: UMI count per barcode against its rank, read from alevin-fry's per-barcode feature dump and flagged against CellBender's cell-barcode list for this route, so it can be compared to the Cell Ranger knee curve for the same sample.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: simpleaf_barcode_rank_knee
  title: Barcode rank plot
  description: |-
    Each point is a barcode ranked by its UMI count, from the richest droplet down, on log axes, with one curve per sample. It answers where real cells stop and empty droplets start.
    How to read: a good library has a plateau of cells with high counts, a steep drop and a long flat tail of ambient barcodes. A curve with no clear drop, or one where the called cells sit on the tail, points to a noisy or low-quality library. Compare it with the Cell Ranger curve of the same sample.
    Lines and annotations: the marked cut-off is where the called cells end. alevin-fry reports every barcode it quantified and calls no cells itself, so the cells are CellBender's cell-barcode list for this sample and the line is a data-defined reference, not a threshold from the tool.
  kind: knee_plot
  roles:
    sample: sample
    rank: rank
    umi_count: umi_count
    is_cell: is_cell

_render.title: Barcode rank plot
_render.description:
Each point is a barcode ranked by its UMI count, from the richest droplet down, on log axes, with one curve per sample. It answers where real cells stop and empty droplets start.
How to read: a good library has a plateau of cells with high counts, a steep drop and a long flat tail of ambient barcodes. A curve with no clear drop, or one where the called cells sit on the tail, points to a noisy or low-quality library. Compare it with the Cell Ranger curve of the same sample.
Lines and annotations: the marked cut-off is where the called cells end. alevin-fry reports every barcode it quantified and calls no cells itself, so the cells are CellBender's cell-barcode list for this sample and the line is a data-defined reference, not a threshold from the tool.

tools.name: SnpEff
tools.description: Functional annotation of variant calls: the consequence, the impact class, the gene and the protein change of every call, plus the run-level summaries SnpEff writes next to the annotated VCF.

output.name: Annotated variant calls
output.description: One row per annotated variant call: the locus and allele the caller reported, its quality, filter status, genotype, depth and allele fraction, and SnpEff's most severe consequence for it (gene, impact class, consequence term and protein change). The per-variant counterpart of the SnpEff CSV summary.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: impact_composition
  title: Calls by impact class
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of annotated variant calls and the ring splits them by the impact class SnpEff assigned to the most severe consequence. It answers how many calls could change a protein.
    How to read: most calls of a typical callset are MODIFIER (non-coding or downstream) and only a small share is HIGH or MODERATE. A ring with an unusually large HIGH share is worth checking against the callers and the filter status.
    Lines and annotations: the classes are SnpEff's own. HIGH is a disruptive effect such as a stop gained or a frameshift, MODERATE a non-disruptive one such as a missense, LOW a mostly harmless one and MODIFIER a mostly non-coding one.
    Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/inputoutput/
  column: variant_key
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - nunique
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: impact
  caption: calls, by impact class

output.name: Gene burden heatmap

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: burden_matrix
  title: Gene burden by callset
  description: |-
    Each cell is the number of coding variants SnpEff assigned to a gene (row) in a callset (column), a sample called by one caller. It answers which genes carry the most variants and whether the callsets agree on them.
    How to read: columns that cluster together call similar variants, so if the callers separate more than the sequencing depths do, the caller matters more than the data. A row that is dark in every column is a robust high-burden gene, and a row dark in one column only is a call to inspect.
    Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/outputsummary/

  id: caller_gene_overlap
  title: Gene overlap between callers
  description: |-

  kind: upset_plot

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: pr_scatter
  title: Precision against recall
  description: |-
    Each point is a callset: its recall on the horizontal axis, its precision on the vertical axis, with the point coloured by its F1 score and sized by its true positives. It answers which caller finds the most true variants without adding false ones.
    How to read: the best callsets sit in the upper right. A callset far to the left misses variants, and one low on the plot adds false calls. The curves join points of equal F1, so compare callsets by which curve they sit on.
    Lines and annotations: the curves are iso-F1 contours at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 drawn by this chart, with F1 the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Recall is tp / (tp + fn) and precision is tp / (tp + fp), as som.py defines them. No cut-off is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  kind: pr_benchmark
  config:
    show_diagonal: false
  roles:
    label: caller
    recall: recall
    precision: precision
    f1: f1
    support: tp

tools.name: nf-core/stableexpression
tools.description: Gene expression stability across public datasets, from nf-core/stableexpression: the stability score of every candidate gene and the measures behind it, the spread of the most stable genes' normalised expression over every sample, the expression statistics of every gene, and what each downloaded dataset went through (platform, gene ID mapping, sample filters, merge).

output.name: Samples through the filters
output.description: The samples of every downloaded dataset at each step, one row per dataset and step: downloaded, after the gene ID mapping, after the zero filter and after the missing-value filter (the samples of the merged matrix), with the samples lost at the step. A step a dataset never reached holds 0, so a step sums to the run's funnel.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: sample_funnel
  title: Samples at each filtering step
  description: |-
    Each bar adds up the samples of every downloaded dataset at one step of the pipeline, split by the platform that measured them. It answers how many samples survive from download to the merged matrix.
    How to read: bars should shrink only a little from one step to the next. A large drop after the gene ID mapping means many datasets could not be mapped, and a drop after a filter means many samples were mostly zeros or mostly missing. Filter by step to see which datasets lose most.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline rejects a sample whose share of zeros or missing values is above 0.9 by default (max_zero_ratio and max_null_ratio), and the run may have changed them.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: step
    y: samples
    color: platform
    histfunc: sum
    labels:
      step: Step
      samples: Samples
      platform: Platform

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: stability_ranking
  title: Most stable genes and their spread
  description: |-
    Each row is one of the best-ranked candidate genes of an expression section, coloured by section: a box of its normalised expression over the samples that measured it, beside the stability score that ranked it. It answers which genes are the best reference candidates and how steady their expression is.
    How to read: a good reference has a short box and a low score. A long box or a long whisker means the gene varies between samples or datasets, whatever its rank. Compare genes of the same section, since sections differ in level.
    Lines and annotations: the box spans the first to the third quartile with the median inside, and whiskers reach the furthest values within 1.5 times the interquartile range (Tukey's rule, computed by this catalog's recipe). The pipeline's report also draws boxes of the normalised expression of the top 25 genes per section.

tools.name: STAR
tools.description: Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference: aligns RNA-seq reads across splice junctions, reports where each read went (uniquely mapped, multi-mapped or unmapped and why) and collapses the junctions it crossed.

output.name: Splice junctions
output.description: STAR's collapsed splice junctions summed per sample into intron motif class (GT/AG, GC/AG, AT/AC, non-canonical) by annotated or novel, with the junctions and the uniquely and multi-mapping reads in each cell. A clean library spends nearly all its reads on annotated GT/AG junctions; novel non-canonical ones with few reads each are alignment noise.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  id: junction_motif_bars
  title: Junctions by intron motif
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample and each segment is the share of its splice junctions that carry one intron motif class. It answers whether the junctions look like real splicing.
    How to read: nearly all junctions should be the canonical GT/AG motif, with a small share of GC/AG and AT/AC. A large share of non-canonical junctions points to alignment noise or a damaged library, so check them against their read counts in the table.
    Lines and annotations: the motif classes fold the intron motif codes STAR writes in SJ.out.tab (0 non-canonical, 1 GT/AG and 2 CT/AC, 3 GC/AG and 4 CT/GC, 5 AT/AC and 6 GT/AT), joining each motif with its reverse strand reading. The folding is done by this catalog's recipe, and no cut-off is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: junctions_pct
    color: motif_class
    labels:
      sample: Sample
      junctions_pct: Junctions (%)
      motif_class: Intron motif

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf

renders.title: Junctions by intron motif
renders.description:
Each bar is a sample and each segment is the share of its splice junctions that carry one intron motif class. It answers whether the junctions look like real splicing.
How to read: nearly all junctions should be the canonical GT/AG motif, with a small share of GC/AG and AT/AC. A large share of non-canonical junctions points to alignment noise or a damaged library, so check them against their read counts in the table.
Lines and annotations: the motif classes fold the intron motif codes STAR writes in SJ.out.tab (0 non-canonical, 1 GT/AG and 2 CT/AC, 3 GC/AG and 4 CT/GC, 5 AT/AC and 6 GT/AT), joining each motif with its reverse strand reading. The folding is done by this catalog's recipe, and no cut-off is drawn.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf

    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  column: junctions

  dict_kwargs:

    labels:

      reads_pct: Reads (%)
      fate: Read fate

tools.name: STAR-Fusion
tools.description: Fast and Accurate Fusion Transcript Detection from RNA-Seq.

output.name: STAR-Fusion calls
output.description: Fusion predictions from the abridged STAR-Fusion table, one row per call. The recipe strips the Ensembl id off each partner gene, sums junction reads and spanning fragments into one evidence count, and derives a log-scaled FFPM plus the fraction of the evidence that crosses the junction itself.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: evidence_dot_plot
  title: Fusion evidence by splice pattern
  description: |-
    Each dot is a fusion call placed under its splice pattern, coloured by its abundance (log10 of FFPM plus one) and sized by the share of its evidence that crosses the junction itself. It answers which fusions have the strongest and most direct support.
    How to read: large, dark dots are abundant fusions backed mostly by junction reads, the most convincing kind. Small, pale dots rest on spanning fragments alone and deserve a second look.
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: splice_type
    gene: fusion
    mean_expression: log_ffpm
    frac_expressing: junction_fraction

output.name: Library correlation matrix

  title: Library correlation
  description: |-

tools.name: SUPPA2
tools.description: Fast, alignment-free differential splicing: PSI per local event and per isoform from transcript TPMs, and the delta PSI between two conditions with an empirical significance.

output.name: Differential splicing of local events (SUPPA2)
output.description: SUPPA2 diffSplice on local events, one row per contrast and event: the parsed event id (gene, type, chromosome, span, strand), the delta PSI oriented treatment minus control, its empirical p-value and the significance call.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: local_event_volcano
  title: Splicing change against significance
  description: |-
    Each point is a local splicing event in one contrast: its change in inclusion (delta PSI) on the horizontal axis and its empirical p-value on the vertical axis, coloured by event type. It answers which events change most, in which direction, and how confidently.
    How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment with strong support. A p-value of exactly zero is drawn at the top of the axis. A cloud with nothing above the line means little differential splicing, so check the transcript quantification before trusting it.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a p-value of 0.05, the default alpha of SUPPA2 diffSplice. No delta PSI line is drawn: the rnasplice template passes its MIN_DPSI variable to this recipe's min_dpsi parameter with a default of 0, so the call adds no floor on the change. A value above 0 is the user's own working value, not a SUPPA2 default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/comprna/SUPPA/master/README.md
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 0.0
    top_n_labels: 10
    effect_label: Change in inclusion (delta PSI)
    significance_label: -log10 p-value
  roles:
    feature_id: event_id
    effect_size: dpsi
    significance: pvalue
    label: gene_id
    category: event_type

How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment with strong support. A p-value of exactly zero is drawn at the top of the axis. A cloud with nothing above the line means little differential splicing, so check the transcript quantification before trusting it.

tools.name: sylph
tools.description: Sylph quickly enables querying of genomes against even low-coverage shotgun metagenomes to find nearest neighbour ANI.

output.name: Containment ANI
output.description: One row per reference genome sylph detected in a sample: the adjusted ANI of the containment match next to the taxonomic and sequence abundances and the effective coverage. ANI against abundance separates confident calls from divergent relatives, which read-count profilers cannot express.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ani_dot_plot
  title: Detected genomes per sample
  description: |-
    Each dot is a reference genome that sylph detected in a sample: its colour is the adjusted containment ANI and its size is the taxonomic abundance as a fraction. It answers which genomes are present in which samples and how close each match is.
    How to read: large dark dots are abundant genomes with a close match. A small dot with a lower ANI is a divergent relative of the reference, so the sample holds a different strain or species than the database. A genome present in every sample is part of the shared community.
    Source: https://sylph-docs.github.io/Output-format/
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: sample
    gene: genome
    mean_expression: adjusted_ani
    frac_expressing: abundance_frac

tools.name: TAMA
tools.description: Transcript models built from long reads: the isoforms of each sample with the reads behind them, and their novelty against a reference annotation.

output.name: Structural category composition
output.description: Share of each sample's isoforms, and of its FLNC reads, in every structural category, stacked to 100 % per sample; the level switches between the two.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: category_bars
  title: Structural categories per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar is a sample, split into the share of its isoforms (or of its FLNC reads, with the level control) in each structural category. It answers how much of a sample's transcriptome matches the reference annotation and how much is novel.
    How to read: a high share of full splice matches means the sample is well covered by the reference. Large novel categories (NIC, NNC) are either real new isoforms or artefacts, so compare the isoform level with the read level: novel isoforms backed by few reads are the first to doubt. Switch the level to see whether the novelty is in many rare isoforms or in a few abundant ones.
    Lines and annotations: the categories follow SQANTI3. FSM is a full splice match to a reference transcript, ISM an incomplete one, NIC a new combination of known splice sites, NNC an isoform with at least one unannotated splice site. Genic intron isoforms sit inside an annotated intron, genic genomic ones overlap introns and exons, antisense ones lie on the opposite strand of a gene and intergenic ones outside any gene.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
  kind: stacked_bar
  config:
    default_rank: Isoforms
    value_title: Share of the sample (%)
    x_title: Sample
  roles:
    sample_id: sample
    taxon: structural_category
    rank: level
    abundance: pct

output.name: Poly(A) tail length distribution
output.description: Share of each sample's FLNC reads per poly(A) tail length removed by TAMA's poly(A) clean-up, pooled over chunks and SMRT cells.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: polya_tail_profile
  title: Poly(A) tail length distribution
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample: the share of its FLNC reads (vertical axis) with each poly(A) tail length removed by TAMA's clean-up (horizontal axis, nucleotides). It answers how long the tails were and whether the samples agree.
    How to read: a pile near 0 nt means TAMA found little tail left to remove, for instance because an earlier step had already clipped it. Curves that differ between samples point to a library preparation difference to check before comparing the samples.
    Lines and annotations: this catalog's recipe pools every tail of 100 nt or longer into the last point, so it is a sum and not a single length. No cut-off is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/GenomeRIK/tama/Home.md
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Poly(A) tail length removed (nt)
    y_title: Share of the sample's reads (%)
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: tail_length
    y: pct

output.name: Isoform structures against the reference
output.description: Exon blocks of every TAMA merge isoform, labelled with its structural category and read support, beside the exon and CDS blocks of the reference transcripts of the same gene (class and sample "reference").

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: isoform_structures
  title: Isoform structures against the reference
  description: |-
    Each lane is a transcript of one gene: boxes are its exons, and the reference transcripts of the gene sit beside the TAMA isoforms of the chosen sample. It answers how an isoform's exon structure differs from the annotation.
    How to read: lanes coloured as full splice matches repeat a reference structure, and novel categories show skipped, extra or shifted exons against the reference lanes. Pick the gene and the sample from the controls, and compare a novel isoform's read support with the reference before trusting it.
    Lines and annotations: the lane colour is the structural category, following SQANTI3 (FSM full splice match, ISM incomplete, NIC new combination of known splice sites, NNC at least one unannotated splice site). Reference lanes are coloured as the reference class.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
  kind: transcript_structure
  config:
    colour_by: transcript_class
  roles:
    transcript_id: transcript_id
    gene_id: gene_id
    chrom: chrom
    start: start
    end: end
    feature: feature
    strand: strand
    sample: sample
    gene_name: gene_name
    transcript_class: transcript_class
    expression: expression

    log_y: true
    x_title: Isoform length (nt)

  description: |-

output.name: Profiler ordination
output.description: Bray-Curtis PCoA over every profiling run. One point per sample, profiler and database, so runs that agree on the community land together and the spread reads as profiler disagreement rather than as biological distance.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: profiler_embedding
  title: Profiler ordination
  description: |-
    Each point is one profiling run, a sample classified by one profiler and database, placed by the Bray-Curtis distance between taxon abundance profiles and coloured by profiler. It answers whether the profilers describe the same community or disagree.
    How to read: runs that sit together report similar communities, so a tight cluster of profilers agrees. A profiler that lands apart from the others reports a different set of taxa or names them differently, so open the detection overlap and the taxon by run matrix to see which taxa drive the gap. Runs of one profiler from different samples spread apart when the samples differ biologically.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The axes are principal coordinates of the Bray-Curtis matrix, so only distances between points carry meaning.
  kind: embedding
  config:
    axis_prefix: PCo
  roles:
    sample_id: sample_id
    dim_1: dim_1
    dim_2: dim_2
    color: profiler

_render.title: Profiler ordination

Each point is one profiling run, a sample classified by one profiler and database, placed by the Bray-Curtis distance between taxon abundance profiles and coloured by profiler. It answers whether the profilers describe the same community or disagree.

A profiler that lands apart from the others reports a different set of taxa or names them differently, so open the detection overlap and the taxon by run matrix to see which taxa drive the gap. Runs of one profiler from different samples spread apart when the samples differ biologically.
Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The axes are principal coordinates of the Bray-Curtis matrix, so only distances between points carry meaning.

output.name: Telomere length
output.description: TEAL's telomere length estimate, one row per DNA sample (tumor and normal): the raw and purity-adjusted final length, the telomeric fragments behind it and the purity, ploidy and depth it was normalised with. A tumor far above its normal suggests telomerase or ALT activity.

    How to read: a tumor far above its normal suggests telomerase or ALT activity, and a tumor far below it suggests telomere attrition. Compare each tumor with its own reference sample.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/teal/README.md
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sampleId
    y: finalTelomereLength

tools.name: tidk
tools.description: Telomeric repeat identification toolkit: finds the candidate telomeric repeat unit of an assembly and counts it in windows along every sequence.

output.name: Telomeric repeats per window
output.description: One row per assembly, sequence and window of `tidk search`: the repeat unit counted forward and reverse, their sum, and the length of the sequence (the end of its last window). A sequence capped by telomeres lights up at both ends; one lit at a single end was broken there, and repeats in the middle of a sequence are an interstitial array or a unit that is not the telomere at all.

    Each bar is a sequence of an assembly, drawn to its length and shaded in windows by the count of telomeric repeat copies, with one karyotype per assembly. It answers which sequences end in a telomere.
    How to read: a sequence that is dark at both ends is capped by telomeres at both sides, which is the signature of a complete chromosome. A sequence dark at one end only was broken at the other. Repeats in the middle of a sequence are an interstitial array or a repeat unit that is not the telomere.

  roles:

    start: start
    end: end

tools.name: Truvari
tools.description: Structural variant comparison tool for VCFs.

output.name: Truvari SV summary
output.description: Structural-variant accuracy from Truvari (precision/recall/F1). Optional: not produced by the public megatest; recipe uses tolerant column matching; `caller` and `truth_set` come from the pipeline's `Caller` and `File` columns.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: pr_scatter
  title: Precision against recall per callset
  description: |-
    Each point is a benchmarked callset: its recall on the horizontal axis and its precision on the vertical axis, coloured by F1. It answers which caller finds the most true structural variants without adding false ones.
    How to read: points in the upper right corner are both sensitive and precise. A point high but far left misses true variants, and one far right but low adds false calls. Compare callsets of the same truth set only.
    Lines and annotations: the curved lines are contours of equal F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and the diagonal marks equal precision and recall. They are mathematical references, not cut-offs, and Truvari publishes no pass mark.
  kind: pr_benchmark
  roles:
    label: label
    recall: recall
    precision: precision
    f1: f1

output.name: Substitution spectrum

    color: sample
    barmode: group

output.name: Variant calls
output.description: One row per variant call, read straight out of the caller's own VCF: locus, allele, quality, filter status, genotype, read depth and variant allele fraction. Pipeline-agnostic, and the only collection in a variant-calling template that is granular enough for a caller-against-caller comparison at the variant level rather than at the summary-count level.

renders._yaml:

  description: |-
    Each point is a variant call: its read depth on the horizontal axis and its variant allele fraction on the vertical axis, coloured by caller. It answers whether the calls rest on enough reads and whether their allele balance is plausible.
    How to read: a heterozygous germline variant sits near an allele fraction of 0.5 and a homozygous-alternate one near 1.0, so calls scattered between the two bands, especially at low depth, are less reliable. Compare callers to see whether one produces more calls off the bands, and note that no cut-off is drawn, since no source gives one for every data type.

  title: Ts/Tv of kept calls
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median transition to transversion ratio of the calls that carry PASS or no filter, and the box shows the spread across callers and samples. It answers whether the kept calls have the balance expected of real variants.
    How to read: false calls are spread evenly over bases, so they pull the ratio down. A caller whose kept calls sit below the others adds noise, and the expected value depends on the genome region sequenced, whole genome or exome.

output.name: Ts/Tv by quality threshold
output.description: The transition/transversion ratio of the calls above each quality threshold, one curve per sample and caller. Where a curve flattens is where that caller's quality score stops separating real variants from noise, which compares callers on calibration rather than on yield.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: tstv_quality_sweep
  title: Ts/Tv by quality threshold
  description: |-
    Each curve is a sample and caller: the transition to transversion ratio of the SNPs whose quality is above each threshold. It answers whether raising the quality floor makes the calls more like real variants.
    How to read: a ratio that rises with the threshold means quality separates real from false calls, and a curve that stays flat means the quality score carries no information. The level to expect depends on the genome region sequenced, so compare callers on the same data.
    Note: the tool publishes no ideal ratio, so no reference line is drawn. Only bi-allelic SNPs are counted.
    Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Minimum quality score
    y_title: Ts/Tv of the calls above it
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: qual_threshold
    y: ts_tv_above

tools.name: nf-core/viralmetagenome
tools.description: Per-sample and per-genome tables of nf-core/viralmetagenome: read preprocessing and host removal, the de novo contigs with their taxonomic call and cluster, and every consensus genome (de novo or against a constraint reference) with its closest reference, ambiguous bases, CheckV call, mapping, depth and variant counts.

output.name: Contig clusters per sample
output.description: One row per contig cluster: its taxon, its centroid and whether that centroid is a reference-pool sequence or one of the sample's own contigs, the member contigs and their summed length, the share of the sample's contig read depth the cluster holds, and whether a consensus was refined from it or it was filtered out.

renders._yaml:
- component: card
  id: clusters_by_status
  title: Contig clusters
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of contig clusters, and the bar splits them into those a consensus was refined from and those that were filtered out. It answers how many clusters turned into genomes.
    How to read: clusters filtered out are usually small groups of contigs holding few reads, which the pipeline treats as likely false positives. A sample with every cluster filtered out produced no de novo genome.
    Lines and annotations: a cluster is filtered out when the contigs in it hold less than 5 percent of the mapped reads by default (perc_reads_contig), or when it is a singleton and singleton filtering is on.
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  column: member_bp
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: composition
  breakdown_col: status
  caption: clusters, by status

Each bar is a sample and its segments are its contig clusters, sized by the share of the sample's contig read depth they hold and coloured by status. It answers how the reads of each sample divide among clusters.
How to read: one large refined segment is a clean single-virus sample. Many segments or a large filtered-out segment mean mixed or fragmented assembly, so check the contigs and their taxonomic calls.
Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline's own cut-off is 5 percent of mapped reads per cluster (perc_reads_contig), a run parameter.
Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json

output.name: De novo consensus across refinement steps
output.description: Every de novo consensus at every step of its iterative refinement: the scaffold built from the contigs, each mapping iteration and the final variant-calling round, with the ambiguous bases, the mismatches and identity to the closest reference and the depth at each step. Read along a genome, it shows how far the refinement moved the consensus away from the scaffold.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ambiguous_by_step
  title: Ambiguous bases across refinement
  description: |-
    Each line is a de novo consensus genome: its share of ambiguous bases at every step, from the scaffold built from contigs through each mapping iteration to the final variant-calling round. It answers whether refinement fills or creates gaps.
    How to read: a flat low line means refinement left the genome unambiguous. A line that rises means positions were masked as the reads were mapped, which happens where depth is too low to call a base.
    Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Positions covered by fewer than 5 reads are masked in the consensus by default (min_consensus_depth).
    Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Refinement step (0 is the scaffold)
    y_title: Ambiguous bases (%)
  roles:
    series: genome_id
    x: step_order
    y: n_pct

  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: attrition
  attrition_cols:
  - trimmed_read_pairs

  caption: read pairs, at each step

output.name: SINTAX composition
output.description: Per-sample Phylum-level relative abundance, built by joining the SINTAX per-ASV taxonomy to the DADA2 ASV count table written beside it. The classifier publishes taxonomy only, so the counts have to come from the denoiser's table.

renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: sintax_sunburst
  title: Kingdom and phylum composition
  description: |-
    Each arc is a taxon: the inner ring is the kingdom and the outer ring the phylum, sized by relative abundance summed over the samples in view and coloured by phylum. It answers which groups dominate the community.
    How to read: a wide arc is a dominant phylum, and many thin arcs a diverse community. Click an arc to zoom into it, and filter the samples to see how the composition shifts. An Unclassified arc means the reference database could not place those sequences.
    Source: https://github.com/torognes/vsearch
  kind: sunburst
  config:
    colour_by_rank: Phylum
  roles:
    ranks:
    - Kingdom
    - Phylum
    abundance: rel_abundance

tools.name: Wittyer
tools.description: Illumina tool for large variant benchmarking.

output.name: Wittyer CNV summary
output.description: CNV/SV accuracy from Wittyer (precision/recall/F1) per callset, at the two levels Wittyer scores: per event and per base (`stats_type`). `caller` is the tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was compared against. Event-type and size-bin strata are kept when a table carries them. Optional: not produced by the public megatest.

renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: F1 per callset, event and base
  description: |-
    Each bar is the F1 score of one callset against the truth set, with the event level and the base level side by side. It answers how well the large variant calls match the truth, and whether they match in count or in the bases they cover.
    How to read: a high event bar means the callset finds the right events, and a high base bar means it covers the right bases. A callset good at one level and poor at the other has events that match in position but not in extent.
    Note: Wittyer counts an event as a match by percentage or base-pair distance and requires the genotype to match by default, and counts every overlapped base at the base level. The cited README states no cut-off for F1, so none is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/witty.er/master/README.md
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: label
    y: f1
    color: stats_type
    barmode: group
    labels:
      label: Callset
      f1: F1 score
      stats_type: Scoring level
